article_title: The 3 Phases of the AI Layer Most Services-as-Software Founders Get Wrong

text:
i regret to inform you that the ai agents you've been building are not the part that does the work.

the data layer underneath is the work.

the agents are just the wrapper.

here's the right way to do it: https://t.co/drpiYgRZwx

I've sent 23,000,000+ cold emails (and these are the only 100 tips that matter).

Bookmark this.

Deliverability

1. Deliverability is the foundation. Without it, the best copy lands in spam.
2. Your primary domain is sacred. Cold sends go from alternates only.
3. Buy alternate domains. Forward them to your main site.
4. SPF, DKIM, DMARC. Set them before the first send or you've already lost.
5. Warm inboxes before the first send. No shortcuts.
6. Cap each inbox at a safe daily volume. Above that, you cook deliverability.
7. Scale by adding inboxes, not by cranking volume per address.
8. One Google Workspace caps you at a handful of inboxes. Stack workspaces.
9. Microsoft inboxes aren't cold-outreach infrastructure. They flag and burn.
10. Check domain reputation weekly. Catch issues before they cook your sender score.

Infrastructure & Inbox Setup

11. Alternate domains should mirror your main domain.
12. Forward alternates to your real site. Never to a parking page.
13. Auto-warm before the first send. Instantly, Smartlead, and Lemlist all have it built in.
14. Verify every address. Bounces tank reputation faster than anything else.
15. Run a fresh verification pass on every list. Don't trust "pre-verified" data. Verification ages out.
16. Rotate inboxes inside each campaign. Don't blast from one address.
17. Stagger sends across business hours. No single-spike sending.
18. Include an unsubscribe link even if you don't legally have to. Signals legitimacy.
19. Plaintext beats HTML. No images, no fancy formatting.
20. Tracking pixels kill deliverability. Turn them off.

List Quality

21. A list of right-fit accounts beats a list of spray-and-pray.
22. ICP first. If you can't describe your buyer in one sentence, you don't have one.
23. Stack signals. One signal is a guess. Three or more is intent.
24. Job changes, hiring posts, funding rounds, tech stack moves. Those are buying triggers.
25. Title match isn't enough. A "VP Marketing" at a small agency is a different buyer than at a large SaaS.
26. Buy data from Apollo or ZoomInfo. Verify it in Clay.
27. Scrape engagement on competitors with Trigify. People who liked their posts are warm to your offer.
28. Triangulate from two sources before sending. Single-source lists are dirty.
29. Suppress customers, lost deals, and competitors. Suppression lists matter.
30. Re-pull lists regularly. Data goes stale fast.

Personalization

31. Relevance is the unlock. Personalization without relevance is decoration.
32. Personalize the reason for reaching out, not the opener.
33. Skip the icebreaker. "Hope you're doing well" buys you nothing.
34. Reference something the prospect did. Not their LinkedIn About section.
35. AI personalization works when grounded in a real signal. Garbage in, garbage out.
36. Feed AI a real input: a job post, a podcast clip, a tweet. Then the line lands.
37. Don't fake personalization. Prospects clock a template instantly.
38. One specific detail beats three vague ones.
39. If you can't say something genuinely relevant, skip the slot.
40. Test personalized against sharp generic. Sometimes generic wins.

Subject Lines

41. Subject lines are the first filter. Get past the preview or nothing else matters.
42. Lowercase looks human. Title Case looks corporate.
43. Keep them short. A handful of words at most.
44. "Quick question," "intro," "{{firstName}}." All overused. Skip.
45. Personal works: "saw the {company} hiring post"
46. Don't use the prospect's first name in the subject. Triggers spam classifiers.
47. No emojis. No question marks at the end. No ALL CAPS.
48. A/B test the angle, not the adjectives. Big swings move open rate; tweaks don't.
49. Match subject to body. Bait-and-switch tanks reply rate.
50. The best subject is one that doesn't sound like a sales pitch.

Body Copy

51. Keep first-touch copy short. Long messages don't get read.
52. Mobile is the default. Most cold outreach opens on phone first.
53. A few sentences max. One paragraph. White space matters.
54. Lead with the reason you're reaching out. Not who you are.
55. Don't introduce yourself in the first line. They don't care yet.
56. State the trigger. State the relevance. Ask.
57. Drop "I came across your profile and was impressed by." Nobody talks like that.
58. Strip the closer's adjectives: innovative, synergize, best-in-class.
59. Write like a Slack DM. Not a press release.
60. One idea per send. Stack three benefits and you get zero replies.

The Ask

61. One ask per send. Not two. Never three.
62. Soft asks beat hard asks on first touch. Ask for interest, not a calendar slot.
63. Yes/no questions force a reply. "Are you the right person for this?" works.
64. "Want me to send over the breakdown?" is one of the highest-converting asks we've seen.
65. Calendar links on first touch kill reply rates. Save them for later in the cadence.
66. Avoid "let me know if you'd like to learn more." Passive asks get passive responses.
67. Frame the ask around the prospect's benefit, not yours.
68. PS lines work. Drop your strongest proof point there.
69. Never include two links. Each extra link drags response down.
70. The ask isn't where you sell. It's where you make replying easy.

Sequences & Follow-Ups

71. Multi-touch sequences win. Most replies arrive on the later touches, not the first.
72. Space follow-ups a few business days apart. Daily is aggressive without being useful.
73. Each follow-up adds value. New angle, new asset, new question. Not just a re-poke.
74. The "did this get buried?" bump works exactly once.
75. Reference the prior message in the follow-up. Reply chains build context.
76. Vary structure across the cadence. Long, short, question, asset, breakup.
77. The breakup isn't a sad note. It's a final useful nudge.
78. Don't send a breakup if you don't want to break up. Recycle the lead later.
79. Multi-channel sequences outperform single-channel. Add LinkedIn and phone to the cadence.
80. Hand off replies to humans immediately. Auto-responses to replies kill trust.

Reply Handling

81. Respond to replies fast. Speed signals seriousness.
82. Don't sell on the reply. Confirm interest, then book the call.
83. Suggest a couple of specific time windows. Don't just paste a Calendly link.
84. Send a one-line agenda before the call. Cuts no-shows materially.
85. Confirm the day before. Confirm again the hour before for high-value prospects.
86. If they ghost after booking, send one reminder. Then move on.
87. "Not now" isn't "no." Tag and set a reminder for later in the quarter.
88. "Wrong person" replies are gold. Always ask for the intro.
89. Negative replies often convert later. Don't argue. Thank them and exit gracefully.
90. Track reply sentiment, not just reply rate. Positive replies are the only metric that matters.

Mistakes That Tank Pipeline

91. More volume is never the answer when reply rate is low. Fix the input.
92. Don't add SDRs before the system works. You'll just multiply broken output.
93. Don't fix copy when targeting is broken. Targeting is the majority of outcomes.
94. Don't fix targeting when deliverability is broken. Nothing else matters if you're in spam.
95. Don't blame the channel. Cold outreach isn't dead. Bad cold outreach is.
96. Stop optimizing open rate. Optimize for booked calls and closed pipeline.
97. Don't trust "industry benchmarks." Your numbers depend on your ICP, offer, and seniority.
98. Don't run a campaign without a hypothesis. "Let's see what happens" is not a strategy.
99. Don't measure cold outreach in isolation. It works as a layer in a broader GTM system.
100. Don't outsource cold outreach without owning the strategy. The agency should run the playbook. And you should be involved in writing the playbook.

text:
if your pipeline isn't growing and you think it's because one channel is failing or underperforming, stop. read this before you move that budget to a new channel.

oftentimes the channel is doing its job. the real issue is one of the five layers every channel depends on.

here's how to build your GTM system so pipeline grows predictably:

1/ foundation

everything that has to be true before you spend a dollar on any channel.

can you quote a real buyer describing their problem in their own words? if not, your messaging is a guess, and a channel doesn't fix a guess. it just delivers it to more people. we pull those exact phrases from sales call recordings.

the inbox matters just as much: gmail now rejects unauthenticated bulk mail outright. if open rates dropped and the copy didn't change, check SPF, DKIM and DMARC before you touch a subject line.

2/ strategy

most teams run one channel until it has a bad quarter, then call it dead. every channel has a bad quarter eventually, and when it's the only one you run, that quarter looks like the end.

we run three that cover for each other: content warms people up, ads keep us in front of them, outbound starts the conversations. that shift alone took us from $40K to $90K a month.

3/ execution

the channels themselves, where everyone starts and where most budgets get wasted.

the most common version: paying for ads to reach strangers while the audience your content already earned sits there untouched.

we get 100+ inbound meetings a month from linkedin without spending a dollar on ads, and the same people who read that content get our cold emails. by the time we show up in their inbox, they already know who we are.

4/ compounding

most replies arrive on the later touches, but most teams stop following up long before that, look at the thin results, and conclude the channel stopped working.

the follow-up is only half of this layer. the other half is what you count: meetings booked is a vanity metric any tool can inflate. pipeline created and revenue closed live in your CRM, and those are the numbers the business actually runs on.

5/ learning

every tactic decays eventually. the teams that survive it sit down once a week and close the loop: which signal converted, which message landed, which channel paid for itself.

the teams that skip this keep running the same play long after it stopped working, and when results dry up, the channel gets the blame. sound familiar?

find your broken layer:

> replies fine, revenue flat = layer 4
> one great month, then two dead ones = layer 1
> everything works a little, nothing compounds = layer 2
> open rates dropped, copy didn't change = layer 1, the inbox
> busy team, nobody knows what worked = layer 5

fix the lowest broken layer first.

if pipeline feels random, start at layer 1.

one of the domains in your cold email setup is carrying other people's spam complaints.

it's the tracking domain, and your own reporting will never show it.

the shared tracking domain your sending platform hands you by default sits on every other customer's links too, so their spam complaints ride into your emails on the same wrapper. your own sending looks clean the whole time.

that's step 4 of 8.

@Kenny_GTM sets up the cold email infrastructure on every client account we run. we've sent 23M+ cold emails across those campaigns. here's his full build order:

1/ domains

buy 10 to 15 for a launch build, 20 for the full spec, all close variations of your brand. keep the primary domain out of the sending path.

burning a sending domain is routine and survivable. burning the one your contracts and invoices go through means you spend months repairing your company's email rather than a campaign.

2/ mailboxes

run 2 or 3 per domain and never more. past that the domain reads as a sending farm.

split the estate 50/50 between google workspace and microsoft 365, because the two filter on different rules. put everything on one provider and one bad filtering week hits all of your capacity instead of half of it.

3/ dns

SPF, DKIM and DMARC go on every domain before any mailbox sends, warm-up included.

weak copy costs you reply rate over weeks. a domain with no authentication gets flagged on the first send, before anyone opens the email. you read it as a bounce rate that stays high no matter what you change in the copy.

4/ tracking domain

the one from the top of this post. teams skip it more than any other step, and skipping it undoes steps 1 through 3.

one subdomain you own, configured per sending account.

5/ platform

instantly handles pure email. lemlist earns its place when linkedin matters. smartlead comes in when the client brings it.

connect every mailbox before warm-up so the platform builds the sending history for you.

6/ rotation and warm-up

mailbox rotation goes on from day one so sends spread across the estate. every mailbox then gets 2 weeks minimum before it touches a campaign, and 30 days is the safer number now that gmail puts a warning banner on domains younger than that.

cut it short and the failure only surfaces after the campaign is live and the domain is already marked, and warm-up won't repair it from there. you replace the domain and start over.

7/ send limits

cap each mailbox at 20 to 25 sends a day. volume comes from mailbox count.

40 mailboxes at that rate sends 800 to 1,000 a day and none of them looks unusual. set the cap inside the platform itself.

8/ placement

clear 95%+ in the primary inbox before the first real campaign. anything sitting in spam produces no pipeline at all.

if you're running this spec and landing well under 95%, the cause is back in steps 1 through 6.

domains get replaced every 9 to 12 months. stagger the replacements, because rotating all 20 at once puts the whole estate back to zero and every new domain still owes you its two weeks of warm-up.

the two numbers that break first:

> spam rate above 0.1%
> bounce rate above 3%

both shift weeks before reply rate does. by the time reply rate drops, the damage is a few weeks old and the domain is usually past repairing.

all of that is phase 1. phase 2 is data and targeting, phase 3 is the copy.

most teams start at phase 3 in week 1, which is why they spend the next month debugging subject lines for a domain problem.

you just read phase 1. @Kenny_GTM wrote all three, plus the ten-line weekly dashboard and the numbers that mean you already have a problem.

article_title: How to Pick the Right Claude Model

text: Going live in 45min to show you how to do GTM Engineering like the top 1%

if AI looks expensive in your outbound, look at what you're running opus on.

most of a campaign isn't thinking work. it's lookups, filters, checks and dedupes. a frontier model doesn't do any of that better than a script does, it just costs more and adds variance to an answer that was never in question.

so price the step before you hand it to anything. two things decide it:

how open-ended is the work?
how far does a bad output get before someone catches it?

then give it to the cheapest thing that clears both, which is somewhere between a plain python script and a person.

here's where the 7 steps of an outbound campaign sit:

1/ qualifying against your ICP
a python script. no model in the loop, $0. it applies a firmographic floor, scores the signal, and buckets the account. run the same account through it twice and you get the same answer twice, which is the whole reason it isn't a model.

2/ suppression and preflight
claude code hooks, also $0. an account already sitting in an open sequence doesn't get put in a second one, spend caps hold, send windows run on the account's own timezone so nothing shows up at 6am local and gets read as spam. none of that is a judgment call.

3/ signal feeds and list pulls
haiku 4.5, the 1x baseline. 10,000 rows a pull, filtered down to the ones that moved. it needs a model at all because a hiring post and a repost of someone else's hiring post look nearly the same in plain text.

4/ account research and tiering
sonnet 5, roughly 3x. reads the account, interprets the signal, then maps who signs, who evaluates, and who uses it daily. this used to be affordable on the top 20% of a list. it runs on the whole list now, for less than that top slice cost.

5/ QA in front of every send
sonnet 5 again. three checks on every message before it goes out: ICP fit, the claims it makes, tone.

6/ first-draft copy and strategy
opus 5, and fable 5 when the reasoning gets hard. 5x to 10x. this is the one step that earns it. a weak draft here travels into every account on the list.

7/ picking the signal, approving the send
a person, which is the most expensive tier in the stack and is supposed to be. on a 500 account campaign we look at about 50 at the front and read about 50 sends at the back. the other 400 move through steps 1 to 6 without anyone touching them.

i had this backwards for a long time, and i don't think the instinct is stupid. nobody wants to be the person who under-provisioned a step and shipped something bad. so the frontier model ends up running everything.

The problem is that distribution isn't a tool. It's 7 jobs that feed each other, and if you run them out of order it doesn't matter what you bought.

Here's what each job does, in the order they have to run:

1/ Signal
You want to know the moment something moves at an account, whether that's a funding round, a new VP in the buyer's seat, or a hiring spike, and you want it arriving with a note on why it fired. Hold onto that note, it comes back in step 6.

2/ List on demand
When a signal fires you enrich that one account right then, instead of paying upfront for twelve months of records you might never open.

3/ Score and tier
You score every account on six weighted factors, and each one has to be checkable from the outside before anyone talks to you. Nobody finishes this layer, because what it ends up telling you is to stop calling most of your list, and nobody wants to hear that. Finish it anyway.

4/ Channel routing
The tier decides which channel an account gets before anyone opens an inbox, and tier 1 always gets an actual person. A signal can bump an account up one tier, never two, no matter how good it looks.

5/ Content
You post enough that people have heard of you before the email lands, and anyone who engages goes straight back into step 1 as a signal.

6/ Outbound
Remember the note from step 1? It becomes the opener here. If an account has no note on file, it doesn't get sent at all.

7/ Feedback loop
Everything writes back into the same table, the replies, the deals that died, the no-shows. And keep the no-shows, seriously. Those people booked a meeting with you, they were just early.

Running it in this order took us from 1 deal per 1,000 cold emails to 3, out of the same inboxes, without adding a single send.

text:
Found a 22-year-old clip of Peter Thiel and Max Levchin breaking distribution down to what each customer cost PayPal.

In September 1999 PayPal was 22 people, and Silicon Valley had two main ways to get customers.

The first was advertising. A billboard on the highway into San Francisco went from $10K a month in '97 to $100K a month in '99, and drivers got 6 to 10 seconds to read it.

The second was a big partner. They flew to London to pitch HSBC, and the executives told them about the TV ads they had just started running.

So PayPal started paying people to join. 

$10 to open an account and another $10 for every friend they brought in. People called it the most insane scheme of all time. It worked out to $20 a customer, and the next cheapest option was online ads at about $65.

Then eBay sellers started asking to put PayPal's logo on their auctions. PayPal told them no for two months, until it noticed they were joining without the $20.

In 2014 Thiel put the same math into the distribution chapter of Zero to One. The profit you make over a customer's lifetime decides what you can spend to win a customer, and that decides which channel you can afford.

Here's how he lays it out, from the biggest deals down:

1/ Seven figures and up. The founder sells. Palantir's CEO was on the road 25 days a month.

2/ $10K to $100K. A small sales team runs a process it can repeat.

3/ Around $1,000 a year for small-business software. The dead zone. The buyer still needs a conversation, and the price can't cover a salesperson's time.

4/ Low price with mass appeal. Advertising, when other channels are uneconomical.

5/ Viral. The product brings in the next user, the way a PayPal payment could.

PayPal priced its options and went with the cheapest one. Thiel's line on it in the book: "If you can get just one distribution channel to work, you have a great business."

text:
AI only gives you something good when the system under it is right and the data going in is right.

Before you let AI take over your cold email, make sure you do these seven things (below) first. You'll thank me later.

1/ Stop sending to bought lists.

About a quarter of a bought list is dead within a year, and every dead address is a bounce that hurts your domain. Build the list from live sources and keep bounces under 2%.

2/ Score every account for fit before anyone writes to it.

Fit is the company, the role, and the tools they already use. Timing is what changed at that company in the last two weeks. Keep them as two separate scores.

3/ Verify every email with more than one provider.

One provider finds about half the emails. Three in sequence got us to 85 to 90%. For your best accounts, open the LinkedIn profile as well. A verified email only proves the mailbox exists, and people who left last quarter still show up as verified.

4/ Only send when something just changed at the account.

A new VP 12 days ago, a pricing page changed 5 days ago. "They're hiring" is always true, so it never tells you when to send. We track 70 of these signals and send inside 14 days of the change. This is where the reply rate moves.

5/ Let AI write the reason you're reaching out, then read it before it goes.

The agent reads the company's site, news, and job posts and writes one line. Tell it to return "SKIP" when nothing changed in the last 14 days, or it will find a reason for every account. A human reads every message before it leaves.

6/ Run one campaign per account at a time.

Two campaigns on the same account and you lose track of which one earned the reply. Your best accounts get email, LinkedIn, and a call. The next tier gets email and LinkedIn. Everyone else gets email.

7/ Feed what closed back into the list.

Every quarter, take the last 30 to 50 deals you won, pull the company domains, and score the next list against them. All of them paid you and stayed.

Most teams we audit get to step 3 and stop. Clean, scored, verified list, then they send it on a Tuesday. Instantly's 2026 benchmark puts the average cold email reply at 3.43%. Our signal-based campaigns get 5 to 18% on the same AI models.

The full build for each step is in the article (bookmark for later).

If you're a founder or running GTM, build one account list your whole growth engine can use.

Start with your 10 best customers. Put their domains into AI Ark's lookalike search, find similar companies, and pull 2 to 3 buyers per account. Verify their emails and fill the gaps with Prospeo.

Keep the company domain, segment, buying trigger, outreach tier and status together in Clay. That record should tell the next tool who the account is and what's already happened.

Then build the campaign around it:

→ Outbound: tier accounts by segment fit and a live buying trigger. Accounts with both get email, LinkedIn and a call from your team. Those with either one get email and LinkedIn. Keep broader-fit accounts with neither on email.

→ Paid: use the company list for LinkedIn ads and Vibe’s streaming TV ads. Match the data to each platform's requirements. Google Customer Match needs first-party contacts. Keep the offer consistent as you adapt the creative.

→ Search and landing pages: answer the questions buyers ask about pricing, alternatives and how the work gets done. Give each segment a page with a clear promise, proof and next action. Use the same brief for the page, ads and outreach.

→ Workflows: build a workflow that connects reply events across your tools. When someone responds, have it stop their other sequences, update the CRM and write the result back to the account. Add a monthly refresh to re-verify emails and update the tiers.

→ Reporting: bring matched ad exposure, tracked site activity and CRM deals into an account-level view. Compare results by segment. Use what you find to choose the next audience, page or follow-up to improve.

2/ Open rates.

3/ Impressions from people who could never buy.

→ Count the accounts on your list that saw you.

4/ Meetings booked that never turn into pipeline.

→ Search your account list in Clay by the job titles you sell to, and keep each person's name, title and LinkedIn URL.
→ Run them through a waterfall. Prospeo checks first for a verified email and mobile, and whatever it can't find goes to the next provider. Ours is LeadMagic.

6/ Most of the GTM advice you read online.

7/ More SDRs sending more cold email.

→ More volume on a weak list gets you more of the same result. I'd fix the list before I added a seat.
→ Then let content warm the accounts up.
→ Give Claude last month's call transcripts. Ask it to list every question and objection in the buyer's words and count how often each came up. Write a post for each of the top 5.
→ We pull our topics from sales calls, and those posts book us 50+ meetings a month.
→ Each week, export who reacted to or commented on those posts. Anyone at a target account gets enriched in Clay and goes into a sequence that opens on the post they engaged with.

8/ One template sent to 10,000 people.

→ A funding round or a new hire changes what a company needs that month.
→ Clay can watch your account list for both, plus job changes for the champions you already know. Stack them. Once an account has 3 or more signals, email it that week.

9/ Which team gets credit for the lead.

→ Omniscient Digital had 189 leads say an AI tool sent them. HubSpot's first-touch tracking credited 28.
→ Log 2 sources on every deal: what your software tracked first, and what the buyer told you on the first call.
→ That second source is where AI search shows up. Ahrefs studied 75,000 brands, and the ones with more web mentions showed up more in AI answers. Backlinks barely mattered.

→ Name the trigger: a new role, a funding round, a recent post
→ Ask who handles it on their team
→ Send something useful first

Whatever booked meetings becomes your template. Run it for 30 days, keep the winner and test the next step. Eventually you're running a template that gets better every campaign.

We've sent over 23M cold emails and built GTM systems for 300+ B2B companies at $7M ARR.

Here's how the top 1% make cold email work in 2026:
(Based on 1,000,000+ emails analyzed via @InstantlyAI)

1. Small Targeted Lists > Big Broad Lists

> Micro-lists of 500-1,000 hyper-targeted prospects beat blasting 100,000 contacts every time. Reply rates: 20-30% vs. 2-3%.
> Stop praying someone bites. Start targeting the actual people who have a reason to reply.

2. Hyperenriched Data > Basic Data

Go beyond name + email. Collect:

> LinkedIn headline & profile
> Job postings (signals growth/hiring needs)
> Technologies used
> Funding announcements
> Website case studies
> Department & industry
> Company size & connections

Personalization at scale requires data at scale.

3. AI Personalization > Generic Openers

Instead of: "Hey John, hope all is well at [Company]"
Try:

> Job postings → "Saw you're hiring 3 AEs..."
> Funding news → "Congrats on the $25M Series B..."
> Case studies → "Just read your case study on..."
> Tech stack → "Noticed you recently added [tool]..."
> Product launches → "Saw you rolled out 5 new SKUs..."

Make every email feel 1:1.

4. 4-Step Sequence > 1 Single Email

Most replies come from the first emails, but follow-ups increase overall sequence reply rates significantly.

> Email 1: Personalized opener + value offer
> Email 2: Short follow-up (3-5 days later)
> Email 3: Different angle (3-5 days later)
> Email 4: Breakup email (3-5 days later)

Keep them short. 2-4 sentences. Reference the original. Add new value.

Pro tip: Layer in LinkedIn touches between emails for omnipresence.

5. Value-First > Ask-First

Stop asking for their time immediately.

❌ "Can we hop on a call tomorrow at 2pm?"
❌ "Do you have 15 minutes to chat?"

✅ "Would it make sense to send over a quick example deck?"
✅ "Happy to share what's working best right now."
✅ "Can I send you something that could help [specific pain]?"

They raise their hand first. Then you've earned the conversation.

6. Fundamentals > Fancy Tactics

Master the 3 core pillars:

> ICP – Who exactly are you targeting?
> Offer – What specific outcome do you deliver?
> Copy – How do you communicate value?

Depth > Width. No shiny object syndrome.

7. Long Game > Quick Wins

Cold email isn't a magic pill. It's a compounding client acquisition system.
Quality over rushing. Pipeline over quick wins. Be there when they're ready to buy.

8. Deliverability > Volume

None of this matters if you land in spam.

> Multiple domains (not just one)
> 30 emails per inbox per day max
> Proper technical setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
> 30 days minimum warm-up
> Clean, validated lists

Sending 100 emails/hour from one email = spam city.

9. Tech Stack

Most founders quit LinkedIn after six months. They write technically correct posts, get a handful of likes from coworkers, and decide B2B buyers don't live on the platform.

B2B buyers do live there. They scroll past 200 posts a day and most of those posts get less than a second of consideration before the scroll continues.

I sat down with @PierreReddot (runs Content Path, one of the most-followed B2B marketing creators on LinkedIn) to pull apart what makes a post survive that first second. We've installed a version of his anatomy across 24+ ColdIQ profiles. LinkedIn drives 65% of our inbound and added $80K+ MRR on its own.

A few things actually moved the needle:

1. The image does 95% of the work. The visual is what stops the scroll, what gets screenshotted into a Notes app for next Thursday's meeting, what gets reposted with a one-line caption from someone else's profile. We design the visual first now and write the copy around whatever it's doing.

2. The high-performing posts almost all collapse into one of four archetypes: the comparative table, the pyramid, the iceberg, or the visual metaphor. Pierre's most-copied post pairs a glowing button labelled "what people think marketing is" against a Rubik's cube labelled "what marketing actually is." Pick one archetype and run it across different topics. The reason most accounts plateau is they try to invent a new visual every week instead of building muscle memory on one.

3. The hook has one job. Open a curiosity gap in the first two lines, then pay it off in the line right after "see more." Pierre's name for the most common failure mode is the "deceiving hook," which promises something in line one and resolves it fifteen lines down. It kills more posts than weak openings ever do.

4. Most bodies fail because they read as dense walls of text. We keep posts inside 140 words and 1,300 characters and we vary sentence length deliberately. A six-word punch sits next to a twenty-word analytical sentence, which sits next to a one-word emphasis. The eye needs the rhythm or it bounces.

5. The metric that actually moves the algorithm is saves. Saves correlate with dwell time, and dwell time is what LinkedIn watches across the first 72 hours after publication. We roughly doubled our save rate after three changes: we embedded tool logos like Clay, Lemlist, Apollo, and HubSpot inside the infographic so readers save the post for the stack, we made the framework self-contained enough that a screenshot of the image alone delivers the playbook, and we added one small animated element per post which pushes average dwell from about two seconds to seven.

Most LinkedIn advice is about output. Post cadence, time of day, hashtag strategy, tagging peers. None of it matters if your individual post can't survive a half-second scroll.

Build the anatomy at the unit level first. The volume conversation comes after.

Verify every email before you send. Skip it and it costs you: a dead address bounces, and enough bounces train Gmail to file you under spam. An unverified guess is worse than an empty cell.

Every row comes back with the email, the source that found it, and whether it cleared verification. The few nobody could place get flagged, so you skip them and move on.

Starting it was the only part that needed you.

This is the GTM funnel behind ColdIQ, every layer & the tools that run each one (it books us 100+ meetings a month)

Top to bottom:

1. Traffic

Five channels feed the top. LinkedIn posts, cold outbound, YouTube, X & the blog.

40,000+ people a month land on our website. The biggest sources: the blog and the rest of our AEO & SEO ~12,000 visits/mo, LinkedIn ~10,000 with 10+ of us publishing, cold outbound ~3,000. (YouTube is the one I keep failing to stay consistent on.)

@prospeo_io and @FullEnrich do the enrichment up here, @predictleads for the buying signal, taplio(.)com the post inspiration.

2. The four surfaces

Company page, LinkedIn profile, the website, form fills. Every capture surface we own is one of those four.

3. The eight buckets underneath them

→ page followers, pulled with getleads(.)io
→ connections, profile viewers, post engagers & DMs, all covered by @expandi_io
→ website visitors, caught with vector(.)co, Warm & posthog(.)com, including the ones who never fill anything in
→ newsletter subs in beehiiv(.)com
→ demo bookings through default(.)com, ColdIQ & attio(.)com

Eight streams, eight different shapes, and plenty of the same people showing up across them.

4. Data routing

All eight land in one place. ColdIQ sits there and holds one row per human, so someone who followed the page in spring and booked a demo in summer stops being two separate records.

It dedupes, enriches, timestamps, and keeps the origin bucket. Keep that last one forever, it's what eventually tells you which source was worth funding.

5. Lead scoring & prioritization

Claude Code and Codex do the modelling, ColdIQ holds the records, PredictLeads brings the intent signal.

Train on closed-won first. Those are the accounts you actually want more of. Then feed it closed-lost, so it learns which good-looking accounts never close. Skip the lost deals and everything scores well.

6. Three motions, picked by the score

→ Automated outreach. Email & LinkedIn sequences through @InstantlyAI and @lemlist. Mid score, good fit, unclear timing. Most of the volume ends up living here.

→ Manual sell-by-chat. Email, call, DM, text through Gmail, LinkedIn & nooks(.)ai. High score with live intent, a human the same day. It stays deliberately small, it costs real rep hours per contact.

→ Marketing. Ad retargeting & nurture sequences through LinkedIn, Google & customer(.)io, holding frequency until something in the score moves.

Nothing is permanently assigned. Re-score on every event and people move lanes on their own.

7. Sales process, closed deal

70% of deals are sales-led, usually 1 to 2 calls on Google Meet depending on package size. I record them with claap(.)io and turn them into coaching, cobl(.)ai drafts the proposals off the transcripts.

That's the map, and it reads top to bottom.

You build it middle out. Start dead centre with the router, then scoring, then the lanes, then work back up to claim the eight buckets, and open the channels last. Build it the other way round and everything above the router is collecting records that nothing can join up.

Tier 1 = dream accounts, manual and high touch. They get your DM slots and your call blocks.

2. Check what each channel can physically carry

→ LinkedIn: ~100 DMs or connection requests a week, platform enforced. Push past it and you risk an account you spent years building.

→ Email: ~25 sends per mailbox per day before spam risk climbs. Mailboxes stack though, so 10 of them is about 1,250 a week (one number is the per-mailbox threshold, the other is a full sending setup).

→ Calling: 50 to 100 dials per rep per day. A parallel dialer lifts the connects you get out of those hours, but you're still buying capacity in rep time, which is the most expensive kind.

Those are starter weights. Your reply and meeting data should tune them.

Most teams work them the other way around: they automate the public announcement every competitor can see, then let the strongest intent die inside a dashboard.

The signal alone is not the entire system. You still have to decide what matters, how long it matters and what a rep should do next.

Here is the starter model I use (that you can copy too): 

Only track signals your offer can act on.

Budget-gated product → funding, leadership hire, expansion.

Replacement product → tool added or dropped, review-site activity, competitor ad shifts.

Role-attached product → job openings, champion moves, team growth.

Self-serve product → product usage, pricing-page visits, content engagement.

Pick three from the relevant row. Do not add a fourth until those three produce meetings.

Score the full account.

Start with:

First-party signal: 40 points
Second-party signal: 25 points
Third-party signal: 10 points
Then apply four modifiers:
×2 when the signal is inside its freshness window
+15 when signals from 2+ tiers stack on one account
+10 when the signal resolves to the actual buyer
−20 when the same event was counted twice

That last rule matters. A round surfaced by PredictLeads, Crunchbase and a news monitor is one event. Count it once.

Suppress before a rep sees the queue.
Remove open opportunities, active sequences and anyone touched in the last 14 days. Then enrich the accounts that survive with the person who actually owns the problem.
Let the score determine the treatment.
80+ → work today, manually. DM or call.

40 to 79 → sequence this week with the context built in.

Below 40 → nurture. Wait for another signal.

If 400 accounts hit the manual band, the model is not calibrated. Raise the threshold until the queue matches the team’s actual capacity.

Expire every signal.

Hours → pricing-page visit, demo form, product-usage spike.

Days → content download, ad engagement, LinkedIn engagement.

1 to 2 weeks → job post, champion move, review-site visit.

2 to 6 weeks → funding round. Skip week one, when every vendor is sending congratulations.

Months → technographic change, leadership hire, expansion.

The fastest-decaying signals tend to convert best. They also punish slow operations the hardest.

Use the signal to choose the situation without exposing the surveillance.

Funding → the hiring plan or target the money created.

Job opening → the work behind the role.

I recently spoke to a video agency founder about improving his LinkedIn content and using it to attract buyers.

During a content exercise, he showed me a viral post he liked and wanted to replicate.

But copying its hook and framing would have told his own buyers they didn't need his agency in the first place.

He'd picked it because he liked the visual. But the hook positioned Claude Code as a replacement for the service he was trying to sell.

So we kept the visual concept and changed the angle: how his agency could use Claude Code to deliver better videos on smaller budgets. Same source of inspiration, now giving buyers a reason to hire him.

Here's how to work out which parts of a viral post you can use for your own business:

1. Find an outlier, then check what you're comparing it against.

Look at the author's surrounding posts. You're looking for something that performed unusually well for that account. A big like count on a huge account tells you very little on its own.

In the session, I used Scripe to search relevant keywords and filter by date and likes. Start with your niche, then look at adjacent ones for formats you could explain through your own expertise.

2. Open the original post and separate its parts.

Save the hook, the supporting line, the body structure, the proof, the visual and the CTA.

Check whether the post was edited. In our example, the updated copy pointed to a resource. I thought the lead magnet helped drive the engagement; the graphic wasn't the whole explanation.

Read the comments too. Are people discussing the idea, asking for the resource or arguing with the claim? Those are different reasons for a post to take off.

3. Translate the idea into a problem your buyer has.

"Claude Code for marketing" could become "Claude Code for video."

But "AI replaces video agencies" would undermine what he sells. And "small agencies can compete with bigger agencies" would interest his peers.

His clients cared about production quality and budget. So we discussed an angle about using Claude Code to improve production on smaller budgets.

Before writing, finish this sentence: "The person who would hire us wants to know how to ___."

4. Supply the knowledge the original format leaves out.

A list of prompts might work in one niche. Video production also needs context: product images, existing footage, brand material and visual references.

If your reader needs those inputs to use the advice, explain them before the prompts.

Build the body from work you can show. For each example, include the input, what you did, the output and anything that still needed a person to fix it. Use your own results as proof; don't inherit the original author's numbers.

5. Write the hook and sub-hook together.

The hook gives the reader a specific reason to open the post. The next line handles the obvious objection or explains what they'll get.

For a video-production tutorial, that could be:

"AI prompts for product videos."
"Including the source images and reference shots each prompt needs."

Then deliver those materials in the body. If you promise usable prompts, show tested prompts. If you promise better production quality, show the work that supports it.

6. Rebuild the visual around your version.

In this case, I suggested adapting the image concept into "Claude Code for video" while dropping the replacement pitch.

You can borrow a comparison layout, a list structure or a workflow diagram. Replace its examples, labels and supporting material with your own. Keep only the parts that help someone understand your subject.

7. Make the next action fit what you delivered.

A useful discussion needs a question someone can answer from experience. A resource offer needs a finished resource you can send. A service CTA should explain what you can implement for the reader.

Don't copy a giveaway's closing line if you haven't built the thing it promises.

After publishing, check who responded and what they asked. Track relevant questions, DMs and enquiries alongside reach.

If other agency owners love it but your buyers aren't responding, revisit the angle before abandoning the format. You might likely be creating content that's educating your competitors, instead of attracting your buyer.

Your ICP doc, your campaign notes & your CRM will eventually contradict each other. Rank them & the model stops picking a winner silently while it writes 40 emails.

At the bottom of brain.md:

1. Closed-won CRM data
2. This file
3. Last quarter's campaign notes

→ Rewrite brain.md after every closed deal. Weekly is the floor.

3. Connect the tools

claude mcp add --scope project coldiq --env 'COLDIQ_API_KEY=${COLDIQ_API_KEY}'

→ Single-quote the variable. Unquoted, your shell expands it first & the real key lands in .mcp.json, the file you're about to commit.
→ Always write the "type". A typeless entry gets read as stdio, so a remote entry carrying only a url gets skipped.
→ Edit .mcp.json & a running session won't pick it up. Restart claude, or reconnect the server from /mcp.
→ Never @ your .env. It loads, & the contents go into the prompt & the session transcript. Put a deny rule in .claude/settings.json & hand the agent a .env.example instead.

4. Run these 7 steps, with a checkpoint after each one

1. Detect the signal. Hiring, funding, tech-stack changes, job posts. The filter should name an event that happened, with a date on it.
2. Score & tier. T1 = strong fit with a live signal. T2 = strong fit, no signal yet. T3 = adjacent, watchlist only. Removes ~80% of the manual sorting.
3. Find the contacts against the tiered list, filtered to the personas in brain.md.
4. Enrich & validate. Email first. Phone on T1 only, it runs ~10x the cost of an email lookup.
5. Write the copy per tier. T1 gets its own prompt per account, built on that account's signal. T2 runs a template with one variable swapped. T3 drops into the volume sequence.
6. Route & launch. T1 multichannel with a call task & a LinkedIn touch, T2 and T3 to the sequencer.
7. Analyse & save. What worked goes back in the file, so the next run starts from a better rubric.

→ Approve the plan, review the list before enrichment spends credits, read the copy before anything goes live. Approving it end to end on the first pass is how you find out something was wrong after the mail went out.
→ Pull job posts off the ATS layer. Greenhouse publishes an open JSON board API, Lever exposes public postings per employer. Tech stack comes off the company's own front end via BuiltWith or Wappalyzer. No login, no scraping.

5. Turn every winner into a skill file

Ask Claude to build the same list 5 times from a typed prompt & you get 5 different lists. You never type it the same way twice, & the output tracks the wording.

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md in it, holding one procedure written down once.

→ When a campaign lands, that sequence becomes a skill the same day. Six weeks later nobody remembers the send window that made it work.
→ If the description of your skill needs an "and", it's two skills. Split it.

6. The commands you'll actually use

/compact on long list jobs, before quality drops.
/clear between unrelated clients, so the last one doesn't bleed into the next.
/model Opus for planning & copy, Sonnet for bulk mechanical work.
/mcp to see what actually connected.

→ @data/input/ gives you a listing & leaves the files unread. Name the file: @data/input/leads-raw.csv
→ Batches of 100-200 rows, /compact between them. Push 1,000 through in one pass & it degrades partway.
→ Keep approvals on for anything that sends. --dangerously-skip-permissions uploads to your sequencer & starts the campaign with no confirmation step.

7. Put your proof where it gets read

Best cold email I ever got ran the sender's own product on me & put the result in the subject line.

→ Do that with something public. Their open role, their tech stack, the page they read.
→ Lead with something they keep. "Want the list of 1,000 HR directors at companies hiring 5+ roles?" beats asking for 15 minutes.

Your next customer could be in a court filing, a lost deal, or a LinkedIn comment you never followed up on.

We mapped 26 GTM plays for finding opportunities like these and turning them into campaigns. Each includes the data sources, qualification checks and outreach steps you can run through Claude Code and the ColdIQ MCP.

Here’s where I’d look first, based on the business you run and the data you already have:

1. If you have past customers or lost deals, start there.

Export your past users and champions from your CRM. Check Apollo’s job-change alerts for your saved contacts, then verify their current role and company.

Only look up their new email once the company fits your ICP. Prospeo and FullEnrich handle that step. If the company doesn't fit, keep the person on your watchlist.

The message can open on the work you already did together. They know you, so you can ask whether the same problem exists at their new company.

For lost deals, have Claude read the call transcript and extract the objection. Check whether your product changed or something changed at the account. A funding announcement only matters if budget actually stopped the deal.

If the blocker is unchanged, leave it parked. When it moves, explain exactly what's different before asking to reopen the conversation.

2. If people already engage with your content, qualify them before reaching out.

Collect the people who liked or commented on a relevant LinkedIn post. Use Explorium to research the accounts, then have Claude score company fit and the person's role against your ICP.

Check your CRM before email enrichment. Someone already in a sales conversation shouldn't get a fresh cold sequence.

Write from what they engaged with and what the company research found. A like tells you which topic caught their attention; you still need a reason your offer fits.

You can apply this to profile visitors and event attendees too. For newsletter subscribers, start with repeated engagement. Leave the others on the newsletter.

3. If you sell a service, put a sample of the work in the email.

Use the ColdIQ MCP and Explorium to collect what the company sells, who it sells to and what the recipient owns.

Write a few campaign ideas yourself first. Give those examples to Claude, then ask for 3 ideas per company. Review a sample before running the rest of the list.

Each idea should point to something you found about that business. If you can swap the company name and keep the idea, research further.

You can go further with a rewritten post, a redesigned banner or a landing-page teardown. Check whether the original needs improving, do the work, and review it yourself before sending.

If your buyer serves local businesses, use Openmart to find nearby companies that match your buyer’s customer profile. Send 3 relevant businesses with a reason for each. Skip prospects where you can't find enough useful matches.

4. If you're starting cold, build from a result you can prove.

Pick a case study with a specific outcome. Enrich that customer's company in Apollo or Explorium, then find similar accounts.

Check the business model as well as size and industry. A company can look similar in a database and still have no use for the work you did.

Open with the relevant result and offer to send the case study.

Once replies come in, connect Instantly or lemlist to Claude. Classify the positives, objections and “not now” replies. Enrich the responders and look for patterns in who wanted what.

Use those patterns to propose 3 smaller segments. Review them before GetLeads sources more accounts. An objection about timing needs a different response from an objection about the offer.

5. If you're targeting named accounts with ads, use engagement to decide the follow-up.

Build the account list with ColdIQ, Explorium, PredictLeads or Apollo. Create LinkedIn content for the buyers inside those accounts.

Track company engagement through ZenABM or Fibbler. Use ColdIQ to find relevant contacts at engaged accounts, then qualify them before outreach.

Company-level engagement alone doesn't tell you which person saw the ad. Keep that distinction in the copy.

For your highest-priority accounts, combine calls, LinkedIn and email. Keep the account context with the sequence so each touch follows the same conversation.

6. If your buyer is hard to find in a database, identify the public record that reveals them.

The deck includes court filings, aircraft ownership and company ownership registers. Each answers a different targeting question.

For a law-firm offer, a relevant filing can identify the firm, attorney and case. Check the attorney's actual seniority before treating them as the buyer.

For a product sold to independently owned companies, check ownership before buying contact data. Remove subsidiaries when they don't meet that requirement.

Write the qualifying condition first. Then choose the register that can establish it. A broad industry filter won't answer an ownership question.

7. If you sell recruiting, look at the vacancy behind the signal.

Check saved contacts for job changes in Apollo, and use PredictLeads for publicly reported executive hires and departures. Confirm the company the person left, then find their former manager.

Ask whether they plan to backfill the role. A departure gives you a reason to ask, but it doesn't prove they're hiring.

When a job is already posted, have Claude read the full description and identify the requirement that matters most. Offer 3 real, anonymized candidate profiles that match it.

Another play is companies with several openings and no recruiter listed. Verify who's handling hiring before approaching the founder.

Use BuiltWith to find companies where Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby was first detected recently. Verify when they adopted it, then ask about their hiring process. A detection date doesn’t prove a recent install or a hiring surge.

Check how the companies on that list actually make their money.

A software consultancy and a SaaS company can both show up in a broad technology search. One sells client projects. The other sells access to a product.

If your offer only fits one of them, a verified email address at the other won't fix that.

Take an example: selling outbound support to UK B2B SaaS companies with 50-200 employees. Here's how I'd go from that brief to a list ready for outreach:

1. Define the companies before looking for contacts.

In @prospeo_io, open People Search. Set company HQ to the UK and employee headcount to 50-200. Under Type & Business Model, set Company Type to SaaS and How they sell to B2B.

Company HQ and person location are separate filters. A London-based sales leader at a US company could pass the wrong one.

Export customer and open-deal company domains from your CRM. Upload that CSV under Company > Bulk include/exclude companies and select exclude.

2. Make the title search match the job you're selling to.

Include Head of Sales, VP of Sales and Sales Director. Prospeo lets you choose Exact, Contains or Smart matching.

For this example, I'd start with Exact and inspect the titles before widening it. Contains can pull in adjacent roles. Smart can help find variations, but you still need to review what it includes.

3. Check the records that look close enough to slip through.

Preview names, titles and companies before spending credits on contact details. Then manually check company websites and public profiles where the business model or person's responsibilities are unclear.

For this campaign, the decisions would look like this:

A Head of Sales at a UK B2B SaaS company, with responsibility for new business: keep.

A sales leader whose remit is renewals: reject from this campaign. The offer needs someone responsible for winning new customers.

A Sales Director at a consultancy selling custom projects: reject from this SaaS campaign, even if the title fits.

If you can't establish someone's responsibilities, hold them for review.

I'd record each decision and the evidence in a separate spreadsheet. If the same mismatch keeps appearing, adjust the search before exporting more contacts.

4. Pull contact data for the people who passed.

Under Contact Details, choose Work email and tick Verified. Select the people who passed your review, click Export, and choose Contacts with verified email.

Exporting triggers email enrichment, so do the review before that step. Check the credit estimate before confirming.

Save the search so the next batch starts with the corrected filters.

If you're trying it on your next campaign, review who you'd reject before clicking Export. Those records can show where to tighten your search or add a manual check.

Your CRM still says “closed-lost.”

I'd have Claude Code check that before buying another list of cold prospects.

We connected Claude Code to folk, our CRM, and the ColdIQ MCP. Alongside tracking our 2,000+ product signups, this lets us work the opportunities buried in our own deal history.

Before building another list, make the CRM show you where you already have a reason to start a conversation:

1. Find a reason to reopen the deals you lost.

Pull your closed-lost deals from the last 12 months. Have Claude read the call transcripts and put the buyer's exact objection beside each account.

Then investigate that objection. If an integration was missing, check whether you now support it. If someone blocked the purchase, verify whether they're still at the company.

Have the agent return the old objection, what changed and the source.

Only draft a follow-up when you can explain why the conversation would be different this time.

Leave everything else parked. “Just checking in” isn't a change at the account.

2. Find out where your best champions went.

Pull the people who helped get your deals approved. Include the person who spent weeks convincing their boss, even if they never signed anything.

Check their current company through the ColdIQ MCP. When someone moves, qualify the new company before opening an opportunity there.

Keep the old deal attached to their history. Your rep should know what you helped them with before writing the first message.

And assign someone to meet their replacement at the existing customer. Losing your internal supporter is worth acting on too.

3. Check whether your ICP describes buyers or just companies you like.

Set aside some closed-won AND closed-lost deals before giving Claude the rest.

Compare company size, industry, tools used and the signals available at the point you would score a new lead.

A characteristic that's just as common in lost deals as won deals doesn't distinguish the two on its own.

If your winners and losers all use the same software, that tool alone shouldn't earn an account a higher score.

Keep the criteria that separate the groups. Test them against the deals you set aside, and check whether winners tend to score higher there too.

If you revise the model, test it on fresh unseen deals before applying it to new leads.

Save the reason beside each score. Your reps need to see which assumption put an account at the top.

4. Turn a closed-won deal into the brief for your next list.

Send the customer's domain through the ColdIQ MCP to find similar companies. Then check what made the original customer a good fit.

If they bought because they needed to connect a warehouse to their CRM, another company with the same headcount isn't enough.

Check whether the same problem could exist there.

Remove existing accounts, apply your ICP criteria and keep the original customer attached to each match.

For the accounts you work individually, give the rep the shared problem and the relevant customer example.

If you can't explain that connection, research further before writing the email.

5. Follow up on what a signup did inside the product.

Our signups land in folk as enriched, scored people and companies. We track API-key creation, first requests and checkout starts.

For your own product, connect the product events to folk first. Then alert the owner when a checkout starts so they can offer help with the plan.

Send inactive signups an example they can run. Have the owner draft a personal note for strong-fit accounts that have started using the product.

Write down the trigger, owner and follow-up before connecting the events. Otherwise, you've built a dashboard that still needs someone to watch it.

Compare users who were still unpaid at the same point after signup. Use only behaviour recorded by then, and give each user the same follow-up window to convert.

If an event is equally common among converters and non-converters, don't treat it as strong buying intent on its own.

6. Give every new record enough context for these plays to work.

Normalize company domains, verify emails and check for duplicates before adding more records. Enrich the empty fields, then apply your ICP score.

We use Claap for call recordings. Have Claude extract the objection, named competitor and next step into fields on the deal, with the transcript linked.

Keep the buyer's words. “Need warehouse integration” gives the reactivation play something specific to check months later.

“Not interested” gives it very little.

7. Ask the CRM which deals need someone to act.

Our Slackbot and company-brain MCP let the team and agents query the same records.

For your first question, try: “Which deals are expected to close this month but have no agreed next step?”

Return the owner, stage, expected-close date and latest buyer conversation for each.

Give that list to the deal owners to agree the next step with the buyer.

Define “expected to close” once, using your stages and dates. The Slackbot and the agent preparing the sales meeting should return the same deals.

Ask it to pull the objections and next steps, with the source for each. Keep that first run read-only.

If the answers are missing, connect your call transcripts and fill the fields. Then run the play you have enough data for.

Once the checks work, put changed accounts into the deal owner's queue before the next list-building run.

Include the old conversation and the new evidence, so the rep can reopen it without researching the account from scratch.

Since then I've helped 15+ people past 10,000 followers with the same methods, so if I had to get my first client from LinkedIn again, starting from zero, this is the order I'd do it in:

1. A posting schedule you can keep. 3 posts a week for 3 months before judging anything. The biggest reason people never grow an audience is that they give up beforehand... I nearly did at post 30.

2. Know who pays you. Other GTM agencies found my content "too basic". Good. I wanted revenue leaders reading it. Write down the questions your buyer asks before hiring you, that's your first batch of topics.

3. A profile that shows clients what you do. Your content brings people to the profile and the profile does the closing, so fix the banner, the headline & the featured section before the first post goes out.

Tag every account by region, industry and company size, which gives you segments like UK Tech or DACH Services. Then have AI validate those filters. Is it SaaS or agency? Self-serve or sales-led? SMB or enterprise buyers?

If you sell to both a US SaaS and a German manufacturer, they can't get the same email. Each segment gets its own offer later on.

4. Pick a path per segment

Path A is for the big segments: blast first. A free offer goes to the whole segment and you only enrich the ones who reply. I'd recommend Instantly for email & Expandi for LinkedIn.

Path B is the other way around, for when every account counts: enrich first. Filter the segment down, add intent signals & tech stack data (PredictLeads, BuiltWith), then enrich everyone left.

5. Score every account

Have Claude score each account against your ICP model and sort it into 3 tiers. This is where your TAM becomes your TAL (target account list).

T1 gets priority on every channel.
T2 gets volume, cold email only.
T3 gets nurtured and re-scored every month, which is where an unlimited data endpoint comes in.

6. Find the right people

3 personas per account, in the best case: who signs (the decision maker), who uses it (the champion) and who weighs in (the deal influencer).

Enrich the people with unlimited data first. Then get their emails, and even phone numbers if necessary, from single providers in our waterfall (Prospeo, FullEnrich, Findymail...).

T1 × Persona 1, the decision maker, gets the first email.

Hope this helps you build a TAM/TAL you can (finally) trust.
This would explain why AI labs are paying so much to get their hands on companies’ internal data

Stop giving every account the same cold email.

Rank every account on 2 things: how well it fits, and how ready it is to buy right now. Your best effort goes to the top of that list.

6 steps to set it up:

1) Map every company that could buy from you

Start in your CRM. Your closed-won and closed-lost deals define your ICP (ideal customer profile).

Build the full list from there and split it by region, industry and size.

2) Grade every account on 5 things

Industry, headcount, geography, tech stack and contacts. Each account comes out a best, good or weak fit.

Drop 4 kinds on sight:

> an industry you don't sell to
> a market you can't serve
> a competitor already locked in
> nobody inside who matches your buyer

3) Track 3 kinds of signals

1st party: site visits, product usage, calls, LinkedIn.

2nd party: review sites, a champion changing jobs, ad engagement.

3rd party: funding, hiring, tech stack changes, news.

4) Rank every account by fit × timing

Fit tells you who. Signals tell you when.

A good fit visiting your site lands in Tier 1, ahead of a best fit with no signal yet.

Rerun the tiers every Monday.

5) Warm the accounts ahead of the first email

Ads get you seen, and the posts inside them earn the trust.

Run thought-leader ads (your founder's posts, run as ads) to your target accounts for 2 weeks. The Companies page in LinkedIn Campaign Manager shows which ones engage.

By the first email, they already know you.

6) Match the effort to the tier

Tier 1 (1:1): a hand-researched first message to 3 people per account, by email, LinkedIn and phone in the same week.

Tier 2 (1:few): clusters of similar accounts, 1 angle per cluster, sequences plus LinkedIn messages.

Tier 3 (1:many): a short automated sequence, plus ads and content to stay visible.

Open with something useful. AirOps, one of our agency clients, got 112 positive replies by inviting buyers to a webinar and asking for their input.

Cold email isn't a numbers game. It's a fit and timing game.

(I ranked 25 buying signals from S to F. There's no way to be 100% sure... but the top ones get you pretty close)

0:00 Intro & why listen to me
0:42 The 3 families of signals
1:39 Website & product usage signals
3:57 Content signals: ebooks, webinars, newsletters
6:08 LinkedIn engagement signals

20:13 Job openings
21:21 Competitor & industry news

If you send cold emails, you might want to save this...

(I ranked 25 buying signals from S to F, based on growing my agency from 0 to 7M ARR and sending tens of millions of cold emails)

Quick context first. Every signal comes from one of 3 families:

- First-party: people who already know you (your site, your product, your content)
- Second-party: one step away from you (someone checking your G2 page, a customer who moved to a new company)
- Third-party: public data or data from external providers suggesting a company could benefit from your solution (funding, job openings, news). The ones we usually use for outbound.

Here's every tier, & how I'd use most of them:

S tier

1. Webinar or event attendance

Someone signs up a few days in advance, actually shows up and sticks around for 30-40 minutes... even if they never add you on LinkedIn after, that's a strong interest in the topic. An actual event they attended, even more.

A tier

2. Pricing or contact page visits

Pricing = they're evaluating a solution. Contact = they were thinking about reaching out. A much stronger signal than a random visit.

3. Multiple website visits

Some genuine buyers just keep coming back.

→ If you can find their contact information, send them a message.

4. Newsletter & email opens

We've looked at who opens 80%+ of our newsletter emails.

→ Same on cold email: someone opening your email months after you sent it usually means their circumstances changed.
→ Careful though, open tracking isn't as accurate as it used to be and it can kill your deliverability. Still worth looking at.

5. LinkedIn comments

Depending on the comment, there's more or less intent. Some are literally a question about the outcome your product gets them.

→ Extract the engagement on your posts with the content of each comment, have AI analyze which ones sound interested in your product, and send outreach based on what they wrote. Some of these can be extremely good leads.

6. Champion job change

A happy customer moves to a company that isn't a customer yet. Usually a high-converting play.

→ Monitor your CRM for job changes, then something along the lines of: "Congrats on your new role. Looks like you were a very happy client of ours at {old company}... perhaps there's a use for us at {new company} too?"
→ Only an A, because unless you have a large list of customers, it doesn't happen that often.

7. Review site activity

→ Look at your competitors' bad reviews on Trustpilot, TrustRadius or Capterra (e.g: a review saying their data is inaccurate), identify the person, and position your product as the alternative built so that exact problem doesn't happen.
→ Only works if your competitors have lots of bad reviews.

8. Job openings

"They're hiring SDRs, so they might need help with outbound" is a bit too simplistic.

→ The description tells you way more. Have your AI agents scan it and position your product as a way to help the new person in their job.
→ That's an A only when you actually use the description.

9. Industry news

→ A big event that hits a whole industry, e.g: a few banks get hacked, a cybersecurity company reaches out to other banks. Great if you catch it at the right time.

B tier

10. A single website visit. They probably searched for a solution like yours, but it's difficult to read strong intent from one visit.

11. Product usage spike (SaaS). Set thresholds (a specific workflow completed, a specific amount of time or data used), and when a user crosses one, trigger an action like a discount or an onboarding call.

12. LinkedIn likes. Suggests close to nothing on its own, sometimes people like random stuff. But a lot of the high-converting campaigns we run are based on re-engaging people who engaged with our content, so it depends on the topic of the post and whether they fit your ICP.

13. LinkedIn profile views. If they're in your ICP, it's worth asking whether there was anything specific they were looking at.

14. Lookalikes of your best customers. Not really a signal, it's a static list (I added it anyway haha). Take your most profitable segment (or the easiest to acquire), and ask the ColdIQ MCP (or any lookalike tool) to find 100 companies similar to it. Then: "We helped {company}, which shares similar traits to you, by {what you did}..."

15. Hiring surge. A growing company probably has more budget. What's interesting is which departments are growing (sales vs engineering)... that gives you an idea of their priorities.

16. Competitor news. A competitor increases their price, has a big outage, gets acquired or just stops... can be a great moment to reach out to their users.

C tier

17. Ebook downloads. They're interested in the topic as a whole. Nothing special.

18. Public asks ("who's the best email finding tool?" on Reddit, Quora or LinkedIn). Nothing's more explicit. But the comments get flooded with "use me", and you won't find enough of these posts to do volume.

19. New exec hire. A new VP of Sales can signal a change of strategy, and new leaders want to show impact quickly. Never a bad idea to reach out, but it lacks context for a very personalized approach, so layer other signals on top.

20. Tech stack change. BuiltWith shows you who started using lemlist. If they're doing outreach, they might need data... that's where your data solution comes in.

21. New market expansion. A US company going to Germany might need offices, people hired in the country, help with regulation. Pretty good if you can find more context on it.

D tier

22. Engaging with your competitor's posts. People are becoming fed up with cold emails that start with "Hey, I saw you engage with this person". Open on the topic instead, e.g: "Hey, looks like you interact a lot with posts around go-to-market"... then, if they're in your ICP, share your value prop.

23. New office opening. They'll usually need supplies, tables, computers. Useful if you have the information early enough, but only some companies can actually use it.

24. Mergers & acquisitions. The magic is in the details: the news usually explains the objectives, so link those objectives to how your product helps.

F tier

25. Funding rounds. Might be the most overused signal of all time. Every department can justify reaching out to a company that just raised, so they get bombarded with irrelevant emails. Use it as a confirmation that budget most likely won't be the reason they don't buy, and that's it.

text:
"B2B SaaS, 50-500 employees, VP of Sales" is 3 answers.

A full ICP has 34.

We went through 1M+ cold emails in @InstantlyAI. Tight lists of 500-1,000 people with a reason to reply got 20-30% reply rates, 100K blasts got 2-3%... and your ICP is how you know who has that reason.

So I broke it into 4 parts (every question is in the infographic, feel free to save it):

1. Company fit

Our example: you sell a tool that helps SDR teams book more meetings.

Before opening any tool, export 2 lists from your CRM: the companies that paid you, and the ones that paid you then left. Every answer gets checked against those 2. We use folk as our CRM, plugged into Claude Code, so pulling both is 1 prompt.

Data tools answer the first 6 questions:
→ Limadata for what they sell, to whom & where
→ Prospeo for industry, headcount & location
→ ColdIQ company search for funding stage, with the hiring filter on to catch the teams that are growing
→ BuiltWith for the tools running on their site

The last 3 (the job they need you for, what's blocking their growth, what your churned accounts share) come from your deal notes.

Then run your Prospeo & ColdIQ filters against your won list. If a best customer drops out, one filter is too tight. Whatever your churned accounts have in common becomes a "do not target" line, which in our example is teams with only 1 SDR.

2. User persona

The user feels the problem first, so most of your messaging is written for them, starting with the number their boss checks.

An SDR Manager running 4 reps is judged on meetings booked per rep, and also cares about pipeline generated & how fast new hires ramp. Every email to them should hit one of those 3.

A Head of Growth running 2 people can be a second user. A Marketing Intern working alone is out, since they don't run a team or push a purchase.

Then pull the exact phrases they use to complain from your call transcripts, and reuse them word for word in your emails & posts.

3. Buyer persona

The buyer is rarely the user, so map every seat that has to say yes: the SDR Manager brings you in, the VP of Sales signs, Finance checks the budget... and IT or Legal can still kill it.

Apollo or Prospeo find who sits in each seat (domain + job title in, names out). Do it on 3 of your won deals and write down the proof that got each one signed: a case study, a trial, a reference call.

4. Signals

Visitor ID in ColdIQ (a pixel on your site) shows which companies hit your pricing page. Job-change data from Signalbase & LeadMagic flags past users who moved to a new company. PredictLeads picks up hiring, funding & new tools, with the date each tool was first and last seen.

But the signal worth finding first is in your won deals. Go back through them, check what happened at each company right before the deal started, and watch whichever signal keeps showing up.

That said, a signal on its own only means the timing is good. An account only becomes Tier 1 when the company passes Part 1, your user works there & you can name who sits in each buyer seat.

Those get your first emails: open on the signal that fired, tie it to your user's number & add the proof your signer needs.

And if a company fails Part 1, it stays out (even with a strong signal).

Every single intent signal worth watching in 2026:

JOB

1. Job postings. They opened a role you can map to a pain you solve. Send the hiring manager three lines, quoting the JD back at them. Don't pitch the product yet.

2. Reposted jobs. Same role, listed twice. The first attempt didn't close. Show up with the candidate-shaped alternative before they burn another quarter.

4. Job changes. Your champion moves, or a buyer you lost lands somewhere new. Reach out in week one with something useful. New hires get a 60-day budget window. Almost nobody hits it.

SOCIAL

1. Competitor tracking. They engage with a competitor's content or page. The highest-intent social signal you'll buy. Skip the us-vs-them copy. Lead with the second-order problem the competitor won't solve, the one their customer hits in month three.

2. Social mentions. A decision-maker writes about a topic in your space on LinkedIn. Comment in their thread before you DM. Send a useful resource before you send a pitch.

3. Post reactions. They liked or reposted industry content. The thinnest signal you'll work with, useless on its own and worth something only when stacked under heavier signals.

4. Influencer post reactions. Engagement on a thought leader's post. Read it as topic curiosity and nothing more.

5. Company post reactions. Someone reacted to your target company's page. Useful for warming an account already in your pipeline. Don't open a new account off it.

6. New followers. New follows on a competitor or partner page. Treat this as market-map intel. It tells you who is interested in the category weeks before they show up in a job posting or an RFP.

COMPANY

1. New companies. A company was just registered. No vendor relationships, nothing locked in. Be the first one in their inbox with a starter package. Save the enterprise pitch for later.

2. Tenders & RFPs. Procurement opens. The highest stated intent on the entire list. Budget approved, scope written, timeline locked. This is a response motion, not an outbound one, and without an RFP playbook the signal is wasted.

FUNDING

1. Fundraising. The company just raised. Budget opens in the quarter after the close, rarely on the day of it. Time your outreach to 30-60 days post-announce. Day one their inbox is a graveyard.

2. Mergers & Acquisitions. They bought or got bought. Stack consolidations and vendor reviews follow inside the first 90 days. Pitch the migration help, the integration, the thing that survives the post-deal cleanup.

Take things further by stacking the intent signals on top of each other, and get better response rates as a result.

> Reposted jobs + Fundraising on the same account is a scaling team with budget approved.
> Tenders & RFPs + M&A on the same account is a company rewriting procurement rules after a consolidation.

Note: Two signals together aren't additive, they multiply.

No fake urgency, no "circling back"
No em dashes

The difference from ads is that no report ever shows you this happening.

Say you catch four funding rounds one quarter and none of them convert. Bad timing, and two were bridge rounds.

So the system does the sensible thing and lowers the weight on funding.

Now accounts that just raised stop making your list. You stop reaching them, so none of them book anything, because nobody asked. Next quarter funding looks worse still, and the weight drops again.

The signals that die this way are always the rare ones.

Post reactions fire constantly, so they carry enough volume to climb back out. A funding round or a new VP landing in the budget seat shows up a handful of times a quarter. Two bad ones bury the signal that was probably worth the most.

Two different questions, both answered in the same month.

Most setups reward the second kind, because social fires constantly and a pair of them is easy to find.
