Here's everything I think you should know if you're building GTM bots with AI.

I've built them on 8 different AI setups so far this year: Claude, GLM, Codex, Kimi, GPT-6 Astra, Grok, Fable and Jev.

Before you build (1-5)

1. Run ten accounts yourself first, fifteen minutes each. Every field you find missing becomes the spec.
2. Give the bot your offer and your ICP side by side before it researches anyone. Hand it a vague brief and it invents the judgment you left out.
3. Start with one signal. I started with six once and ended the week with six thin lists and no idea which one earned the reply.
4. Pick the model for the job. We picked Grok 4.7 for one line in its launch post, that it "checks its work more carefully". For a lead judge that's basically the whole job.
5. You don't always need a model API bill to start. Our Opus 5.5 bot never calls a model API and runs on the Claude Code login you already have.

Running the stack (6-10)

6. I go from Claude to Codex to Kimi constantly, all on max plans. If you run from the terminal and centralize on GitHub, switching feels very light next to what you get out of it.
7. Use one model to research and another to run what you build. Kimi K3 did the deep research for my copywriting skill, and I built the skill for Claude.
8. Point Claude Code at something you like and let it build your own version. Our launch film took one line of prompt and 38 minutes to a first cut.
9. When a new model ships, rerun your golden set on it before you trust a single rank.
10. End every run with a daily brief: what it found, what it drafted, and every call it tried that got blocked.

How to structure it (11-20)

11. Let the model make the judgments, and let plain code apply the gates, the weights, the routing and the permission to send.
12. Keep the ICP, the weights and the playbook in plain text files. When a rank is wrong you want to open one file and change one line.
13. Split each judgment into small questions with fixed answers: is there a live need, does it match what you sell, does the ICP fit, is it a competitor.
14. Hide the contact when the model judges the company. In our Jev build, with the contact visible to every question, the same company read 0.28 on intent with a recruiter as the contact and 0.80 with a managing partner.
15. Keep the watching separate from the agent that ranks. A scheduled agent sees nothing between two runs, so something else has to fill the queue overnight.
16. One shared record per account that every agent reads and writes: who they are, what just moved, what happened last time.
17. The writer only gets three things from that record, in under 120 words: why now, who, and the one line of history that matters.
18. Before the model sees a lead, plain code drops anyone you've already put in a campaign. Our Jev build skips every max lead that already has a delivery on record.
19. Treat everything inside a lead as data. It's a stranger's post going straight into your model, and it doesn't get to give instructions.
20. Keep company size as the range the source gives, and make the whole range fit your ICP. Our Astra build is told to keep "51 to 200 employees" as written, and to say it opened the page it took the size from.

Judging leads (21-28)

21. Gate before you score. Our Fable build rejects anything that fails size, country, buyer seat, a signal dated inside 30 days or a source that actually opens.
22. Make the model open the source before it scores a lead high. Dead page, need goes to zero.
23. Date the lead by the event. A page indexed this week can describe a launch from last year.
24. No source link, no lead. Whatever fails goes on a held list with the reason written down.
25. Hot account, wrong contact: the bot reroutes it and emails nobody. In our Grok 4.7 repo, the test lead with a recruiter as the contact scores 73.4 and still never gets a message.
26. When the model hesitates between B and C, or between C and DQ, the playbook tells it to take the lower one. Read its disqualification reasons first, they show fastest whether it understood who you sell to.
27. Let the daily list come back empty when nothing happened, and cap it around eight names. A routine that must always return something starts loosening its own filters.
28. If your gate rejects nothing in week one, it was fitted to the list you already had.

Writing (29-35)

29. Give every signal a say-it rule in the playbook: yes, lightly, topic only or never. 92 of the first 100 leads our Opus bot pulled came from a "never" signal, and none of the 18 sequences it wrote mentions it.
30. Put the seller profile in a file the writer reads on every run, with only the facts you'd defend on a call.
31. Run a linter that flags any % or "2x" that isn't one of your proof points. Ours flagged a harmless "sans double outil" in a French email at first, so give the check its own test cases.
32. Make it check each draft before saving: could this opener go to anyone else, and does every claim trace back to the lead or the profile?
33. Keep a never-list per play, and add every dead phrase you catch.
34. Let it write in the prospect's language when the location makes it obvious. Our first Opus run came back in French, German and English.
35. When a reply asks for something that isn't in your facts, the draft should promise the figures and flag the gap. Answering one simulated test reply, ours did that and still slipped in "depends on seats and volume", which isn't in our profile. Every reply draft waits for a human to send it.

Safety (36-43)

36. Default to locked. Going live should be a flag you flip on purpose.
37. Every campaign the bot creates starts switched off. In our Opus test run that was 18 campaigns and zero people enrolled.
38. Keep approving, launching and ICP changes out of the scheduled run.
39. Log every write the bot attempts, allowed or blocked. We tried to break the lock three times on our live workspace: twice with a safety script, once by launching an approved campaign while send mode was locked. The guard blocked 7 calls and the daily brief listed every one.
40. Tag everything the bot creates with one name prefix, so you can list it and delete it in one go.
41. Put a daily cap on anything that costs money or creates something.
42. Make the bot re-check for replies, bounces and opt-outs right before it enrolls anyone. A human review sits between building a campaign and launching it, and people can reply or opt out in between.
43. Read at least 20 sequences in review before you flip send mode to live.

Testing and learning (44-50)

44. Build a small golden set with the traps in it: a recruiter at a hot account, a competitor, a company stacking press releases. On our Jev starter set the ranker gets 10 of 10, the offline baseline gets 7.
45. Write tests for the routing too. Someone who already replied should never land in a new sequence, whatever the model thinks.
46. Make the reason a required field in the outcome log. A bare "no reply" teaches the next run almost nothing.
47. Leave the weights alone until each bucket has 30 real contacts. After its first run our Opus bot called its 15 simulated outcomes "not evidence". Fair.
48. Cap how far a weight can move in a day, and give every signal a floor so the rare ones don't get buried.
49. Route a few leads below your line to a one-touch lane. If the bot only ever contacts the top, you never find out the line is in the wrong place.
50. Change one thing per round. Our Codex build proposes one change at a time as a pull request, and a human merges it.

In the article I walk through a real job post. It's a company hiring its first outbound rep to work on account selection and the prospecting playbook.

If you sell outbound consulting, that looks like the perfect reason to reach out. It may also be the best reason they won't need you. They're hiring someone to build it in-house.

So my call was HOLD, until I'd checked who owns that decision and whether the job post is still current.

The prompts ask for that kind of objection up front. Run them in order, each one feeds the next:

1. The signal brief
Give it your offer, who it's for, who usually buys and who's a bad fit.
It comes back with:
- three changes you can verify
- the decision the company may now face
- the strongest reason your offer might not be needed
It isn't allowed to guess budget or urgency from an event.

2. The search plan
It turns the brief into search phrases and the original pages to open.
For every candidate, save the URL, the exact excerpt, when it happened and when you checked.
A search snippet never counts as proof.

3. The account brief
One account at a time. It gives you:
- facts, each tied to a source
- the decision they might be facing

Most bad AI outbound comes from one thing: the model can't see what you know.

I turned Claude into a prospecting analyst with five prompts (in the article below). Here's what we learned to tell it, so the emails come out right.

If it makes things up:

1. Give it the actual page, the job post, the funding announcement. Don't let it work from a search snippet. That's where the congratulations email for a round nobody raised comes from.

2. Ask it to put the source next to every fact. If it can't point to one, delete the fact.

3. Keep two dates on every fact: when it happened, and when you found it. A page you found this morning can be about last spring.

The job post in the article had no date at all, so part of the hold was checking the role was still open.

4. Tell it what it's not allowed to guess. Ours can't guess budget, urgency or whether someone is ready to buy from a single event. A funding round that says nothing about sales is a weak reason to pitch sales.

If every email could go to anyone

5. Give it the reason you'd matter to them this week. Twenty cold emails a day can name the city I posted from. Not one of them knows if I have a problem.

6. Be exact. Which role they reposted, how much they raised, what the tender actually says. "They fit our ICP" gives it nothing to write with.

7. A test I like: cut the line about what you found and read the email again. If it still sounds like a decent email, send it. If it falls apart, that one line was doing all the work.

8. Keep a short list of things it may never write, next to the instructions. A model can follow every tone instruction and still write the exact email buyers delete on sight.

Ours started as four lines: no buzzwords, no em dashes, no fake urgency or "circling back", no "Hi {{firstName}}". It's longer now, and it does more than the instructions do.

If it pitches the wrong person

9. The person in the news isn't always the person who buys. A company posts its first SDR role. The person they hire is nobody to you.

Whoever runs the sales team is probably who you want, and even that stays a guess until someone has checked. Never let it make up a name.

10. Ask it to make the case against the lead in the same answer. A company hiring its first outbound rep looks like the perfect lead for outbound consulting.

It's also a company that just decided to build it in-house. My call on that one was hold.

If it opens with what it found

11. "Saw you raised your Series B" tells them a tool found it. Counting their pricing-page visits out loud is worse. What you found sets the timing and the topic. The first line is about something they did in public.

If it says yes to everyone

12. Let it say "not yet". Ours says hold when the fit looks right but something still needs checking, and nothing goes out until a person has checked it. A reason to stop is a useful answer.

13. Keep the first email small. 70 words at most: one thing you can back up, one thing you can actually send, one simple question. If what you're sending is a blank template, call it a template.

If it never gets better

14. Log the reason behind every no, in one line. "Wrong quarter" is a date to come back. "Already with a competitor" is a different angle later. "Not the buyer" is a contact to fix. Same word, three different next moves.

15. When the answer is wrong, change what it can see before you rewrite the instruction. Anthropic's own prompting video gets Claude from a wrong insurance ruling to the right one without really touching the instruction. Most bad answers are missing a fact.

Our first paid ads campaign at @heyreach_io hit 20x ROAS. Profitable from day one. I'd love to tell you the ads were genius. They weren't. Let me back up, because this is the most expensive lesson I've got, and I learned it by NOT doing something.

At a previous startup I had everything I needed to run paid. Organic was humming, funnels built right, growing 10-15% MoM. And I never put ads on top of it. Told myself organic was enough and left it there.

Organic was fine. That's not what eats at me. It's the ceiling I never tested. The campaign I never ran.

So at @heyreach_io I made a rule out of it. Roughly:

→ 2/3 of my time and budget on the compounders. Word-of-mouth, content, organic funnels. The foundation. Slow as hell, takes a year before it shows you a clean number, still our #1 channel and I'll love it forever.

→ 1/3 on the fast layer. Ads, retargeting. The stuff that pays back this month.

And most people get the order backwards. It matters more than the budget does.

The instinct is to reach for the fast channel first, because it's measurable and it feels like progress. Money into ads before there's anything underneath worth amplifying. That's a jetpack on a parked car. You don't get speed... it's just an expensive fire.

So I ran it the other way. Didn't touch ads until WoM and the retargeting funnels were actually built, then turned them on. That sequencing is the only reason 20x was even on the table. (And yeah, I'm still just playing with paid, my crew does the technical lifting. But the numbers are the numbers.)

It's worth noting that these ads didn't create that momentum in the first place. They just multiplied what was already there.

Last one, because I see it everywhere: channels run in silos.

Someone clicks your ad and bounces. Someone starts a trial and stalls. You write it off as a dead lead. It's not dead. It's your two layers refusing to talk to each other. Organic feeds paid, paid feeds organic, or you leave most of the compounding on the floor.

The order I run now: foundation first, fast layer bolted on top, the two wired together so nothing falls through the gap.

I'll forever be an organic guy. My one real marketing regret was never the ads I ran.

It's the ones I didn't 🫡

I spent years stuck in the "personalization vs automation" debate. Deep custom research on one side, automation at scale on the other, both camps convinced their way books more meetings.

Wrong question. Both work. I've gotten results from slow, hand-written outreach, and I'm seeing wild results from heavy automation across the @heyreach_io universe right now.

The only thing that actually decides whether you get a reply is relevance. And relevance isn't something you write. It's something you prepare, before you type a single word.

I got this badly wrong early on. I ran marketing for a moving-industry startup and never once sat down with actual movers, even when my boss basically begged me to. The work got results, but it always felt like accidental basketball, points on the board without really knowing why. I was guessing at a world I hadn't bothered to understand. Never again.

Now the prep is the job. What I figure out before writing anything:

→ Their pain today. Name the problem they're living with right now and show I can fix it. That's a meeting.

→ What they want next. Know where they're trying to go and prove I help them get there. That's a meeting.

→ Signal orchestration: mixing 1st party and 3rd party signals, sending warm leads to sales

Nail those three and the message almost doesn't matter. Which is the funny part, because the stuff people argue about endlessly is the stuff that barely matters:

→ Deep vs light personalization

→ Short vs long messages

→ Automation vs human-in-the-loop

Pick whatever fits you. None of it saves a message that wasn't relevant to begin with.

That's the whole system. Relevance, built in the prep, before a single line of copy. Everything else is just your signature.

Between zero and $15M ARR we (@heyreach_io) walked into 6 death traps that could've ended us. Almost none of the fixes were clever. Most were slow, expensive, and boring. Here's each one and what actually pulled us out.

1. The support apocalypse

Turns out when a lot of people use your product, they expect it to work. We were drowning in tickets, response time was glacial, and you could watch the brand bleed in the reviews in real time.

No tool fixed this. We hired Ebru, handed her full control, and she dragged CS from "please hold while I cry" to "solved before your coffee's cold." The fix was a person with real ownership and the authority to change things.

2. The infrastructure meltdown

Our servers handled traffic about as well as I handle spicy food. Badly. This one took two full quarters, and the bill was brutal: we killed basically every cool feature on the roadmap to pay for it. Senior devs in, shiny stuff out. All hail Stefan and the dev team.

3. The churn wave

Late 2024, churn spiked and we genuinely didn't know why (nothing like a new year's surprise that isn't the fun kind). On marketing's side I owned the leaks: a proper cancellation flow, instant notifications, counter-offers, and finally going after the involuntary churn we'd just been eating. The revenue side took prevention, breaking it down by ICP tier with retention plays per segment. No single fix did it. It took about ten small ones.

4. The PLG mess

We somehow built a $15M business on an onboarding experience that was, roughly, "here's the login, good luck, we believe in you." I didn't ship a real onboarding flow until the end of Q2 2025. The only reason it didn't bury us is the product is genuinely simple and the success team is fast. And honestly? PLG is getting better now, but we can still do so much more

5. Shiny object syndrome

We said no to so many exciting distractions that I sometimes wake up at night just to say no to ideas in my own head. You would not believe how many features, deadlines, and marketing channels we sacrificed to hold the pace. Focus isn't sexy. But neither is bankruptcy.

6. Duplicated effort

At $10M+ ARR, you take on more projects and hire more people. If your cross-department comms don't level up, you'll end up with teams working in isolation. This leads to wasted energy, duplicated effort, extra costs, and competitors catching up. The fix isn't another all-hands. It's a system where 5 players score 5 points each instead of 1 player scoring 25. One wins championships. The other ends the season early.

The pattern across all of it: every fix that saved us was slow, unglamorous, and cost us something we actually wanted to build. Growth rarely dies from the exciting problems.

It dies from the boring ones you keep putting off.

I joined @heyreach_io with one dream: make word of mouth and growth loops run like a single machine. Today WoM is our strongest channel and ~90% of revenue is inbound. Here are the 5 loops that got us there, brick by brick.

Loop 1: engage every single mention

We made one rule. Every time someone mentions HeyReach on LinkedIn, we're in the comments. Not with "thanks 🙏", with a genuine reply. The data backs it: if you engage, that person is 3x more likely to mention you again, and you pick up followers and traffic for free. Most companies let mentions just sit there.

We treat every one as the start of a loop.

Loop 2: put your users in the spotlight, not your logo

Every piece of content we ship features a user, not us. Their playbook, their results, their face. They get the visibility, we get an organic ambassador who now has a reason to share it. Win-win isn't a buzzword here, it's literally our content operating system.

Loop 3: build a product people actually want to talk about

This is the foundation, and there's no hack under it. If people genuinely win with your product, they talk about it on their own. No campaign required. Everything below is just amplification, and if loop 1 isn't true, none of the others save you.

Loop 4: build personal brands inside the company

We have 10 people actively posting and building their own brands, with an internal competition (and rewards) to keep it fun and a little ruthless. One person posting is 1x reach. Ten people posting is a distribution network you don't have to rent.

Loop 5: rethink the influencer program entirely

The standard "you post, we pay" deal was never going to cut it. We built expert and creator programs around long-term collaboration with proven GTM operators, people who actually use the thing. Buying shoutouts is faster. This compounds.

Then I pour ads and inbound-led outbound on top, because all five loops throw off a mountain of content and a warm audience that already knows us. That's the machine.

And let's be clear, none of this is a solo act. Every loop is the team.

I treat content like leftover chicken.

Cook it once and eat off it all week. Sure, you could cook a brand-new meal every day instead. One post, served once, gone by morning. (That's also the quickest way to start calling content a hamster wheel.)

One good piece molded right has endless uses. Sandwiches today, tacos tomorrow, soup on Friday. And if you keep adding layers that same piece eventually turns into a funnel.

This is how I carve it.

Start with one meaty source, like a recorded breakdown or a user's campaign torn apart step by step. That's the whole chicken, and everything else comes off it:

→ the long-form article or video, which is the full thing start to finish

→ native clips and a thread, pulling the sharpest three or four moments out to stand on their own

→ standalone tweets, quotes, and an infographic, the bits most people never bother to reuse even though they quietly pull their own reach

One source, and you've got a week of content for a fraction of the effort.

The thing that turns repurposing into an actual system is making each piece do more than one job. My best content works for acquisition, onboarding, and retention at the same time. The breakdown that pulls in a cold prospect is the exact same one your team sends to a trial that stalled.

Then you add a small layer every time it ships, a CTA or a link to the next piece or a lead magnet at the end, until that one chicken stops being a meal and becomes a funnel.

None of this is about being clever. Organic only gets efficient when one unit of work produces ten outputs, and cooking something fresh every single day is how teams burn out and quit three months in, right before content starts to compound.

So stop shipping a piece and walking away. Cook one great thing and eat off it all week.

Your distribution has an off switch. It's you.

Go quiet for a month and the whole thing cools with you: newsletter, SEO, YouTube, personal brands. That's rented distribution, and almost everyone is renting.

There's another kind. The kind that keeps moving when you don't, because other people are doing the pushing. For us that's word of mouth, our strongest channel and the reason ~90% of our revenue is inbound.

And it comes down to two channels almost nobody builds properly:

1. Users sharing your stuff, without being asked
2. Partners spreading the word, and actually meaning it

Here's how you build them, because "be remarkable and they'll talk" isn't a plan.

Channel 1: users sharing on their own

Three things, in order:

→ Build a product people genuinely win with: No shortcut under this one. If they don't win, nothing below matters.

→ Put the user in the spotlight. Every piece of content we ship is about the user crushing it: their playbook, their results, their face. They share it because it makes them look good. We just get an ambassador out of it.

→ Engage every single mention. Everytime someone names drops us. Our whole team is in the comments + the data proves that person is 3x more likely to mention you again. Most teams let mentions sit there and then wonder why WoM "isn't working."

Channel 2: partners who actually mean it

The standard influencer model is "you post, we pay." That's rented enthusiasm, and everyone can tell.

We built it the opposite way: long-term collaborations with proven operators who actually use the product:

- Expert and creator programs
- Integrations
- Co-marketing

The kind of partnership where they promote you because they'd recommend you anyway. Pay-to-post spikes and dies, this compounds. Because you can feel the enthusiasm and it keeps going long after the invoice clears.

The whole point:

The channels everyone obsesses over are distribution you rent. You push, it moves, you stop, it stops. Most teams pour everything into what they rent, then act surprised when growth stalls the second they ease off

For 2 years, every marketing win I got felt like an accident. Turns out it was.

I'd been marketing a product without ever really understanding the people I was selling to.

I started as a copywriter at a US startup, and within 3 months I'd become the "marketing chameleon", a generous way of saying "the guy who says yes to everything because he doesn't know any better."

I learned just enough about the moving industry to ship what was needed. That should've terrified me. It didn't, because it worked. My stuff brought results. For 2+ years I was net positive for them on paper.

But every project took twice as long and went through three rounds of feedback, because I was always half-guessing. Kobe had a name for winning without knowing why: accidental basketball.

That was me. Every result felt like it could fall apart any second, because I was building on guesses.

I could've blamed the setup. We had no marketing leader, just 5 C-level execs throwing tasks at me from every direction. We even talked about me spending a few days riding along with real movers.

I wasn't persistent enough. I could've emailed customers to hop on calls. I could've researched 10X harder. I didn't, mostly because I wasn't passionate about the industry, partly because I wasn't disciplined enough to push past that.

So I made myself one promise: never again.

Everything in marketing starts and ends with how well you understand the person you're selling to. Funnels, copy, ads, all of it sits downstream of that. Get it wrong and you can still grind out results, but they'll always feel like accidental basketball.

These days I go full Sherlock Holmes on every industry I touch. Minus the pipe and the hat

The marketing playbook that gets a SaaS to $1M is usually the same thing that stalls it at $2M.

I've taken two companies past $10M ARR (plus my own agency to six figures in year one), and it broke in the exact same two spots every time. Around $1M. Again around $2M.

What has to change at each break:

$0 → $2M (survival mode):

→ Marketers wear every hat, no specialists yet

→ Lead with the one feature nobody else has

→ Go global from day one

→ Pick one or two battles that win the war and ignore the rest

→ Stay off paid ads until PMF is confirmed

→ Run sprints, not marathons

$2M → $10M (build the machine):

→ Hire T-shaped marketers full-time

→ Get the motion off the founder's back

→ Run pricing experiments often, even when it's scary

→ Layer paid ads on top of organic proof, never in place of it

→ Widen the ICP only when the data tells you to

What people call "the SaaS playbook" is really two playbooks pretending to be one. The teams that stall are running the first one long after it stopped working.

When I joined @heyreach_io, it was doing $15K MRR. today we crossed $16M ARR. Here's the growth and distribution playbook that got us there:

1. Distribution is 51% of the game. Great content nobody sees is just an expensive diary, so from day one we put as much work into getting @heyreach_io seen as into what we made.

2. We engineered word of mouth like a channel.

Year one we went from $15K MRR to $2M with zero paid, on word of mouth and content alone. We built a product people talk about, engaged every single mention, and put 10 of us on personal brands to compete for reach.

The loop only spins if someone feeds it every day.

3. AI beat everything else we ran this year.

We leaned in hard, from shipping HeyReach MCP, the first in LinkedIn outreach, to running AI across how we plan, build, and distribute content.

4. Our biggest lever was already inside the funnel.

We stopped leaving pipeline on the table by giving every lead tier an owner. Self-serve handles the ones who want to move on their own, and marketing, sales, and success each cover the tiers that need a human.

We enriched and scored the 2,500 to 3,000 trials we get a month with Clay so each one reached the right hands. That took free-trial to paid from 9% to over 26%.

5. Fast growth hid everything we'd skipped.

Support drowned before we staffed it properly, the servers buckled and took two quarters to rebuild, and we ran a $7M business on onboarding that was basically "here's your login, good luck."

We paid for all of it later, with interest.

6. Paid ads came last, on purpose.

We only turned them on at $7M ARR, once word of mouth and retargeting funnels could feed them. The first campaign was profitable from day one, and waiting that long to start is my one real regret.

We closed 2025 at $10M ARR and around 90% inbound. $13M in March, $16M today. The next number on the wall is $22M by December, carried the whole way by a lot of people I was lucky to have.

There's one thing I check before deciding to work with a marketer a second time: do they own the outcome, or just their slice of it?

Most of the ones I don't bring back are genuinely good. A few are T-shaped, real range across paid, content, and brand, fluent in the revenue number too. That range is rare and I value it.

But ownership is much more rare, and it's the actual reason someone earns a second project with me. After enough hires, it shows up as four behaviors:

→ They run the channel end to end. None of that "I wrote the brief and handed it off" energy.

→ When something breaks, they've usually started fixing it by the time they tell me. No tidy explanation of why it broke.

→ A missed target lands on them personally. They chase down why it happened instead of logging it and moving on.

→ They know exactly how their channel feeds the other three in the stack, and they build with that in mind.

A skilled marketer without it just produces really polished reasons things didn't work.

Ownership doesn't show up on a resume, and it barely correlates with talent. You see it the first time something goes wrong.

I held myself to this standard for years before I ever held a team to it.

I don't believe in marketing vs sales attribution.

I've got nothing against tracking. My problem is how much time gets burned fighting over it.

Marketing and sales arguing over who gets credit for a deal is the most expensive meeting in the building, and it moves revenue by exactly $0.

At HeyReach I stopped asking who touched the deal. Here's what I run through at every pipeline review instead:

→ Did they close?

→ What's the real revenue impact?

→ Are they winning with the product, or just paying for it?

→ Who's the next lead exactly like them, and how do we run that motion again?

Not one of those needs a credit fight to answer. They keep the whole team staring at the only number that pays the bills, and they let us repeat what's working instead of debating who gets the trophy.

Revenue is the score. Attribution is an internal sport.

After building marketing teams at two $10M+ startups, here is my system to hire top-tier social media managers:

I like to ask them six questions.

These questions separate talk from execution faster than any interview does, because none of them can be answered with a vibe. Each one asks for a concrete proof of work:

1. Your own profile. When did you last actually touch it?

2. You missed the target. What's your next move, and are you taking it personally or just filing it away?

3. Last book, podcast, or event you genuinely geeked out on? What did you take from it?

4. That brilliant idea from two weeks ago. Where is it now?

5. Show me three brands crushing it on social right now. Why are they winning?

6. You posted on the company page. Did you engage with it? Did you pull the team in? Or is it just us liking us?

Last quarter we went back through the system behind 1.19M LinkedIn replies. 26% average reply rate. What separated closed deals from dead threads came down to one thing:

How fast we replied once someone wrote back.

A LinkedIn reply has a shelf life of minutes. People reply from their phone, mid-scroll, in a small window where you're the thing they're thinking about. Get to it the next morning and you're a stranger interrupting them again.

And that points at a trap most outbound teams walk into: past a certain point, more replies work against you.

Open warm conversations faster than you can service them and every reply that sits for a day cools into a cold lead. It's demand you paid to manufacture and then can't catch.

So we treat response speed as a real metric, not reply volume:

→ One inbox for every reply, across every sender (we run ours in HeyReach's unibox so nothing dies in a stack of tabs)

→ A clean CRM, no duplicate campaigns firing at the same person, because a duplicate means two reps answer or nobody does

→ One person owning reply velocity

→ A same-day SLA on Tier 1 replies, triaged, no exceptions

Most teams optimize the message right up until the reply lands, then go quiet. The reply is the moment the deal actually goes live. That's the part worth obsessing over.

We shipped this at HeyReach (our MCP, CLI, and powerful API that lets you run outreach straight from Claude, Cursor, or any LLM). But the shift is bigger than any one tool: the campaign builder is turning into a chat box you talk to.

If you run outbound, this is the year your dashboard starts to disappear.

I've helped scale two SaaS tools past $10M ARR. Neither had the biggest ad budget in its category. Both won on distribution. This how you should get a product in front of people:

1. Stop picking a channel. Build a loop into the product instead. The tools that scale have marketing baked into how they work: a branded output, a referral moment, a result worth screenshotting.

2. People are your best distribution: People prefer following operators more than company logos. A founder or team member posting will out-distribute your polished brand account by a mile.

3. Bet on channels that compound: Paid ads stop the day you stop paying. Content, community, and word of mouth keep paying you back for years.

4. Repost your winners: Your best idea, posted once, is money left on the table. Run it again with a fresh angle every few weeks.

5. Favorite move: make your customers the distributors. Turn their wins into content where they're the hero. They share it to a network you could never buy your way into.

The best product rarely wins. The best-distributed one does. I've watched it happen twice.

Your lead list quality is set in 4 decisions you make before the campaign launches. Get them right and everything downstream works better.

Step 1: Choose your source based on relationship proximity.

Warmer sources like post reactors and event attendees accept far more than a cold Sales Nav pull. The source sets your acceptance ceiling before you write a word.

Step 2: Clean your list before it touches a campaign.

Warm lists import raw, with no title filter, so every off-ICP reactor comes in with the rest. Cut them by title and company fit first.

Step 3: Remove the wrong leads before launch.

Exclude your existing clients, anyone you've already contacted elsewhere, and your 1st-degree connections from cold sequences.

Step 4: Stop running warm and cold leads through the same sequence.

Split the list by connection status. People you're already connected to get a direct message, everyone else gets a connection request.

- Skip Step 1 and you're targeting the wrong people.
- Skip Step 2 and bad-fit leads enter the campaign.
- Skip Step 3 and someone gets contacted who never should have.
- Skip Step 4 and warm audiences get cold outreach logic.

Get the list right and the message barely has to work. Get it wrong and no copy saves you.

4 things that make the your LinkedIn A/B tests meaningless :

1. You ran the versions as two separate campaigns: LinkedIn caps sends per sender account, so delivery is uneven. The campaign that launched first gets sent more. Campaign A didn't win because of the copy. It won because it launched first.

2. You changed more than one thing: New opener, new CTA, new ICP filter, all at once. When the number moves, you can't tell which change did it.

3. You edited mid-flight: Day 2, replies look low, so you tweak the opener. Now half your data is one message and half is another. The test is dead.

4. You read it too early: Checking before you have enough data and acting on it splits the pool, the same way a mid-flight edit does.

The fix: run your variations in one campaign, change one thing at a time, and don't read the result until you have at least 100 leads per version.

If you can't trust the test, you're just guessing with extra steps.

This is the best growth advice I've heard all week. And it's something we have been implementing consistently at HeyReach to make word of mouth our #1 channel past $16M ARR in 3 years.

Lovable's Head of Growth on how they hit $200M ARR in 12 months with 100 people: "The only way to create a word of mouth loop is to blow their socks off."

She's right. And having done this at a bootstrapped company, this is what I think: the socks-off moment is step zero. The loop is what you build on top of it.

The exact 5-step system we used at HeyReach:

1. Put the user in the spotlight
Every case study, post, and screenshot celebrates the operator winning. A screenshot of someone's own reply rate travels further than anything with our branding on it.

2. Engage every single mention
A user who gets a real reply from the team is ~3x more likely to mention you again. This one needs zero budget, just someone who owns it every day.

3. Give the playbooks away
Templates, teardowns, real numbers, free. The product gets mentioned because it sits inside the workflow people are copying.

4. Amplify only what's proven
We never guess what to promote. If a piece already resonated organically, that's the one that gets ad budget behind it.

5. Treat mentions as sales signals
Who mentioned us, which segment they're in, what triggered it. That feed goes straight to the sales team, and it books meetings.

I was always against the notion of one person owning the distribution channel and this study by @emilykramer proves it.

This is a study of 100 B2B companies: under $100M raised, 60% of founders have more followers than their own company page. And it's one founder carrying it. The second and third add about 17% between them.

So the entire channel sits on one guy's calendar.

We run 10 of us at @heyreach_io , each building their own audience, competing with each other internally.

5 players scoring ten goals each beats one player scoring fifty. The one-man team looks unstoppable right until they get marked.

I once joined a cold email tool closing in on $250K ARR as a head of growth with a blog nobody read. We put around 80% of our time into producing content and almost none into getting it seen.

My first articles all tanked, apart from one content catergory: cold email templates

Last month, @randfish pushed the numbers on why that split is now fatal.

68% of Google searches end without a click, up from 45% ten years ago. AI Overviews sit on more than 20% of searches and cut clickthrough by almost 60% when they show.

SEO on its own doesn't cut it anymore. It still matters, it just stopped being a traffic channel.

This how I run it now:

1. Treat content like leftover chicken. One real piece gets molded into posts, clips, replies and emails.

2. Every piece has to sell the product. If it doesn't, I don't ship it. That's fishing with gourmet bait instead of grabbing at fish with my bare hands.

3. Distribution runs through people, not through domain. 10 of us build our own audiences with internal competition.

It had led @heyreach_io  to $10M ARR with zero paid ads, around 90% of revenue inbound. Now it's at $16M ARR.

I've taken two outbound tools past $10M ARR and I still could not have told you what a normal LinkedIn campaign looks like. Nobody publishes it.

You get guru screenshots and cherry-picked case studies, so there's no comparison bar.

So we went through nearly 100k campaigns that ran through @heyreach_io, and published the whole thing for free.

What you get out of it:

1. Ten minutes with your last three campaigns and you'll know exactly where you sit against 96,051 others. Weak, typical or strong, on each of the three numbers that decide a quarter.

2. You'll find the stage that's leaking instead of guessing at it. Four checkpoints in order, and the first range you fall under is the only thing worth touching this month. Everything downstream of it is wasted effort.

3. If the opener really is the problem, there's a Claude prompt that takes yours, hands back three versions, and shows you why the current one keeps getting archived.

4. You'll get the cheapest fix in the whole report. One agency in the dataset messages every new connection within 3 hours of acceptance, they run a 26% positive reply rate.

5. You'll walk out with a Q3 order of operations. What to fix this week, what to close out by end of August, so September is only scaling.

The line from it I keep coming back to: hitting the median isn't a win, it just means you stopped losing.

Comment LEAK and I'll send it over (follow me first, otherwise the DM doesn't go through 😇)

I can buy the exact same list as my competitor, from the same vendor, on the same afternoon. That stopped being an edge a long time ago.

@jjen_abel goes further than me here. She won't  touch an outreach tool at all.

She's right about the databases. Where I'd push back is on manual being
the reason it works.

Her signals can't be bought. No vendor sells a list of people who just did something that makes them ready for you. Jen finds those people by hand. We built a system for it.

We look for three things before anyone sends a message:

1. The account is a real tier one fit for us, judged properly and not by a job title filter.

2. Someone from that account visited our site. That signal exists nowhere except our own data.

3. They engaged with our content, so there's a reason to be in their inbox before we ever arrive.

When the three line up, the message writes itself.

I've been doing cold outreach since 2019 and I've watched the personalized first line go from an edge to a cost.

It worked for a while.

Then every tool shipped it as a feature, and now it's the thing that tells someone a machine wrote the message.

 @jjen_abel’s fix is to cut the opener everyone expects and personalize the subject line or the framing instead.

Our own numbers back her up on LinkedIn too. Blank connection requests get accepted 27% of the time and personalized ones get 22%. The note costs you five points at the door.

It pays off later though.

Once someone accepts, a short specific line about why you reached out gets you a lot more replies.

So I skip it on the request and put the effort into the message that comes after.

The test on that message is whether software could have produced it without knowing anything true about the person. If it could, it's costing you.

Timing decides far more of this than copy ever does now.

We got HeyReach to $10M ARR without spending a cent on paid ads. Then our first campaign did 20x ROAS, profitable from day one.

First try. And we weren’t any expert at ads, because we'd never run one.

What was different is that word of mouth and retargeting funnels were finally built underneath, so the spend had somewhere to land. Five months in: $21,404 spent, 24.9x ROAS.

A basketball is worth about $0 in my hands and millions in Steph Curry's. Nobody blames the ball. The value was always in everything around it.

@poyark did a study of 195 companies here, and the winning motion keeps moving depending on where you're standing.

The one thing I'd take from it: a channel can be early or late for you, but never dead. Most people who buried one were running it at the wrong time.

The best argument I have heard against my own job came from Shopify's head of growth.

They do not have a CMO and it's a deliberate choice:

- Brand marketing sits with their president
- Growth marketing sits inside the growth org,
- Revenue marketing sits near sales
- Product marketing sits with the PMs.

Our setup is not far off. We run 12 channels and initiatives at HeyReach and 10 people on the team are building their own personal brands. Almost none of that is me, and it works better for it.

Whoever sits closest to a channel runs it better than I would. The campaign approvals, the channel decisions, the content calendar, none of that runs through me anymore.

What is left is much smaller than the title suggests.

For me it is ads.

We got to $10M ARR without running a single one. I run them now and the first campaign came back at 20x, so this was never about ads being a bad channel.

But for two years the answer to "should we try paid yet" stayed no, while the team grew and the pressure to try it grew with it.

So everything my team does can belong to whoever is closest to it. But one person has to hold a no and take the blame in public when it turns out wrong.

I don't buy the 3-reasons version of what happened to AI SDR.

The first two are consequences of the third, and keeping them separate is how the category gets to blame the tooling instead of the strategy.

AI runs the strategy that was already sitting there, faster, and everything a human used to fix in their head before hitting send went out as written.

I've been in outbound since 2019. The teams who got value out of these tools had already done the unglamorous work of deciding who they were for.

Buying the tool first and hoping it would decide for you was always going to hand back your own vagueness, at volume.

Our rule at HeyReach is three signals before a campaign goes out:
- Tier one ICP
- Visited the site
- Engaged with something we published.

When all three land on the same person, 100 messages a week turns into eight or nine real conversations. When they don't line up, no amount of copy rescues it.

Our users have averaged 26% reply rates in Q1 across 1.19 million replies.

This is where I stop. LinkedIn is the one channel where more output makes you worse at it.

Everywhere else volume is an asset. Here every account has a finite amount of goodwill and each request spends some. Acceptance rate is the meter on it. Send generic at scale, acceptance falls.

LinkedIn lowers your ceiling, and next month you're allowed to send less than you could this month.

So an agent that raises output per account is spending the budget faster and putting "scale" on the invoice.

The only AI worth pointing at LinkedIn is AI that raises acceptance rate.

Fewer requests -> more of them accepted ->ceiling goes up instead of down.

Nobody builds that because it demos badly. "We helped you send 40% fewer messages" is a rough slide to put in front of a VP.

text:
If you run LinkedIn outreach, you are almost certainly guessing whether your numbers are any good. Guru screenshots and cherry picked case studies are not a benchmark.

So we built one. 96,051 campaigns, twelve months, and here is the entire scoreboard (in the article below)

Score your last three campaigns against it in about a minute:

1. Acceptance rate, accepted divided by requests sent: under 13% weak, 21% typical, over 32% strong.

2. Reply rate, replies divided by conversations started: under 13% weak, 22% typical, over 33% strong.

3. Reply to acceptance, replies divided by accepted connections: under 10% weak, 18% typical, over 29% strong.

Score them in that order and stop at the first one you fall below. That is your leak, and everything downstream of it stays wasted effort until you close it.

Both of the first two under 13% and the list is wrong, so no opener rescues it. Acceptance healthy with replies weak and they let you in, then your first message lost them.

Almost nobody calculates that third one. It decides your quarter and I have never seen it on a dashboard. 10.7% of the campaigns that got connections accepted never got a single reply back.

I think integrations are one of the most underrated distribution channels in SaaS.

We've got 31 of them and I count every one as distribution.

Because every one of them puts us inside a workflow somebody else is paying to grow. Someone's already living in Clay or n8n. They hit the point where they need LinkedIn, and we're just sitting there.

Clay, HubSpot, n8n, Make, Instantly, Smartlead, Zapier, Trigify, RB2B, and a bunch more after that. Some we built, some the platforms met us halfway on.

Most of your distribution has an off switch and the switch is you or your team. Go quiet for a month and it all cools with you. The newsletter, the content, the ten of us posting.

Content nobody distributes dies in 48 hours. Ads stop the day you stop paying.

An integration doesn't have that switch. It sits in someone else's docs and keeps working while nobody on my team thinks about it.

I've helped take two bootstrapped SaaS tools past $10M ARR, and at @heyreach_io (past $17M ARR now) I handle all things growth. 

Here's how I'd rebuild our entire distribution engine if I started from zero tomorrow:

1. Fix what the traffic lands on before scaling the traffic

Our onboarding was "here's the login, good luck, we believe in you." 9 of every 100 trials paid. Fixing that took conversion past 26% and moved more revenue than any campaign I've run. The test: if traffic doubled tomorrow, would the business be better or just busier? Answer that before you spend anything.

2. Put the audience on people instead of the logo

10 people on our team build their own brands, with names and opinions I don't approve first. The company page posts into the void and we made peace with that. Emily Kramer's data says at companies under $100M, 60% of founders out-follow their own company page.

3. Build word of mouth on purpose

Engaging a mention makes that person ~3x more likely to mention you again. That runs while I'm on holiday, which is the only test I trust. Reach is rented. A loop compounds. Word of mouth is our strongest channel now and ~90% of revenue is inbound.

4. Reach out to people who already know you exist

Cold first touch gets more expensive every year. We stack three signals (tier-1 ICP, visited the site, engaged with something we published) and only then reach out. The message writes itself because there's a reason to be talking.

5. Be findable by machines too

A third of search happens inside AI answers now, by Kyle Poyar's count. Make sure the model has something accurate to say about you, and let agents use the product directly. We shipped our MCP early. No clean attribution yet: I'm telling you what we did, not what it returned.

6. Run paid last

Our first campaign hit 20x ROAS, profitable from day one, and the ads weren't genius. They worked because word of mouth and retargeting funnels already existed underneath. The same ads at $2M ARR would have burned the money and taught me nothing.

7. Say no to almost everything else

AI made every new channel cheap enough to try, and that is the trap. Each yes eats attention, mine and the team's. So before adding one, I ask a single question: what does this stop us finishing?

Making your outreach "cold" is a choice in 2026.

Prospects give off buying signals all day: they visit your pricing page, stall in a free trial, engage with your ads, comment on your team's posts. And what does the average team do with all that? Nothing. Buys a list and blasts 1,000 strangers.

Here's a flow you can copy instead. All it needs is a signal source or two and one place to collect them:

1. Tier your accounts. Have a person make the fit call, job-title filters get it wrong all the time.

2. Pull every signal into one view: site visits, ad engagement, LinkedIn engagement on your team's content, trial activity. Scattered in 5 tools this data is useless. In one view it's a work queue.

3. Don't reach out on one signal. A lone site visit could be a student or a competitor. 2-3 signals on the same person = real intent. That account goes to the front.

4. Enrich with Clay, let an AI agent make the first qualification pass. The team only sees a short list, already sorted.

5. Write the message about the signal. Trial stalled at the integration step? The message is about the integration step, nothing else.

6. Route warm replies straight to sales while the signal is fresh. Everyone else stays in retargeting until a second signal lands.

We run a version of this at HeyReach. We crossed $10M ARR before we ever spent a dollar on ads.

The math for one LinkedIn sender: 100 messages a week, roughly the platform's cap, at 26% replies (our users' Q1 average) = 8-9 real conversations = 2-3 customers a week.

Run it for a month and see how much of your list was never cold to begin with.

article_title: How to engineer word of mouth: the 6-loop playbook behind $17M ARR

text:
2,500 to 3,000 people start a free trial with us every month. ~90% of our revenue is inbound.

It took us ~3 years to build the word of mouth machine behind those numbers, and I broke down the whole system and how we built the WoM loops along the way.

First, I'd like to define what I mean by "loop", because the word gets thrown around a lot.

Someone likes your product, tells a friend, that's word of mouth. Great, but also unrepeatable.

A loop means you build something around that moment so it creates the next one.

So we created six of them:

Loop 1: a product people actually talk about. When growth slows we audit the product before any channel. It's usually the problem. Marketing teams hate that answer (me included).

Loop 2: engage every single mention. One owner, every day, small accounts too. Our data says an engaged mention is ~3x more likely to mention you again. Cheapest loop on the list, and the one I'd ship first if we started over.

Loop 3: put users in the spotlight. We take a real operator's campaign, tear it apart, publish the playbook. That's Outbound Outliers (named after Commissaire Gilbert from the Taxi movies. Watch Taxi). The story is about them winning, we're just the tool in the screenshots. They share it, their audience steals it, some of those readers become the next teardown.

Loop 4: 10 teammates building their own audiences. People trust people, a logo account never reaches that far. Plus there's no off switch on 10 people.

Loop 5: creators on long-term deals. Pay-per-post gets forgotten in a week. These still pull months later.

Loop 6: inbound-led outbound. Everything above gathers warm people around us. Site visit + trial activity + ad engagement = our team reaches out while it's fresh, and the message opens with whatever the person did.

Ads came dead last, once all of this was already running.

The full system below (bookmark for later):

If you're running ads or outbound and your pipeline still feels stuck, you might want to hear me out.

Running ads, content, and outbound as three separate machines is the most common mistake that prevents you from growing your pipeline.

Combine all of them and run them as a single motion, and you can see a noticeable pipeline lift. And wiring them together is simpler than it sounds:

1. Stop ignoring everybody who didn't buy.

Someone clicks your ad and doesn't convert, and most teams write that off as a wasted impression, when the person was interested enough to click in the first place.

Same goes for somebody who stalls halfway through a trial, or spends two weeks liking everything your team posts. All of them go on one list.

2. Then go through that list.

You could run it through AI agents the way we do, or if you're small enough you could simply read the list yourself every Friday morning. Both work. The problem is when nobody reads it at all.

2. Send the warm ones to sales while the signal is still fresh.

Leave the rest in retargeting until they give you a second signal.

3. Then run it backwards.

When a post from your team takes off on its own, put the ad budget behind that one. You already know it works, so you're buying more of a proven result instead of testing a new creative.

Apart from running channels together, you might also want to add channels on top of the ones that are working well.

For instance... at a previous startup I had organic going well, funnels built right, growing 10-15% MoM, and I never put ads on top of any of it. But if I did, the entire thing would have produced even better results.

If you do one thing from this, do the first one.

1,000 people walk into Store A. 50 buy.
500 people walk into Store B. 100 buy.

Store B looks 4x better at selling.

But check how many people walked in actually looking for what the store sells.

In Store A, only 250 were. 50 of them bought.
In Store B, all 500 were. 100 bought.

Both stores close 20% of the shoppers who showed up wanting to buy. The selling is identical. Store A just pulled in 750 people who were never buying anything.

Every campaign I've run has this math buried in it somewhere. Leads are the foot traffic. Qualified leads are the people who walked in to buy. The funnel is the rest of the store, everything between the front door and the register.

Blend it all into one conversion rate and the number can't tell you which problem you have. Most teams default to rebuilding the funnel, because that's the part they control.

I studied our ICPs very carefully before I even joined @heyreach_io. One of the insights unlocked our entire 2025 playbook: our buyers were already building personal brands as their own growth engine.

So we made word of mouth and ambassadors the main channel. Every piece of content we ship gets one question before it goes out: does it fuel word of mouth?

A lead ignores your LinkedIn message.

Three days later, they reply to your email.

Then LinkedIn sends them another follow-up as if nothing happened.

This is the stupidest version of multichannel outreach: more channels, zero memory.

So here's how you build a smart multi-channel outreach system with memory:

a way to add the lead, a shared identifier, a reply event and a lead-level pause action.

Here's the flow:

1. The workflow starts on LinkedIn.

It views the profile, sends the connection request, then waits.

Once they connect, it sends the first message. If they reply, the flow ends there.

2. Switch channels when LinkedIn goes quiet.

If the request stays pending, or the message gets no reply after the set window, that branch moves the lead into the right email campaign.

In HeyReach, that handoff can run natively through Smartlead, Instantly or EmailBison.

Other email tools can follow the same logic through Make, n8n or an API, provided they support the same add, reply and pause actions.

3. Carry the memory with the lead.

The CRM record stores the LinkedIn URL, email address, LinkedIn status and last action.

That record routes the lead to email copy that continues from what already happened instead of starting the conversation again.

4. Stop the other machine when a human answers.

Replies in either channel trigger the control layer.

Make uses the email address or LinkedIn URL to find the CRM record. It marks the reply there first, then pauses the same lead in the other active sequence.

Without that step, your “multichannel” system congratulates itself for sending more messages while the prospect wonders why two versions of you are talking at once.

5. Let the CRM keep score.

Each lead has one owner, one current status and one next action.

Every channel reads from that record.

P.S: The smartest multichannel workflow knows when to switch channels and when to shut up.

I've taken two outbound tools past $10M ARR.

And I still couldn't tell you what a normal LinkedIn outreach campaign looked like.

So we analyzed 96,051 of them and built the benchmark nobody publishes.

These are the 100 rules you can use to diagnose a campaign before you touch the copy or add volume.

1. The median is the more useful starting benchmark because a few exceptional campaigns can pull the average above what most teams experience.

2. The typical campaign had 21% of its connection requests accepted.

3. Acceptance below 13% fell into the weak range.

4. Acceptance above 32% entered the stronger range.

5. The typical message-reply rate was 22%.

6. A reply rate below 13% was weak.

7. A reply rate above 33% entered the stronger range.

8. Reply-to-acceptance conversion, or RTA, measures replies divided by accepted connections.

9. Typical RTA was 18%.

10. RTA below 10% was weak post-acceptance performance.

11. RTA above 29% was strong post-acceptance performance.

12. I read those three stages in order because the first one below range is the leak I fix first.

The first lesson killed a bad habit of mine. I used to see a weak overall reply rate and start rewriting. That number can hide two completely different problems.

Read the funnel in order.

13. A typical batch of 100 requests produced about 21 accepted connections.

14. Fewer than four of those 21 accepted connections produced a reply.

15. The sharpest loss in the typical funnel happened after acceptance.

16. In 10.7% of campaigns with accepted connections, nobody replied.

17. Another 15% converted fewer than one in ten accepted connections into a reply.

18. Combined, roughly one in four campaigns got through the connection stage and still created almost no conversations.

19. Acceptance can make a campaign look healthy while the conversation layer is completely broken.

20. Overall reply rate is an outcome metric. It cannot identify the broken stage by itself.

21. RTA equals replies divided by accepted connections, multiplied by 100.

22. RTA belongs at campaign level because one account-wide average hides differences between audiences and messages.

This was the part I had been missing. Acceptance tells me we got through the door. It says very little about what happened once we entered.

Diagnose the post-acceptance leak.

23. Directional RTA patterns begin to stabilize around 100 accepted connections in one campaign.

24. An A/B message test needs about 50 accepted connections per variation before the result becomes directionally useful.

25. Low RTA that stays flat across campaigns points first toward the opening message.

26. The RTA guide uses roughly 15% as the warning line for that low-and-flat pattern.

27. The first message has one job: make replying feel worthwhile.

28. A low-commitment question is easier to answer than a calendar request from someone the prospect just accepted.

29. When early cohorts reply and later cohorts stop, sequence depth becomes the next thing to inspect.

30. Fewer than three useful steps after acceptance can leave good prospects with no second reason to engage.

31. A follow-up that only says “just checking in” adds another notification without adding another reason to answer.

32. Time-series RTA requires an export because the native dashboard does not currently show that view.

33. When RTA varies sharply between campaigns, compare the audience before blaming one universal opener.

34. The same message can fit a Head of Sales and miss a RevOps leader because the problems they own are different.

35. Comparing the roles, company sizes and seniority levels in the top and bottom campaigns reveals where the message stopped fitting.

36. A winning opener's structure can survive across segments, but the problem it names has to change with the buyer.

37. The clean diagnostic order is acceptance, opening message, ICP-message fit, then sequence depth.

I expected bigger campaigns to fall apart. They did lose some acceptance, but reported replies stayed surprisingly stable.

Understand what scale actually changed.

38. Campaigns with fewer than 100 contacts recorded 21.43% acceptance.

39. Campaigns with more than 1,000 contacts recorded 19.35% acceptance.

40. That is a decline of only 2.08 percentage points between the smallest and largest reported volume groups.

41. Reported reply performance stayed between 21.67% and 23.08% across volume tiers.

42. Higher volume was associated with slightly lower acceptance, while reported replies stayed broadly stable.

43. A large campaign with weak results deserves a list-quality inspection before an automatic copy rewrite.

44. Broader lists can introduce weaker segmentation and lower-fit prospects as volume rises.

45. Campaigns using six to 20 senders recorded the strongest median reported reply rate at 25%.

46. Single-sender campaigns recorded 22.22%.

47. Campaigns using 50 or more senders recorded 20.33%.

48. The dataset does not isolate why six to 20 senders performed best, so sender count remains a benchmark to test rather than an explanation by itself.

49. Campaigns under 30 days consistently underperformed the older groups in the report.

50. Acceptance in the first seven days was 13.33%.

51. Reported reply performance in that early period was 14.29%.

52. Campaigns running for 180 days or more reached 26.99% acceptance.

53. The duration gap does not prove that campaigns improve with age. Survivorship is one plausible explanation for the association.

54. A two-week campaign below the benchmarks is a diagnostic flag. Waiting for day 180 is not a fix.

This is where the report ends and the operating work starts. A benchmark can point at the leak. Someone still has to crawl into the pipe.

Build a list that gives the campaign a chance.

55. The audience and campaign goal are defined before anyone writes the first message.

56. Warm sources such as post engagers, event attendees and website visitors stay separate from cold prospecting lists.

57. Warm and cold prospects get different sequences because only one group already has context.

58. Every imported list is filtered by role, company fit and geography before it reaches a sender.

59. Customers, active opportunities, disqualified leads and do-not-contact records are removed before launch.

60. Previous outreach across LinkedIn and email is checked before a lead enters another sequence.

61. First-degree connections are separated from new prospects because they can be messaged without another request.

62. Every lead keeps its source, segment and trigger so performance can be traced back to the audience that produced it.

63. A trigger_reason field records why the outreach is timely.

64. A proof_link records where that trigger came from, so a personalized line can be checked before it ships.

65. High-value, low-volume lists get manual research across the profile, company, careers page and recent activity.

66. Larger lists use structured enrichment so every lead carries the same minimum set of usable fields.

67. One or two adjacent stakeholders are mapped inside important accounts before launch.

I've watched decent messages lose because the sender profile gave the prospect no reason to trust the person behind them.

Treat the sender like part of the message.

68. The sender profile functions as the landing page behind the connection request.

69. The headline explains who the sender helps and which problem they understand.

70. The About section carries the proof that would make the outreach credible.

71. Recent profile activity stays relevant to the audience the sender is contacting.

72. New or idle accounts start with lighter activity and increase only while account health holds.

73. For new accounts, HeyReach's current guidance starts with 100 manual connections, then ramps from 5 requests a day in week one to 10 in week two and 15 to 20 from week three.

74. Once an account is warmed up, HeyReach recommends 25 requests a day by default. Going to 30 is reserved for accounts with more than 1,000 connections and healthy acceptance.

75. Activity is spread across the day instead of arriving in one obvious burst.

76. Profile views, requests and messages are mixed so the account does not repeat one robotic action pattern.

77. Old pending invitations are cleared before a new campaign starts.

78. Sender-level acceptance is compared inside the same campaign so one weak profile cannot hide inside the pooled average.

The blank-request result was the awkward one. I had spent years hearing that personalization wins, then our benchmark put blank requests five points ahead.

Use the connection request to earn access.

79. Empty connection requests averaged 27% acceptance in one HeyReach benchmark.

80. Requests containing text averaged 22%.

81. That five-point gap is an association worth testing. It does not prove that every audience prefers a blank request.

82. Blank and written requests are tested against comparable audiences before either becomes the default.

83. A written note gives one current reason to connect and stops before becoming a pitch.

84. Links and attachments stay out of the request because they add friction before trust exists.

85. Dynamic variables always have a fallback so a missing field cannot send a broken message.

86. Every variation is previewed against real leads before the campaign launches.

87. The deeper personalization belongs after acceptance, where relevance can create a reply.

The request gets us through the door. The first message decides whether anyone talks to us once we're inside.

Build a sequence people can answer.

88. The operating sequence is simple: connect, send value, follow up, then stop on reply.

89. The first post-acceptance message names one true signal and one relevant problem.

90. Personalization is capped at two meaningful inputs per contact because more inputs add work faster than they add relevance.

91. Each follow-up has a different job: reconnect to the context, offer something concrete, or close the loop.

92. One agency in the report messaged new connections within three hours and recorded a 26% positive reply rate.

93. That result makes timing worth testing, but one agency case does not establish a universal three-hour rule.

94. “Stop on reply” is enabled before launch so automation cannot continue after a human conversation begins.

I don't care about winning an acceptance-rate screenshot. The campaign has to produce a conversation that Nadja and the sales team can actually move forward.

Make the system produce pipeline.

95. Total replies and positive replies are tracked separately because objections and buying intent have different pipeline value.

96. Campaign-and-sender performance lives in one dashboard, while segment performance lives in another.

97. A clean test changes one meaningful variable, keeps the rest stable and waits for enough accepted connections.

98. One suppression system and one set of stop rules govern every sender in the workspace.

99. The CRM receives the sender, campaign, first touch, acceptance, reply and current stage so sales inherits the full context.

100. The final scoreboard reaches beyond replies: positive conversation, opportunity, revenue. The order stays the same: earn acceptance, earn the reply, then add volume without losing control.

Marija had the best line in the whole report: hitting the median isn't a win. It only means you stopped losing.

My version after 96,051 campaigns: find the first leak, fix it, then earn the right to scale.

The marketing playbook that gets a company to $1M is usually the same thing that stalls it around $2M.

@nikolak47's article explains why. 

You see there are six different growth jobs hiding inside one ARR chart.

At $2K MRR, the job is to buy time and learning.

You need enough runway to stay alive and enough users to tell you what is broken. For HeyReach, AppSumo created both. One launch brought a year of runway and 1,117 users into a product that still had no PMF.

That move could not run forever. It only needed to buy another year.

At $10K MRR, the job is focus.

More traffic into a weak offer gives you a larger churn problem. So Nick and Ilija took 597 of the first 600 sales calls, found the agency use case, and used the customer's own language: unlimited senders.

One ICP with one painful job and an offer people immediately understood.

That turned six flat months into 26% MoM growth.

At $1M ARR, the job is to make the promise stick.

The agency wedge only keeps working if the product fits the agency's stack. APIs, webhooks, integrations and permissions turned HeyReach from another campaign dashboard into infrastructure.

This is where product starts doing part of marketing's job. It becomes easier to adopt, harder to remove, and useful inside workflows other companies already distribute.

At $2M ARR, the job is capacity.

More demand can destroy a machine that is already full. HeyReach had around 1,000 customers on software built for 200. The app crashed daily, Support reached 200+ tickets a day, and churn went above 15%.

Acquisition was still working. That was exactly why the underlying problem was easy to miss.

At $3M ARR, the job is to make service part of growth.

Reliability, Support, billing and customers getting the outcome they paid for became the work. Once the service around the software could carry the volume, the business started adding close to $100K per week.

At $6M ARR, the job is compounding distribution.

Creators teach the workflows. 
Affiliates turn trust into traceable revenue. 
Customer results keep word of mouth moving.
Integrations make the product easier to discover and harder to remove. 

That engine kept running even when LinkedIn deleted the founder profiles and company page.

So the simple version is:

> $2K MRR: buy time and learning
> $10K MRR: find the ICP and offer
> $1M ARR: become infrastructure
> $2M ARR: protect capacity
> $3M ARR: make service part of growth
> $6M ARR: build compounding distribution

Every stage has a different constraint. You have to keep evolving your playbook along the way.

In summer 2024, we ran an internal churn-reduction program at @heyreach_io called Operation Churn.

It saved 235 users. We recovered 55.7% of involuntary churn across three methods, and churn dropped and stayed stable for the next three months.

The lesson was mildly annoying for a CMO: a lot of acquisition work is just replacing revenue the company already earned once.

Marketing can ship more content, turn up spend, and celebrate a bigger signup chart, but if the same amount of revenue leaves through the other side, the company is buying the same growth twice.

So we worked on the cancellation process, instant notifications, counter-offers, and failed payments before doubling down on acquisition.

True growth starts after we subtract the revenue used to replace last month's leaks. Everything below that line is running to stand still.

I spent almost four years selling cold email. Employee #1 at the tool. They were doing like $250K ARR when I joined. $13.5M when I left.

For most of those years our number one cancellation reason was "cold email doesn't work for us." 

Turns out it worked fine. Nobody knew what to send. 

We solved that problem by publishing templates that actually worked (among many other things) and it still took us months.

Don't get me wrong, I'm not anti-email. It's just slow even when it's working. You warm domains for weeks before anything goes out. Then you send, and you have no idea what's happening in there. Two months in you find out the list was bad.

Our users got 1.19 million LinkedIn replies in Q1, 26% average reply rate. 

Per sender: 100 messages a week, 26% reply, most of them no's, 8 or 9 real conversations, 2 or 3 customers. 

You know inside a week whether the channel is working for you or not. 

So go to LinkedIn. Keep email running under it, and get ads going behind both.

Yesterday I was going through Demandbase’s latest B2B referral data. Yes my idea of fun is quite niche.

And this press release was such a great way to flex:
ChatGPT referrals to their B2B websites grew from ~645K to 2.6M monthly visits in one year.

My brain went straight to how were they able to achieve this.

When someone asks ChatGPT which tool to use, our homepage is only one input. Reviews, comparison pages, customer stories, and what others say about us can all shape the answer.

This changes how I think about content:
→ fewer interchangeable SEO articles
→ more customer proof
→ more operator stories with receipts
→ more useful content people actually cite and share

Traffic still matters. But the bigger game is becoming part of the answer before the buyer ever visits your website.

Doubling down on distribution is how a weak product burns through a market.

Doubling down on distribution can keep the signup chart moving long enough to make a product problem look like a growth problem. 

More traffic goes in, churn comes out, and the answer is somehow another channel.

Our first paid campaign at @heyreach_io returned 24.9x. 

The ads weren't genius tbh. We turned them on after word of mouth and organic funnels were already working. Paid multiplied something people already wanted.

Every channel I run eventually sends people into the product. I can change who sees it, what we say and how we sell it. I can't fix what happens after the login with another campaign. 

So by all means, go ahead and distribute your SaaS aggressively, but ensure that you also spend time to improve the overall experience. 

And this just doesn't stop with finding PMF. If you get the next product call wrong, more distribution only puts the mistake in front of more people.
