article_title: 7 prompts to run LinkedIn outreach from Claude code terminal

text:
Claude Code + LinkedIn to grow your pipeline:

Setup, once:

1. Ask Claude in the browser how to install Claude Code. Paste the command into your terminal, type claude, log in.

2. In HeyReach: Settings, Integrations, HeyReach MCP Server. Click New MCP key. Copy the key and the connection URL.

3. Paste both into Claude Code's MCP configuration. Claude hands you the exact command if you ask for it.

4. Run /mcp in the terminal. HeyReach should show up under Local MCPs.

5. Write one markdown file into that folder with your DM rules: who you write to, what a good first message looks like for you, the things you never say. Claude Code reads it at the start of every session.

Building the campaign:

6. Drop your CSV in the folder. "Read this CSV in the current directory. First, show me the column names and the first three rows so I can see the structure. Then filter it to only rows where the first person is a CEO."

7. Same prompt does the boring stuff. Drop duplicates, remove anyone under 50 employees, score against a criteria list you paste in.

8. "Can you load those CEOs into the HeyReach campaign for Blank CEOs?" It finds the campaign by name, creates the list, maps the columns, enrolls the contacts.

9. Rows with no LinkedIn URL get handled on the way. Ours called Prospeo on its own and found 4 of the 7. The other 3 stayed out of the campaign and it told us which ones.

10. That segment gets a blank connection request. Blank requests get accepted 27% of the time, personalized ones 22%. The note costs you five points at the door, so I skip it and spend the personalization after they accept.

11. "Enroll the [list name] lead list into a new campaign. Use three messages spaced three days apart. Generate custom variables for the first ten leads based on their LinkedIn profiles, using my DM rules file."

12. Add the line "ask clarifying questions before actioning" to every prompt like that.

13. Run it in plan mode, so Claude shows you what it intends to do before it touches the account.

14. The message it writes is five parts: a greeting off something you genuinely share, a compliment kept at roughly five out of ten in enthusiasm, one observation that shows you know their space, one curiosity question that can't be answered with a yes or a no, and a closing line tied to their city, industry or network.

15. Then open Edit campaign in HeyReach, read every message, set the gaps to three hours, and fix the copy by hand.

The inbox:

16. Write a brain doc first. What you sell, who you sell it to, the pains you're looking for, your current process, and an FAQ with pricing, onboarding time, delivery and the objection you hear every week.

17. Claude drafts most of it from your website and your past chats in one prompt. Save it in Notion, read it once, fix the two things it got wrong. Those two are exactly what would have gone out to a prospect.

18. "Using the HeyReach MCP, pull the conversations that are unread or unreplied. For each one, read the full thread, then draft the next reply using the brain document in Notion. Show me each draft with the lead's name and the thread. Tag anyone asking for a call as Hot and anyone asking questions as Warm. Do not send anything."

19. Four tags: Hot, Warm, On hold, and Multi-thread for accounts with more than one contact. A single interested tag works fine for one account and falls apart at ten.

20. Put it on a schedule. Monday and Thursday morning it runs and DMs me the drafts in Slack. I approve five replies and close Slack.

After the campaign ends:

21. Only on campaigns that have finished. A metric dropping mid-flight is a diagnosis problem, and this is a post-mortem.

22. "Pull acceptance rate, reply rate, and reply-to-acceptance conversion for my last campaign, broken down by lead list and segment. Then compare each metric against the HeyReach benchmark averages and flag the segments that clearly beat or missed them."

23. The benchmarks it compares against, from our study of 96,051 campaigns: 20.75% acceptance, 22.22% reply rate, about 18.1% reply-to-acceptance.

24. Read reply-to-acceptance first. Under 10% is weak, over 29% is strong.

25. Under 10% and the leak sits after the accept. Either the first message or how long you waited to send it. Ours goes out within 2 to 3 hours of them accepting, tops.

26. "Rank my segments by reply-to-acceptance conversion. Show me the two that beat the campaign average and the two that dragged it down, and tell me how each compares to the HeyReach benchmark."

27. Then: "Compare reply-to-acceptance conversion across my opener variants and my send timing after acceptance. Tell me which opener and which timing window earned the most replies." Out of that I pick one segment to scale and one to kill.

28. "Pull my replies from this campaign in Unibox and cluster them into themes: interested, wrong timing, wrong person, price or priority pushback, and not relevant. Tell me what share of the negative replies fall into each theme."

29. How I read them. "Not a priority" is timing and list hygiene, go find better signals. "Wrong person" means the seniority filter in Sales Navigator or Clay is off. "What is this?" means you started selling too early.

30. Then: "Based on the objections in this campaign, draft three opener variants that address the most common one head-on. Use the wording my prospects used in their replies."

Two more worth stealing:

31. Relaunch with one prompt. Everyone in a finished campaign who never replied drops into a new campaign with a different angle, no export and no list-building in between.

32. Point an n8n agent at the MCP and trigger it from Slack. Each client types "how did last week go?" in their own channel and gets the answer, without logging in at all.

One warning:

33. It amplifies whatever system you already have. Messy segmentation goes in, messy truth comes out, just faster. If the campaign was one lead list with no segments, there is nothing in there to rank. I would fix the structure before connecting Claude to any of it.

If you're looking to grow your pipeline through LinkedIn, one of the most underrated hacks is to increase your sender accounts.

Every profile is capped at about 100 connection requests a week. 

> At a typical 21% accept rate that's 21 new connections. 
> Ten accounts gets you 1,000 requests and about 210 connections.

It helps the quality too. 

Across 96,051 campaigns we recently analyzed for a report, single-account campaigns have a median reply rate of 22.22%. 

Campaigns running 6 to 20 accounts sit at 25.00%.

Here's the catch though...LinkedIn looks at your accounts as a group.

Ten accounts sending thirty messages in the same hour looks very different from ten accounts spreading them across a whole day. Every account can be under its own limit and the pattern still shows.

That's how it usually goes wrong... 

So once you're past three or four accounts:

→ Spread the sends across the day. Same volume, quieter pattern and less likely to get flagged.
→ Start new accounts slow. Profile views and light activity in week one. Add volume only while your accept and reply rates hold.
→ Check pending invites. Over 35 on one account is your warning, and you get about 3 to 5 days to fix it.
→ Match the sender to the prospect. Founder profile for C-suite, SDR profile for director and below.

Here's how I'd turn them into a LinkedIn campaign, right out of Claude: 

1. Connect HeyReach to Claude

Add @heyreach_io's MCP connector, then ask Claude to list your campaigns. Our MCP supports building the sequence, assigning senders and launching. Get the connection working first.

2. Upload your email non-responders

Export the leads from your email platform and upload the CSV to Claude. Include names, companies, roles, LinkedIn URLs and campaign/reply status wherever available.

"Read this CSV. Keep leads who finished the sequence without replying. Flag missing or unclear statuses."

3. Give Claude the rules for who gets through

Upload your ICP criteria, current CRM export and do-not-contact list. Keep qualified matches; exclude unsubscribes, negative replies, open sales conversations and active LinkedIn outreach. 

Ask Claude to show why each lead qualifies. Hold uncertain records and missing or unverified LinkedIn URLs.

4. Write a new opening for LinkedIn

Give Claude the original emails and a verified detail about each prospect. Ask it to draft a short message around a relevant problem.

If the company is hiring sales reps, for example:

"How are you building pipeline for the new reps you're hiring?"

That hiring signal has to exist in the research. Please spare them "just following up on my email."

5. Build the campaign in HeyReach

"Create this as a draft. Start with a connection request, then send the approved message after acceptance. Add a follow-up with a different reason to reply. Use these sender accounts, this timezone and these delays."

Supply the actual accounts and timings. Have Claude show the full sequence before anything goes live.

6. Preview the messages against real leads

Check the names, companies, opening lines and missing-field fallbacks. Confirm the exclusions and schedule, fix anything you'd never send, then tell Claude to launch the approved campaign.

7. Check what LinkedIn added

Keep these leads in a separate campaign. Ask Claude to pull the replies and separate buying interest, questions, objections and rejections. Read the actual conversations behind those labels.

Note: The best way to evaluate this is to check whether qualified people who haven't responded on email start replying on LinkedIn. If not, it might be a case of poor fit, and you might want to fix targeting before reaching out to another set of leads.

Your lead list quality is set in 4 decisions you make before the campaign launches. Get them right and everything downstream works better.

Step 1: Choose your source based on relationship proximity.

Warmer sources like post reactors and event attendees accept far more than a cold Sales Nav pull. The source sets your acceptance ceiling before you write a word.

Step 2: Clean your list before it touches a campaign.

Warm lists import raw, with no title filter, so every off-ICP reactor comes in with the rest. Cut them by title and company fit first.

Step 3: Remove the wrong leads before launch.

Exclude your existing clients, anyone you've already contacted elsewhere, and your 1st-degree connections from cold sequences.

Step 4: Stop running warm and cold leads through the same sequence.

Split the list by connection status. People you're already connected to get a direct message, everyone else gets a connection request.

- Skip Step 1 and you're targeting the wrong people.
- Skip Step 2 and bad-fit leads enter the campaign.
- Skip Step 3 and someone gets contacted who never should have.
- Skip Step 4 and warm audiences get cold outreach logic.

Get the list right and the message barely has to work. Get it wrong and no copy saves you.

Imagine two restaurants running the same coupon offer.

Restaurant A gets 100 diners.
Restaurant B gets 80.

Restaurant A looks like the winner.

Now suppose 90 of A’s diners were already planning to eat there. They found the coupon on the way.

At B, only 20 were coming anyway.
A added 10 diners. B added 60.

The campaign with fewer redemptions brought in 6x as many additional customers.

Restaurant A mostly gave a discount to people who were already sold.

That’s the question I keep coming back to with marketing attribution. How many of these people would have bought anyway?

Our first paid campaign at @heyreach_io hit 20x ROAS. We were profitable from day one.

But we’d already built word of mouth and the retargeting setup before running it. The ads went into a business where people had reasons to know us.

I can be happy with that result and still admit the ROAS number doesn’t tell me how much revenue the ads added. Some buyers might have come through another route. The dashboard can’t settle that just by assigning them to a campaign.

That matters when I’m deciding where the next dollar goes. If I mistake people taking the easiest route to checkout for people we persuaded to buy, I’ll keep funding the channel closest to the sale.

Meanwhile, the work that got them interested starts looking expensive.

I want to know what happens to total sales when the spend changes. More sales credited to the campaign, on their own, aren’t enough.

Before you rewrite a cold message that isn’t getting replies, take another look at the companies receiving it.

You may be sending the same pitch to businesses that need very different things from you.

Your list might look specific: B2B SaaS, 50 to 200 employees, Head of Marketing.

But those filters don’t tell you how each company gets customers, or which part of that process you can help improve.

Take two companies on that list.

One lets people start a trial and pay without speaking to sales. The other routes buyers through demos and a sales team.

If you sell conversion audits, those are two different conversations.

With the first, you could discuss the journey from trial signup to first use to payment.

With the second, you could discuss what happens between a demo request and a qualified sales opportunity.

Before writing the message:

1. Follow the signup or demo path on the website.
2. Find the person responsible for the step you can help improve.
3. Group companies that share that need, then write a message for each group.

Use the website to decide what to ask about. It won’t tell you where their funnel is actually underperforming.

Credit to @KellenCasebeer for this approach to segmentation.

Once you’ve grouped prospects by the problem you can help with, you have a clear starting point for the message: why this conversation would be useful to them.

Our partner and affiliate program has brought HeyReach over $3.1M in revenue.

When you plan a joint campaign, it’s easy to focus on the promotion: the emails, registrations and getting both audiences to show up.

All of that matters, but the campaign also needs to help an interested attendee become someone who actually uses the product.

Someone can leave a webinar thinking, “That could work for us,” then never come back to it.

They still have to figure out the setup and make time to try it, so the campaign needs to make that easier.

With Trigify, we built the campaign around helping people try it. Here’s how you can apply the same approach:

1. Start with a campaign people can reproduce.

@nikolak47 and the Trigify team brought in Alexander Tsvetkov from OneAway to walk through a real campaign using both products.

2. Give attendees a specific task.

With this pairing, you could ask people to use Trigify to find prospects engaging with LinkedIn posts about a problem they solve.

Then have them check who fits their target customer and build a HeyReach outreach campaign for those people.

3. Make sharing the work part of the entry.

Our challenge required people to build with both tools and share their workflow online.

For yours, ask for a short recording of the setup, the message and what happened, so the next person can learn from it.

4. Pick a prize your ideal customer wants.

We put a year of both tools’ top plans up for grabs. The reward was more of the products participants were learning to use.

5. Give the winning workflow another audience.

Choose a winner based on how useful and reproducible the workflow is, then invite them to teach it in your next webinar.

The LinkedIn flow I run holds a 40%+ reply rate, and every second reply books a call. The 2 messages that open it are under 20 words combined, and neither one pitches.

Almost all of the work sits after the connection is accepted. Teams fight for the acceptance, then open with "I help companies like yours" and wonder why the thread dies.

Here's the whole thing, request to booked call. Copy it as is:

1. Send the request blank, or with one line and no pitch. The request only has to get accepted. Save the personalization for where it can earn a reply.

2. The moment they accept: "Thanks for connecting {name}." That's the entire message. Linkunity, an agency in our benchmark report, messages every new connection within 3 hours and runs a 26% positive reply rate on it.

3. 1-2 days later, the opener: "Saw {company} is doing {specific thing}, how's that going?"

{specific thing} comes from the research: a hire, a launch, a post they wrote. 1 or 2 inputs per person, never more. People reply to curiosity. They ghost a pitch.

4. Give every follow-up a different job: the first reconnects to the context, the second offers something concrete, the third closes the loop. "Just checking in" is a notification with no reason to answer. Stop-on-reply switched on before launch.

5. Answer replies the same day, from one inbox across every sender. A LinkedIn reply has a shelf life of minutes. Get to it tomorrow and you're a stranger interrupting them again.

6. Measure replies divided by accepted connections, per campaign. Across the 96,051 campaigns we analyzed, typical was 18% and strong was 29%+.

If it's low and flat across every campaign, I fix the opener. If it swings from campaign to campaign, I go back to the audience. You can't see which from the overall reply rate.

We run this at HeyReach. It's the flow under the 7 templates I gave away in June.

The math for one sender: 100 requests a week, 21 accepted at a typical acceptance rate, 40% of those replying = 8-9 conversations = 4 booked calls a week.

Same 100 requests as everyone else. The difference is what you say once you're inside.

text:
Tier list on how to win your customers back...and which tactics you should leave alone:

S tier
→ Write down the exact reason the buyer gave for saying no, in their words. "No budget" in the CRM tells you nothing

→ Split every "no budget" into 3 buckets: they needed sign-off, they couldn't afford it, or they didn't see the value. Each one needs a different message

→ For deals lost on timing, ask "did the rollout wrap or did the schedule move?" The date passing doesn't mean you're next

→ Before writing about a new feature, check it works on their plan and their permissions. A feature name in an email isn't proof it solves their problem

A tier
→ Sort accounts into 3 groups: something changed, they gave a review date, still blocked. Only the first 2 get a message

→ For deals lost to a competitor, ask if that vendor delivered the one thing they picked it for. Don't ask if they're unhappy

→ Show a 2 minute clip of the one thing you couldn't do last time. They already sat through your full demo

B tier
→ If they said "next budget cycle", send the updated proposal 2 weeks before that review, with the scope you already agreed

→ Count a deal as reopened only if they still have the need, the blocker is gone, and there's a next call booked. "Thanks for the update" is a zero

→ Track wins by why you lost the first time. You'll find out which kind of no is worth going back for

C tier
→ A discount for people who didn't see the value. Price was never their objection

→ A cheaper scope with the parts they cared about removed

D tier
→ Every lost deal on a 90 day timer
→ "Circling back"
→ Making up problems with the vendor they chose

I'm convinced lead gen agencies have the best outbound playbooks.

They run campaigns for businesses that expect paying customers. A nice reply-rate screenshot only gets them so far. The campaign has to keep producing, or the account is at risk.

That's why my team spends time collecting what these operators actually do. @nikolak47 put 8 of their plays into the article below, alongside our campaign benchmarks.

These are the details I'd pay attention to:

1. They check whether the people on the list actually use LinkedIn.

Mohan at @springdriveco used the "Posted on LinkedIn" filter in Sales Navigator to reach active people. The message was two casual sentences and a question about the kinds of customers they work with.

The campaign's published dashboard shows 38.1% acceptance, a 40% reply rate and 291 replies.

I'd check that filter before spending another afternoon rewriting an opener. Someone who barely opens LinkedIn is a difficult person to start a conversation with there.

2. They think about whose profile the prospect will open.

Danilo (@DaniloPrelevikj) at Viralnetix ran outreach for a cybersecurity business. The messages came from a cybersecurity practitioner, and the meeting ask waited until there was a conversation and a clear fit.

The case study reports 62% acceptance and a 56% reply rate.

From my side of marketing, the sender's profile is part of the campaign. A CISO opening it should find someone who understands their work. All the copy edits in the world can't supply that credibility on their own.

3. They keep the topic someone engaged with attached to the lead.

Sönke (@soenkevenjacob) at Platinum Agency collected people reacting to a customer's posts, then split them by topic. Cold email, GPT email templates and LinkedIn DMs went into separate campaigns.

The case study reports 174 leads, 57% acceptance and a 48% reply rate.

This is directly in my team's territory. If marketing hands sales a list called "LinkedIn engagers" and drops which post each person came from, we've thrown away useful information. I'd want the conversation to pick up where their interest started.

4. They give the connection note a job.

Our benchmark found 27% acceptance for blank requests versus 22% for requests with a note. I'd start with blank and test from there.

Luke (@Luke_Bivens) at @QCGrowth shows when a note has a reason to exist: the sender was planning a visit to NYC and asked CS leaders about meeting for coffee.

QC Growth reported 49 conversations, 17 qualified meetings and $2.5M+ in qualified pipeline.

The date and location made that invitation specific. Copying the coffee line without the actual visit would miss the point.

5. They give away a small piece of the work they're selling.

Joel and Cameron at Repify offered prospects a list of people engaging with their competitors, personalized messages for those leads, and a video showing how to launch the campaign.

They reported 15 qualified calls booked in a week, with 6 of those prospects becoming retainer clients.

I like this as a marketer because the giveaway lets someone inspect the work. The prospect can look at the leads and messages and decide whether the agency understands their business before taking a call.

6. They use LinkedIn to arrange a conversation offline.

Tom (@tomsotoschiller) at Grundwerk Digital planned a dinner for 12 CFOs around Frankfurt. His outreach first invited new connections to lunch, using their office ZIP codes to suggest a restaurant nearby.

The campaign had 134 leads and a reported 50% reply rate.

For a service that needs a lot of trust, I'd be comfortable giving LinkedIn that smaller job: help the right people meet. I wouldn't expect a DM to do all the selling.

7. They have a plan for what happens after the accept.

Linkunity messaged new connections within 3 hours and reported a 26% reply rate. Repify also sent its first message 3 hours after acceptance.

Across our benchmark, 10.7% of campaigns with accepted connections got zero replies.

That gap deserves attention. I'd have the first message ready before launching: a specific reason for connecting and a question that's easy to answer. Getting accepted is still only the start of the conversation.

8. They give people a chance to recognize the sender first.

Daniel and the GTM Brigade team picked 738 people who matched their ICP. A rep regularly liked and commented on those people's posts before the same audience entered the outreach sequence.

The campaign saw around 50% acceptance and a 20% reply rate. Daniel reported $250K in pipeline across campaigns in a month from the approach.

This is where content and outbound fit together for me. Marketing can help build familiarity with the people sales wants to reach. Then the outreach can follow something more useful than a job-title match.

What I like about these campaigns is how much thought went into the recipient's side: whether they're active, who they'll trust, what interested them and what would make a conversation worth having.

The messages make a lot more sense once those decisions are visible.

My team collected these so the work behind the results could be useful to other operators. Nick's full breakdown is below, with the examples and numbers together. Plenty here I'd borrow for an in-house team too.

Run LinkedIn outreach with Jev:

Jev is TypeSafe's new model, and it doesn't write. You give it a lead or a message plus a narrow question with the answers you'd accept, and it picks one and tells you how sure it is.

That's exactly what outreach needs, because outreach is a stack of decisions.

Right person?
Signal still fresh?
Message about them or about us?
Which of my three messages will this one person actually answer?

You can't make those calls on every lead by hand, so most campaigns skip them and find out from the reply rate. Jev makes every one of them, on every lead and every message, before anything goes live, for cents.

So we built GTM Bot on it. It tiers the leads in your @heyreach_io lists, scores every message variant, locks the best one to each person, builds the campaigns in HeyReach, and self-improves based on your campaign performance.

Here's the full setup:

1. Two keys and one small file. A TypeSafe key for Jev, a HeyReach key from Settings, Integrations, API. Then a config that says what you sell: one sentence on the product, one on the problem, your target roles, the company type, who to skip. That's all it knows about you, so make it sharp.

2. Run the demo first. Three seconds, under a cent, and you're reading a report of what it does before you touch your own list.

3. Point it at a list. Any HeyReach list (Sales Nav, Clay, CSV) or your 1st-degree network. Give every lead a signal: one line on what they did, and when. A post about your problem beats a like on a random post, and a signal loses half its weight every 21 days, so fresh wins.

4. Write 2 or 3 first messages, not one. It needs options to pick from.

5. Score the leads. Every lead gets asked: right role, senior enough, right company, how close is the signal to the problem you solve, and the disqualifiers (sells what you sell, open to work, on your exclude list). Tier A, B, C or Skip.

6. Score the messages. Every message gets asked: about them or about you, does it use the signal, does it pitch, does it ask for a meeting on first touch, stock phrasing, a merge tag still unfilled. Score and reply chance per variant.

7. Lock the best message to each lead. No more random split putting your best lead on your worst message. Every one of those is a Jev call, and that's where the 2.59 seconds go.

8. Push it into HeyReach. One list and one campaign per tier-and-variant pair. A and B get campaigns, C and Skip don't. Every lead lands with its verdict on it as custom fields, so you can see why it's there. Preview it first, then let it build.

9. The sequence is set for you. Blank connection request, then the message 3 hours after they accept. Blank requests get accepted 27% of the time, ones with a note 22%, and 3 hours is the rule from our 96,051-campaign report. People you're already connected to skip the request and get the message.

10. Launch. In HeyReach, or do what I do: open Claude with the HeyReach MCP and say "start the [GTM] campaigns".

11. Let the inbox teach it. At 30+ conversations it reads the ones you started, scores the lead and the first message behind each one, and learns which ones got a reply on YOUR account. It also prints what moves your replies, habit by habit: using the signal, asking for a meeting too early, going over 60 words.

12. Every Monday: learn from last week, score the new list, build, launch. Each week it knows a bit more about who answers you.

text:
HeyReach was doing $15K MRR when I joined in October 2023. It's at $18M ARR now.

I've been the marketing person the entire way, first as a growth consultant, then as CMO.

This is everything we did to get here, stage by stage.

Stage 1: $15K MRR to $2M ARR (12 months, survival mode)

Nobody in marketing had a single job. Everyone did everything.

→ We led with the 1 feature nobody else had and went global from day 1
→ Zero paid ads, because product-market fit wasn't confirmed yet
→ Everything ran in short sprints

What broke: support got buried under 200+ tickets until Ebru came in and turned it around. Churn was the other leak.

In summer 2024, on marketing's side, I built a proper cancellation flow, instant cancel alerts, counter-offers and failed-payment recovery. That program saved 235 users and recovered 55.7% of involuntary churn.

Stage 2: $2M to $10M (2025, building the machine)

I became CMO in January 2025, and the job changed from doing everything to building a team that could.

→ Word of mouth became our #1 channel. We engaged every single mention, because someone we engage with is about 3x more likely to mention us again

→ Every case study featured a user winning, with their playbook and their numbers, so they shared it for us

→ Free trial to paid went from 9% to 26%+, with 2,500 to 3,000 trials coming in every month

We hit $10M in December 2025 without spending a cent on paid ads, with around 90% of revenue coming in inbound.

What broke: onboarding. We built a $7M business on "here's the login, good luck, we believe in you." The first real onboarding flow only shipped at the end of Q2 2025.

Stage 3: $10M to $18M (2026, adding the fast layer)

→ We finally turned on paid, on top of everything organic we'd built. The first campaign hit 20x ROAS and was profitable from day 1. I'm still a player at ads, and our agency does the technical lifting

→ 5 months in, we'd spent $21,404 at 24.9x ROAS and $2.59 per conversion. The same ad did 5.7x on a broad audience and up to 91x on people who already knew us

→ Sales and success pick who sees our ads. Say a 10K list of trials that didn't convert. It goes into Meta and Google, and sales works whoever engages

→ Our partner and affiliate program has brought in over $3.1M so far

→ Retention and customer success got its own owner. @Vick_Mucunski runs it now, and marketing's job is sending him customers who'll stay

Stage 4: $18M and up (starting now, in-house sales teams)

Sales and GTM teams inside companies are already a bigger share of our customers than agencies, and they're the ICP we're building the next stage around. The first three stages were built for agencies, and most of what worked there doesn't carry over to a sales team as it is.

Distribution first got us through every stage so far. I'll share what it looks like for this one once we've run it.

I've spent 7 years as the marketer inside 2 bootstrapped tools that both went past $10M ARR. If I could send one lesson back to 2019, it's the least exciting one on the list.

Distribution is 51% of the game.

At the first company we were close to $250K ARR with a blog nobody read.

We wrote about outreach, LinkedIn, entrepreneurship, basically whatever might stick, and around 80% of our time went into writing. Traffic was close to zero and so were signups.

So we changed 2 things.

- First, we only published content that could make money. That meant cold email templates. We were already running the outreach, so every template came with real results, showed off a feature, and chipped away at our #1 churn reason back then ("cold email doesn't work for us").

- Then we spent most of the week getting it seen. We posted a template of the week in the community and the newsletter, showed up on Quora, Reddit and the growth forums where our buyers already hung out, and traded backlinks wherever we could

We also started our own 10-person LinkedIn chat, which grew into a group in the thousands and got me in front of people I could never have reached cold, journalists included.

2 people ran all of it. Word of mouth and referral traffic turned into one of our biggest early engines, and that company went on to $13.5M ARR.

I'd still write the templates. I'd just skip the 6 months of publishing into a void and start building the pods and the relationships on day 1.

text:
The most underrated number in LinkedIn outreach: reply-to-acceptance rate, or RTA

Gunner Park used it to turn 42 accepted LinkedIn connections into 25 interested leads at @brijforbrands. A recruiting campaign on @heyreach_io got 571 replies from 800 accepted connections in 2 weeks.

More than half of Gunner's connections turned into leads, and 7 out of 10 of the recruiter's answered. The typical campaign in our data gets a reply from fewer than 1 in 5.

So how do you measure it? or what even is it?

- Take the replies, divide them by the people who accepted, and multiply by 100.

- You're only counting people who already said yes to connecting, so you're grading your messages on their own.

Reply rate mixes your targeting and your messaging into one number, so when it drops you're guessing which one broke.

Acceptance only covers the first half. In 10.7% of the campaigns in our benchmark where people accepted, not one person replied.

Here's how I'd measure it:

→ Pull accepted connections and replies per campaign, from the HeyReach funnel or a CSV export

→ Run the math one campaign at a time, and wait for about 100 accepted connections before you trust it

→ Check acceptance first. If it's under ~25%, fix the list before you look at RTA

→ Under ~10% means something's broken, ~18% is typical, and above ~29% is strong

If RTA is low on every campaign, your first message is the problem. If it's high on some and low on others, your message fits one audience and misses the rest, so score the winning segments higher in your lead scoring.

About 90% of @heyreach_io's revenue was inbound when we hit $10M ARR, we hadn't run a single ad. This was possible because we ran word of mouth like a channel we could control, with someone on the team owning it every day. Here are 10 underrated things we did to get there:

1/ We designed our partner program so creators earn more when their customers stay.

→ 50 creators and 16 agencies are in it, and none of them get paid for the post itself.
→ They get a share of what their referrals pay us. Creators get 35% on our Growth plan for the first year, when the usual B2B SaaS commission is around 20%.

→ That partner and affiliate program has brought in over $3.1M so far.

2/ Every mention gets a reply from a real person.

→ Every time someone mentions HeyReach on LinkedIn, 1 of us comments on the specific thing they wrote.
→ 1 person owns this every day, and a small account gets as good a reply as a big one.
→ In our data, people whose mentions we reply to are about 3x more likely to mention us again.

3/ Every mention also goes to sales.

→ We log every mention: who posted, which segment they're in, and what made them post.
→ We send that list to Nadja, our Head of Sales. Her team reaches out while the post is still fresh, and the first message opens with what the person wrote.
→ They posted about us first, so it's never a cold pitch.

4/ 10 of us post under our own names, with money on the line.

→ 10 people on our team build their own audiences, with opinions I don't approve first.
→ We built a quarterly posting competition for it. You opt in and commit to 1 to 5 posts a week. Hit your number and you get a bonus. Miss a post and you pay out of your own salary. (I hate losing, even at ping-pong.)

5/ We publish our users' playbooks as our case studies.

→ We call them Outbound Outliers. We take a real user's campaign, rip it apart, and publish the whole playbook: the steps they ran and the results they got.
→ The user gets the credit, so they share it with their own audience.

6/ We gave webinar attendees a reason to post their results.

→ Attendees run a campaign, post their results on LinkedIn, and the best ones get rewards.
→ Their audience sees HeyReach working for someone they already follow.

7/ We treat engagement on our team's posts as a buying signal.

→ We qualify whoever engages with posts from our team's active LinkedIn profiles.
→ We stack that with other signals: a site visit, trial activity, ad engagement.
→ The warm ones go to sales while the signal is fresh, and the message opens with whatever the person did.

8/ We fixed the product before we pushed more traffic.

→ Before anything else, I ask: if traffic doubled tomorrow, would the business be better, or just busier?
→ If it's busier, we fix what new users see first. We tier every signup against our ideal customer, and the best fits get a human on day 1.

9/ We waited until $10M ARR to run any ads.

→ First 5 months of LinkedIn ads: $21,404 spent, 24.9x ROAS.
→ The same ad made back 5.7x on a broad audience and up to 91x on people who already knew us. I don't fully trust that 91x, because some of them would have bought anyway.
→ When a post from our team takes off with $0 behind it, we test ad budget behind that exact post.

10/ We stopped trusting the attribution report for word of mouth.

→ Picture a buyer who heard about us in a Slack thread, saw 3 posts from our team, then clicked a Google ad. Google gets the credit.
→ So we check 2 other things. The first is what share of revenue comes in without anyone reaching out first. That's the 90% from the top.
→ The second is whether word of mouth keeps running while I'm on holiday.

Quick PSA for any founder who wanted to raise even when the business didn’t need it.

(Coming from someone who's doing $13M ARR now).

I was once in this EXACT position. The urge to raise was tied to 3 things that had nothing to do with strategy:

1. Scarcity mindset

If you've never lived in a home where your ceiling is someone else's floor, this part might not land. But for me, raising was about making sure I never had to go back.

Money in the bank meant safety. Safety meant if HeyReach blew up, I could build something else. If that blew up, I could build something after that. I was buying myself permission to keep trying.

I used to tell myself "I cannot NOT make this happen. I'm not going back there." I meant it. I still mean it. But I was treating a fundraise like an emergency exit when what I actually needed was to trust the thing I was already building.

2. I wasn't honest with myself about what I actually wanted to build

I wanted to compete with Clay or Apollo and build the biggest sales engagement platform in the world.

> I said it on calls
> I said it in pitch decks
> I said it to my team

At some point I started believing it.

But deep down I knew it wasn't true. I didn't wake up excited about becoming a multi product beast. I woke up excited about making HeyReach the best LinkedIn outreach tool anyone had ever used.

The problem was, "build the biggest" sounds like ambition. "Build the best version of one thing" sounds small. When you are chasing the VC's "idea of success", building a "non-billion dollar business and being independent" sounds small. But actually it's not - it's the key to freedom, and a true success.

I was repeating someone else's definition of success back to them and calling it my goal. 

3. The startup rat race

The whole VC industry pushes you to be a workaholic. Sleep-deprive yourself. Grind 12 hours a day. 

I was watching 20-something-year-olds in San Francisco who raised millions live like this:

> Windowless bedrooms
> Mattresses on the floor
> 12 hour workdays
> 10 years of grinding to build something that might get disrupted anyway

That's not the life I wanted.

Raising is a tool. It's not an accomplishment. If you can't use the tool well, it's cheaper to not use it at all.

It depends entirely on what kind of business you want to build and what kind of life you want to live while you build it.

One of my sales reps DOUBLED his reply rate on LinkedIn last month.

He didn’t rewrite his copy or “optimize” his offer. 

All he did was implement 3 simple signals into the process:

1. The company is hiring for ops or fulfillment. 

Job posts for ops, account managers, or fulfillment roles tell you they have capacity issues right now. reference the role directly in your outreach and it beats any generic opener you could write.

2. Someone recently left the company. 

This gives you 2 angles.

Either that person is now at a new company and might need what you offer there.

Or the old company just lost capacity and now has a gap to fill.

Both are stronger triggers than spraying the same message at a static list.

3. A prospect gives a positive reply. 

The signal here is not the reply itself, it is how fast and how relevantly you respond to it.

text: It took me three years to realize that you’re almost always better off bootstrapping your company than raising money.

You can just:

- Start an account on X
- Share your wins, your failures, and the lessons 
- Engage with everyone in your space 3-4x a day
- Connect with the creators and founders worth knowing
- Get your whole team posting alongside you

And slowly, you build a content loop where you're everywhere.

It was the best decision I made when I was just starting. 

My only regret is not starting sooner.

I remember the moment we hit $400K ARR.

Our investors from my previous company said: 

“Nice, from here everything is upside.” 

But before that, it was really hazy, just a loop of trying to do this and that.

> Hundred times of quitting
> Nobody believing
> Investors saying ‘no’ anytime we mentioned our product

We'd been stuck between $8-9K MRR for like six months, and we couldn't scale past it. 

That was the moment we decided we needed to niche down, so we niched down to lead gen agencies, and that's when we doubled. We hit $19K, then the next month we doubled again, hit $30K-something, then doubled and doubled.

It was proof that we had potential product market fit, and our ICP was lead-gen agencies. 

The product was good for a given ICP, so we doubled down on that. 

> We iterated 
> We listened to the feedback 
> And we were super focused on that segment

Lesson there.

We hit $10M ARR on pure word-of-mouth. 100% organic, 2,600+ free trials a month, basically $0 on ads. If I had a chance to do it all over again, I wouldn’t do it this way for sure.

Because word-of-mouth is an effect. You can earn it, you can engineer the conditions for it. What you can't do is open a dashboard and turn it up when you need $200K more in pipeline this quarter. It speeds up when it feels like it, and slows down when it feels like it. You're always slightly at its mercy.

The moment this realization dawned upon me was mid-2025. After months of adding $1M a month, our MRR stagnated for three weeks straight.

We just... stopped. I panicked hard. I thought this was it, we'd hit the ceiling, the "stuck" stage @RetentionAdam talks about.

And I had no lever to pull. There was no campaign to launch or budget to push, nothing I could turn on to fix it. All I could do was wait and pray it was seasonality.

2/ $1M - $10M

4. Suppress anyone you've already touched.

5. Never send a connection request to someone you're already connected to.

Split the list by connection status. The ones already in your network get a direct message. The rest get a request. Sending "let's connect" to a 1st-degree connection is the fastest way to look like a bot.

6. Open with the exact post they reacted to.

Reply rate is the most misleading number in outbound.

I looked at 96,000 campaigns on HeyReach. For most teams, reply rate was the wrong thing to watch the entire time.

The number to track instead 👇

Reply rate blends two separate problems into one score:
→ did people accept your request? (a targeting question)
→ did they reply after you messaged? (a messaging question)

When it drops, you can't tell which one broke. So you rewrite your copy when the real problem was your list. Or you rip apart your targeting when the opener was the issue.

The number that actually isolates it:

RTA: Replies ÷ accepted connections.

It measures your messaging alone, and the benchmarks from those 96k campaigns are clean:
→ under 10%: something's broken, stop and fix it
→ around 18%: median, you're average
→ 28% and up: top tier

One stat that stuck with me: 10.7% of those campaigns had accepted connections and still got zero replies. People said yes, and nothing that followed earned a single response.

Average and elite teams send the same volume. The elite ones just say something specific to a tighter list.

An accept and a reply are two different decisions. People accept at almost zero effort. They only reply when it's relevant. Don’t track the both as a single number.

In 2021, while I was still at university and building Howitzer (a reddit outreach tool), I raised money from investors.

It was the biggest investment that ever happened in Macedonia - $500k.

I took money from one VC fund (DayOneCapital), and 2 angels who believed in my idea. I was a 22 year old college student. I blew their money a year after, as Howitzer didn’t work.

Now, nearly 5 years after that, I returned their money.

@heyreach_io became a huge, seriously profitable company, and it was a time to pay back what I owned.

If these guys didn’t believe in me back in the days, I wouldn’t be here.

We took @heyreach_io from one customer paying $139/mo to $17M ARR in a little over 3 years, fully bootstrapped.

One of my friends told me that if I lost all of it today, in a year I'd have a business doing at least $1M ARR again. He's right, and here's exactly how I'd do it:

1. I wouldn't try to innovate much

I'd bootstrap a B2B SaaS selling to SMBs again. Same thing as last time.

Creating a category is expensive, both in money and in time. So I'd find a category that already exists, pick one specific function inside it, and make that function 10x better. Then put it in an offer that's really hard to say no to.

The market is already there, so you're not spending years convincing anyone the problem exists. And if you honestly believe you can be 10x better at something, it usually means you've dug into that problem enough to already have an angle. The offer ends up doing a lot of the selling too. Pylon or Atlas are what I'd point at here.

We launched @heyreach_io into a market that already had 400+ tools in it.

2. I'd go to market way before I felt ready

The moment I had something working I'd start selling it. I'd go at my own network first and try to get any social proof I could, then just get the thing in front of as many people as possible.

If I was starting today I'd go on AppSumo right after the beta. Most of those users won't be the ICP and a lot of them won't stick around... but they tell you everything that's wrong with the product, and it generates a lot of runway. Think of it as a pre-seed round.

3. I'd learn how to sell my own product from zero

Doesn't matter if someone has 20+ years in sales. Selling YOUR product is its own thing and everyone starts at the beginning with it.

The part I'd focus on is picking up the lingo of your customers and saying it back to them. When we first launched the feature of multiple LinkedIn senders, we called it "multi-account outreach". It was the customers that completely changed its name.

4. I'd get profitable, then obsess over PMF

@VukConfidential told me something when he started consulting us: you can breathe more easily once you become profitable.

So I'd obsess over becoming profitable, and only after that go all in on reaching PMF.

The biggest mistake you can make at this stage is focusing on processes, rules, optimizations, missions or vision. At this stage you are not a CEO, you are a product person trying to see if there's a need for the product.

When you don't have PMF, whatever you do just doesn't work. Once you get to PMF, whatever you do just works, to some extent.

PMF is the defining moment of your company, and until you reach it you are dying.

"doesn't LinkedIn ban accounts for using tools like yours?"

No.

Two different things get called a ban and people keep confusing the two.

One is a sending account getting restricted for pushing automation past LinkedIn's limits. The other is LinkedIn wiping your profile and company page off the platform. The second one happened to me. I'll get there.

Sending accounts get restricted for behavior against a limit. LinkedIn caps you at around 200 actions a day, and almost everything counts, a profile view, a like, a message.

The ones that get banned are probably blowing straight past it, or running through some tool that keeps changing their login location so the account looks like it's in four countries a week.

Back in October 2024 we were already pushing 60,000,000 actions a month through LinkedIn, for thousands of customers. If @heyreach_io was what got people banned, there'd be no company here.

So the whole product of ours is built on guardrails:

- Hard caps per account. Hit the limit and it freezes, you can't override it
- Volume spreads across senders. Run 5 accounts or 55, none of them ever breaches a limit

Inside those limits people are making killer money out of LinkedIn.

@Luke_Bivens ran one campaign for a client. 359 connection requests, 17 qualified meetings, $2.5M+ in qualified pipeline, with leaders at Microsoft, Slack and Sprinklr.

LinkedIn is still the best B2B channel on the internet. I've been saying it for years and I'm going to keep saying it.

Now the other kind. LinkedIn nuked my profile. 22k followers. My co-founder's too, and our company page, another 20k. Gone overnight.

That wasn't a sending account tripping a limit, that was our brand presence. Whatever their reasoning was, it's not what this question is about.

I was worried for about a week. Then NOTHING happened. The ban didn't affect our growth. We're at $17M ARR now.

And our users never slowed down. Since March they've sent 50M+ connection requests and pulled 2.6M+ replies out of LinkedIn.

People who get banned on LinkedIn cut corners. People who don't, don't.

That's the whole reason we built @heyreach_io the way we did. Every sender stays inside LinkedIn's limits, automatically, and your outreach scales without burning a single account.

I challenged him a few weeks ago to write an article about the entire thing, and here you go:

The most underrated skill a founder can have is refusing to build the obvious next feature.

@heyreach_io is at $17M ARR with 7,000+ companies using it. We still have not built an email sequencer. Our customers run multichannel every day, they just run it through Instantly, Smartlead or EmailBison, and we built native integrations with all three instead of shipping our own.

The case for owning it ourselves is easy to make... and I've said no every time. Here's why:

1. I won't put our v1 against someone's v40

I know for a fact that no one cares how hard your SaaS or solution was to build for you. They'll just compare it against the best version of what they have already used. Might as well become #1 in your category.

@InstantlyAI is one of the most used email outreach tools. We're the most used LinkedIn outreach tool. There's a reason we got to where we are: focusing on a category we could dominate.

2. I won't sell anyone a compromise

None of the all-in-one tools are better than the two giants individually. Bundle one strong channel with a mediocre second one and you've built something that's a downgrade for everybody's main use case.

3. I count what it costs us every year

Email isn't something you ever finish. It's blacklists, warmup, deliverability tickets, and a potentially endless support queue.

We shipped the first of those integrations in a few weeks. An email product would still be eating into our roadmap today.

4. I integrate where we might (probably) be average

So instead of shipping a mediocre or average email tool we made the handoffs really good. Invite not accepted after 5 days, push the lead to email. Lead goes Interested on email, pull them back for a personal LinkedIn touch. We'll even find the verified email for you.

The customer gets the same outcome and we carry none of the cost.

I do believe the CEO should be the CPO, and most of that job turns out to be saying no to reasonable ideas. Every feature you say yes to is a permanent tax on your roadmap, your support team, and the one thing you're supposed to be best at.

We'd rather be the best at one thing than average at four. That's pretty much the whole strategy.

In the last 12 months, our customers ran nearly 100,000 LinkedIn outreach campaigns through @heyreach_io.

Our team studied acceptance rates, replies, sender setups, campaign size and duration across the whole dataset.

We put everything we found into one report: what good performance looks like, where campaigns break and what to fix before scaling.

Here are 50 LinkedIn outreach rules from the data that can help you build more pipeline:

First, know what “good” actually looks like.

1. Use the median as your primary benchmark. The averages were higher across all three core metrics, so the median gives you a more realistic picture of a typical campaign.

2. A typical campaign had 20.75% of its connection requests accepted, while the average across the full dataset was 23.85%.

3. An acceptance rate below 12.97% was weak. Once it moved above 31.78%, the campaign entered the stronger-performing range.

4. The report’s reply-rate benchmark was 22.22% at the median and 25.19% on average.

5. On that reported reply-rate metric, anything below 13.37% was weak, while anything above 33.33% was strong.

6. Reply-to-acceptance rate, or RTA, had an 18.10% median and a 21.23% average.

7. RTA fell into weak territory below 9.62% and strong territory above 28.89%.

8. RTA is calculated by dividing replies by accepted connections. It isolates what happened after someone agreed to connect and keeps the earlier stages of the funnel separate.

9. Put differently, a typical batch of 100 connection requests produced about 21 acceptances and fewer than four replies.

10. In 10.7% of campaigns, people accepted the connection request and then nobody replied. Not one person.

11. Another 15% of campaigns converted fewer than one in every ten accepted connections into a reply.

12. Combined, roughly one in four campaigns with accepted connections still produced almost no real conversations. Acceptance alone can make these campaigns look healthier than they are.

Use the numbers to diagnose the right problem.

13. When acceptance is weak, start upstream. The likely problem is the ICP, the quality of the list, the sender profile or the connection request itself.

14. When acceptance is healthy but RTA is weak, the list has already done its job. The first message or the sequence is now the more likely problem.

15. Treat overall reply rate as an outcome metric. It cannot diagnose the leak by itself, and any comparison is meaningless until you confirm which denominator is being used.

16. When RTA stays low across every campaign, the opening message is usually the common failure point.

17. When RTA changes significantly from one campaign to another, the message probably fits some segments but not others. That points to an ICP-to-message mismatch.

18. Do not rebuild the whole sequence first. Validate the opener, then check whether each follow-up gives the prospect a new reason to reply.

19. If acceptance suddenly falls, check suppression hygiene first, then the number of pending invitations, and finally the sending pace.

20. If acceptance remains healthy while replies decline, test the first two sentences of the message and the timing between steps before changing everything else.

21. A high total reply rate with very few positive replies can still be a bad result. It usually means the targeting or the relevance is generating objections instead of pipeline.

22. If replies arrive during steps one and two but disappear afterward, the next follow-up probably adds no new angle, proof or useful information.

23. If replies stay low across every step, stop polishing the sequence. Pause the campaign and rebuild a smaller, tighter list.

24. Track how quickly your team answers an interested reply. If that response time is high, adjust staffing windows so someone is available when the segment tends to answer.

Test without creating more noise.

25. Run Step 1 variations against the same audience, with the same timing, and change only one element. Otherwise you will never know what caused the result.

26. Do not judge a variation before it reaches at least 50 accepted connections. Below that threshold, you are mostly reacting to randomness.

27. Track positive replies separately from total replies. A polite rejection and genuine buying intent should never count as the same outcome.

28. Record the audience, timing, message change and result for every test. If performance improves, you should be able to trace the lift back to one decision.

29. Use one dashboard to compare campaigns and senders, then use another to compare segments. Blending both views makes the source of the problem harder to see.

30. Keep every KPI definition fixed from week to week. A changing denominator can manufacture an improvement that never actually happened.

Build the campaign so it can survive scale.

31. One HeyReach benchmark found that blank connection requests averaged 27% acceptance, compared with 22% for requests containing text.

32. Test both within your own audience: a blank request versus a short note that gives one specific, timely reason to connect.

33. If you use a connection note, give the prospect one current reason to connect. Do not turn the note into a product pitch or add a link.

34. Personalization matters most after the connection is accepted. Targeting and sender credibility do more of the work before that point.

35. The guide caps personalization at two meaningful inputs per contact. Adding more signals created more work without improving conversion.

36. Store the reason for the outreach and the source that proves it. Fields such as trigger_reason and proof_link make every personalized opener auditable.

37. Map one or two adjacent stakeholders inside each target account before launching. If the primary contact is wrong, you already know who else may own the problem.

38. Give every follow-up a different job. One should reconnect to the original context, one should offer something concrete, and the final one should close the loop cleanly.

39. Use one suppression list across every sender. Without it, two people from your team can contact the same prospect and destroy the trust you were trying to build.

40. Apply global stop rules for replies, booked meetings and do-not-contact requests. Once a prospect acts, every sender should stop automatically.

Finally, scale the part that is already working.

41. Campaigns with fewer than 100 contacts averaged 21.43% acceptance.

42. Campaigns with more than 1,000 contacts averaged 19.35% acceptance. That is a decline of only 2.08 percentage points from the smallest campaigns.

43. The reported reply-rate metric stayed between 21.67% and 23.08% across the different volume tiers. Volume alone is a poor explanation for falling replies.

44. When a large campaign underperforms, inspect the list before rewriting the copy. Scale usually exposes weak segmentation and lower-fit prospects before it exposes a writing problem.

45. Single-sender campaigns had a 22.22% median reported reply rate. Campaigns using six to 20 senders performed better, reaching 25%.

46. Once campaigns used 50 or more senders, the median reported reply rate fell to 20.33%. More sender accounts were not associated with better reply performance.

47. Campaigns running for fewer than 30 days showed a 13.33% median acceptance rate and a 14.29% reported reply rate.

48. Campaigns running for 180 days or more showed 26.99% acceptance and a 28.26% reported reply rate.

49. Do not read the duration numbers as proof that keeping a weak campaign alive will improve it. Part of the gap is survivorship: campaigns that work stay live, while weak ones get paused or rebuilt.

50. The order (that matters): fix targeting until people accept, fix the post-acceptance message until they reply, and only then add more volume.

$139/mo → $1M ARR
AppSumo bought us time.
We focused on lead-gen agencies.
Unlimited LinkedIn senders for one fixed price.

$1M → $2M ARR

$2M → $3M ARR
Rewrote the backend while keeping customers online.
Added weekend support and helped trial users launch campaigns.
Trial-to-paid conversion rose from 17.5% to 19.1%.

$3M → $6M ARR
Added quarterly and annual plans.
Ran LinkedIn outreach events with Clay across Europe.
Cut ads after two months of testing. Growth sped up.

$6M → $7M ARR
Shipped workspaces and user permissions.
Agencies could separate client accounts and control who had access.
Missing those features had been our biggest reason for lost deals and churn.

$7M → $8M ARR
Launched our creator program and LinkedIn MCP.
Creators taught the workflows. Customers could run outreach through AI agents.
Reached 2,600+ trials a month without ad spend.

$8M → $10M ARR
Gave creators higher commissions and sent them leads for their agencies.
Affiliate links accounted for $1M ARR.
We contacted old trial users who had started visiting our website again.
An $800 ad test brought in 17 customers.

$10M → $16M ARR
@Vick_Mucunski rebuilt onboarding and flagged customers who stopped using the product.
Revenue churn fell from 9% to 7%.
Recovered 30% of failed-payment revenue in four days.
Helped customers use more seats and new workflows. Some cancellation calls became upgrades.

$16M → $17M+ ARR
188 existing customers paid us another $100,865 in 30 days.
The offer: pay for 3 months, get 6.
Discounts on quarterly and annual plans when paid upfront.

What I've added above are some of the major growth plays and decisions at each milestone. Full breakdown below.

Building a SaaS in 2026?

Here's my best advice after we went from almost bankrupt to $17M ARR, fully bootstrapped:

1. Don't invent a category. We launched into a market with 400+ tools.

2. Ship early. We called our multi-sender feature “multi-account outreach” until customers renamed it for us.

3. Pick one ICP. Building for everyone kept us stuck.

4. Get profitable first. Then immediately obsess over PMF.

5. If you're not growing, you're dying.

6. At the start, CEO is a fancy title. You're product, sales, marketing, ops and support. That's why I believe the CEO should also be the CPO.

7. Keep the team as small as possible.

8. Great customer support is the real growth hack. At our worst, we had 200+ tickets a day and 10-hour first responses.

9. Be patient. You probably won't achieve much in the first 3-6 months. That's normal.

Venture was already an unnatural way to build most businesses. AI just makes it more obvious imo.

We're getting tools to build with fewer people and less money... and somehow the thing we're supposed to celebrate is raising a round so big you HAVE to build a huge company.

We bootstrapped @heyreach_io to $17M ARR. If we hire people we can't afford, I can't pay their salaries with a story about where we'll be in 3 years. The business has to pay them.

That's the part of the VC game that bothers me. You can keep buying customers who'll never pay back what they cost, show everyone a growing revenue chart and raise again. More money comes in, more people join, everyone thinks it's working.

Then the next round doesn't happen and suddenly "it didn't work out."

The people who took a pay cut for your equity probably have a longer version of that story.

AI should reduce how much of your company you need to sell to get it built. I don't see why it should buy founders another few years of pretending the numbers will fix themselves.

Cold email has been dying for years already.

It just won't be a sudden snap where everyone wakes up and it's gone. It gets a little more annoying, a little more expensive and a lot more laborious every year.

A few years ago, you could find a billionaire's email, press send and honestly expect it to reach them.

Today? Good luck.

Before the first cold email even goes out, you need a gazillion things set up. Extra domains, inboxes, warmup, DNS, blacklists, deliverability... then you start sending and hope you don't burn the domain before you understand if the list or the copy works.

LinkedIn is the better place to start today.

You can launch a campaign right away and within a few hours start seeing what is happening. The feedback isn't perfect, but it narrows things down fast.

Low acceptance usually points you back to the list or profile. No replies after acceptance still leaves a few things to inspect: the message, offer, timing, follow-up, or the rest of the sequence.

Every profile also has a face, work history, posts and mutual connections. There is context before the first message.

IMO, email still has a place inside a multichannel motion. I'd start on LinkedIn, use email where it makes sense, and let content and warm intros do some of the work around both.

Cold email will probably keep working for a long time. There will just be fewer and fewer teams willing to do all that work for one channel.

text:
Building a SaaS and drowning in good ideas?

So do I, and I've stopped trying to fix that. I built a way to work around it instead.

That's basically the CPO job, and I do believe the CEO should be doing it. Here's how:

1. The roadmap starts with boring inputs

Churn reasons. Closed-lost reasons with their revenue potential next to them. Support tickets. Feature requests never go straight on the list, we write down the problem hiding behind them first.

2. We almost never build what was asked for

Customers care about solving their problem as soon as possible. How it fits the rest of the product is my job, not theirs. Campaign Analytics 2.0 took 50+ user interviews and a rework from scratch.

3. Sometimes the answer is an integration

Our own email sequencer was the obvious next feature. I've said no every time. Our customers already ran Instantly, Smartlead and EmailBison, so we integrated with all three. The first one shipped in a few weeks.

4. We don't have a three-year roadmap

We know roughly 80% of what we'll ship this quarter, maybe 50% of the year. Then we pick three battles and drop the rest.

5. Seven phases, and I'm only operational in the first

Idea, wireframe, design, development, testing, launch, revision. I talk to customers, simplify the feedback, draw the first wireframe, then hand it over and review.

6. When my judgment is wrong, I own the consequences

I switched our support tooling in two days to save $3K a month. It cost us at least $15K a month in churn. I unfckd what I fckd up, then got out of the way of the person who rebuilt the department.

In 2023 we were 3 months away from bankruptcy and stuck at $8K MRR. AppSumo bought us runway that summer, and for the rest of the year LinkedIn outreach we ran ourselves brought in 61.4% of our revenue and 523 qualified meetings we sat in.

If I had to build pipeline on LinkedIn from zero tomorrow, here's how I'd do it:

1. I'd fix my profile before I sent a single request

Everyone you reach out to opens your profile before they decide anything, so that page is essentially doing your selling for you. There are tons of resources and pointers on how to setup your profile up. So I'm not going to repeat that.

2. Most of my time would go into the list

Back in 2023 we measured Sales Navigator handing back around 31% dirty data, and idk what it is today but it isn't zero. So I'd pull the list, check the data is real, cut anyone who hasn't posted in three months, and only then start sending.

The best list I know is free anyway. It's the hundred or so people who reacted to your last 5 posts, it takes 30 minutes to pull, and they already know who you are (given you're posting actively on LinkedIN).

After that I'd stop looking at job titles and start looking for a signal that I can act on, so the outreach is timed well.

3. I'd warm them up before asking for anything

Like something they posted in the last 2-3 days, then send the request. "Nick liked your post" hits their notifications while they're still in there, so by the time the request shows up, you're a familiar name to them.

4. The request goes out empty

27% of blank requests get accepted, against 22% for the ones carrying a note. We arrived at this data point after going through nearly 100k LinkedIn campaigns sent through @heyreach_io.

5. I'd treat the first message like a message

Not an email.

I'd write two lines, ask one thing they can answer without thinking about it, and then leave them alone until they reply.

Don't run NPC sequences like a blank request, then "thanks for accepting!", then a wall of text with a calendar link at the bottom. You've received that one this week. It works 0% of the time.

I'd also answer fast. I try to get to anything that comes in within 15 minutes, cuz that's the cheapest thing on this whole list.

6. Track replies on accepted connections. Not just the reply rate.

Reply rate divides by everyone you sent to, so a campaign can look fine and be dead.

The number I'd prefer tracking is replies over accepted connections.

Low acceptance generally indicates a list problem. But if you get connection acceptance, and still no response, then it might have to do with your copy and framing.

7. I'd only scale once the six above actually work

And I'd do it sideways. Every account carries that same ceiling from step 1 above (200 actions/day on LinkedIn), so more volume has to mean more accounts. 6 to 20 sending accounts is where reply rates peak in our data.

What I wouldn't do is add senders to a campaign that's broken somewhere in 1 through 6. That just spends the limits faster on the same outcome.

Fin.

Paying for Sales Navigator and still getting cut off at 2,500 results is annoying as hell.

2. Check which searches still exceed 2,500 results.

text:
HeyReach was stuck at $8K MRR for 5 months in 2023.

We didn't even know who we were selling to. Recruiters, individuals, sales teams of every size, agencies... basically anyone with a LinkedIn account.

The pricing didn't help either. We launched at $149/mo per LinkedIn sender, way more expensive than anything on the market, for a buggy product with half the features the competitors had. 

Total disaster. 

So we dropped to $79/mo with discounts for 10+ and 50+ senders and thought we cracked it.

Nope. That's the exact pricing that kept us at $8K.

A month before How to Web in Bucharest, Ilija came to me with this:

"Dude, we've had 597 sales calls so far, and the data says we MUST niche down to agencies! This is the way to go!"

It sounded scary and I was pretty sure recruiters were our vertical (our booth poster at How to Web literally said "next-gen outreach tool for leadgen & recruitment agencies", lol).

The people we met and the energy at that conference are what finally made us push toward agencies. First thing I did when we came back was give the green light to redesign the website and the pricing page, and niche down specifically to lead-gen agencies.

We rebuilt the offer around agencies: unlimited LinkedIn senders for one fixed price.

The next month we 2.5x-ed revenue and became initially profitable. The month after, another 1.5x. We hit $1M ARR 6 months after niching down, and today we're at $17M ARR, still fully bootstrapped.

What I took from it:

1. Niche down to grow. After we picked lead-gen agencies & sales teams, we grew 26% MoM on avg during that early stretch.

2. Listen to your sales calls and your closed-lost deals. The calls pointed us to agencies, and after that our closed-lost deals basically built our roadmap.

3. IMO the offer is the biggest growth lever you have early on, and you won't nail it at the beginning. Launch with the price & offer that makes sense to you and listen to the market. Almost always, it will tell you what works.

Wrote the whole story down here 👇

Back in 2023, we opened up the first free beta of @heyreach_io.

More than 200 companies signed up. We gave them 30 days to try it. 126 were actively using it, getting results and telling us they loved it.

Then the beta ended, and we asked them to pay. Only one company converted.

I couldn't understand it. These companies were already getting value from the product. They'd told us that themselves. What was missing?

I was treating signups, active usage and positive feedback as proof that people would pay.

I'd decided those people would become customers.

That's an easy assumption to make when everyone keeps telling you how much they love what you're building.

So before calling a product validated, I'd want someone to buy it.

We still offer free trials at HeyReach. I want people to try the product in their own workflow before paying.

But looking back, my mistake was deciding we'd found the answer while everyone was still using it for free. I was stopping the test too soon.

Getting the payment is the next test. Then comes the work of making sure the customer gets what they paid for.

> Help them get a result.
> Find out where they get stuck.
> Talk to the people who stay and the people who leave
> Use the feedback to improve the product.
> Then try selling it again to people with the same problem.

That's the loop I mean when I talk about finding product-market fit. You keep learning from sales, usage and churn, then taking those lessons back into the product and the offer.

A good sign of PMF is also when a specific type of customer keeps using the product, gets value from it, keeps paying, and you can find more customers like them who do the same.

Until that starts repeating, I wouldn't pour money into getting signups and call it growth. I'd rather understand what happens to the people already brought in.

Before you decide LinkedIn outreach doesn't work, check these 6 things.

I think LinkedIn is one of the best ways to grow pipeline, and it gets better with cold email running next to it.

These six recommendations below are a result of studying nearly 100k campaigns that ran on @heyreach_io over the last one year (link to the full report in the replies):

1. Count how many accept, then how many of those write back

Send 100 requests and about 21 people accept. Out of those 21, about 4 write back. That's a typical campaign.

Look at those two separately, they break for different reasons.

If almost nobody accepts, the problem is usually at the targeting level or to do with your profile. Check: who you picked, how your profile looks, what the request said.

Plenty of accepts and then silence? That's the message you send after.

2. Try sending connection requests with no note at all

Blank requests got accepted 27 times out of 100. Ones with a personalized note got 22. I was sure it was the other way round.

The note does help, just later. Once they accept, a short specific line lifts replies.

Cold list, test both. People who already know you, skip it.

3. Cut the list until you can say why each person is on it

"VP Sales, US, SaaS" gives you about 4,000 people with nothing in common. "VP Sales at 11 to 50 employee SaaS companies that posted an SDR job in the last 60 days" gives you about 400.

Every list starts as a few hundred hand-picked prospects and fills up with "might as wells". Those go first.

4. Fix the profile before you touch the copy

A profile with nothing on it and 200 connections gets ignored no matter how good the connection note or the initial pitch is.

Go in this order: who you're messaging, then how your profile looks, then the copy.

5. Message them within three hours of them accepting

One agency running outreach for real-estate clients got to every new connection inside three hours. Not same day, under three hours. Their positive replies came in at 26%.

Open with the real reason you connected. Ask one question they could answer right away. No pitching right away, sending an elaborate deck, or asking for a "quick call?".

Then one follow up, three or four days later, with something they can use.

6. Go look at the best campaigns in the data

One in six gets 40 replies for every 100 conversations they start. At the very top, a recruiting campaign turned 800 connections into 571 replies in two weeks.

Completely different industries, and all of them doing the boring stuff above:

> They went narrow on who they messaged.
> The accounts doing the sending have real profiles behind them.
> And the first message makes it obvious why they're writing.

When you edit a draft, save the reason in the lessons file. If a pricing answer needs more context, write down what was missing so the Dot has a rule to refer to next time.

Kind 1: software you use yourself. A scraper, a dashboard, a bot that scores your own leads. One user, and it only has to work when you open (or use) it.

Kind 2: software other people pay for. For eg: 7,000+ companies run their LinkedIn outreach on ours.

He's probably right about kind 1. Vibe code it. The maintenance is yours and it's kinda nothing:

- you're the only user, so nobody finds the bug before you do
- nobody paid, so nothing was promised. it can be down for a week
- it runs on your account and your laptop. no caps, no proxies, no permissions, no billing
- when it breaks, you fix it when you feel like it (or you don't)

Our first product, Howitzer, started as a Reddit DM script Stefan and I ran for ourselves. Kind 1.

- the platform you built on changes the rules and you're still able to make things work.

- other people's workflows run through it. Agencies have us wired into Clay, Instantly and Smartlead, so every change we ship has to not break any of that

Sure, the era of personal software is here, but there's far more nuance to it, than calling software or SaaS dead.
