What's the first sign a client is at risk?

One of the first things I built at @heyreach_io was a system to flag clients who are quietly on their way out, while there is still time to do something about it.

We looked at more than a dozen possible signals and shipped 7.

The one that I found to be the most significant is inactivity, and it's the one many companies oversimplify. They read it as "hasn't logged in." No, inactive accounts point to much deeper problems in many cases.

So we track five things together: last login over 7 days ago, no API usage, no webhook activity, no platform actions, and no outward-facing engagement.

One of those on its own doesn't mean much. All five at once is a client who has already started to leave, well before they would say so.

The reason we lead with inactivity is timing.

The difference between catching it at day 7 and catching it at day 30 is huge.

At day 7, the client still remembers you and is probably just busy or stuck.

By day 30, they have usually found another way to work and moved on in their head.

I asked a former client once why they left. They said, "Honestly, we never really figured out how to get value from it."

That's how most of these go.

By the time someone clicks cancel, the real decision is weeks old, made in the stretch where the product slowly stops feeling necessary and nobody on our side notices.

A few weeks into running retention at @heyreach_io, I went deep into the churn data across dozens of accounts, looking for the pattern that repeated across the ones who left.

It was almost embarrassingly consistent. Users who get a real result in their first two weeks stay. Users who don't, leave. After that window, no discount and no win-back sequence brings them back.

So if a client hasn't had a genuine win by around day 14, calling what you're doing "retention" is generous. You're mostly just delaying the cancellation.

The product rarely failed those users. They were lost earlier, before they ever worked out how to get a win from it. Wrong targeting, unclear messaging, no real sense of what "good" was supposed to look like.

So we stopped treating it as a retention problem and treated it as an onboarding one.

We redesigned the first-touch guidance, shortened the time to first campaign, defined what a good first result looks like, and added nudges before the day-7 silence. That gave us our lowest churn rate on record.

I went into this assuming a lot of the churn was about price. The data barely backed that up. People left because the product never got them an early win.

Retention in outreach is just momentum. Get someone a win early and they build on it. Miss that window and they're already gone.

At that scale, 9% is a lot of revenue leaving every year.

Almost all of the company's attention was on the other side of the equation. Signups, trial conversion, pipeline.

Every week there was a new acquisition number to talk about. The clients who had quietly stopped using the product weren't really tracked anywhere, and nobody had mapped what happened between a client signing up and a client leaving without telling us why.

So that's where I spent my first few months. I didn't touch acquisition.

I mapped more than a dozen risk dashboards, reworked the cancellation experience, and redesigned the delinquent recovery flow.  Then we rebuilt the onboarding, because the churn data kept pointing there, and that redesign gave us our lowest churn rate on record.

Most of the clients we lost went quiet long before they cancelled. Around day 7 they would stop running campaigns. By month 3 they were gone, and from the outside it looked sudden, even though the signs had been there for weeks.

Acquisition gets all the focus at most companies, but without a strong retention play in place, new revenue will just keep replacing the leaky bucket that the pipeline is.

We built an in-house delinquent recovery flow at @heyreach_io and four days after it went live, it had clawed back 30% of what was failing. And two of those days were the weekend with nobody in the office.

Failed-payment churn is the cheapest revenue you will ever win back, and most teams leave it sitting on the floor. Here is the flow we built, step by step.

1. Stop treating failed payments as billing's problem.

Treat a failed card as a retention event. The customer didn't decide to leave. Their card expired, or hit a limit, and then silence did the rest. The moment you own that as churn instead of filing it under billing, you start saving it.

2. Retry on a schedule that matches why cards fail.

One retry and a shrug is why most recovery never happens. Cards fail for boring, fixable reasons, so we retry on a rhythm that gives those reasons time to clear, spaced across days instead of fired off all at once. Smart retries alone pull back a real chunk before a human is ever involved.

3. Make the message about fixing a card, not chasing a debt.

Tone is the whole game here. Nobody answers a payment demand. People answer a clear, friendly heads-up that something needs a quick fix, with the link sitting right there. Take the friction and the faint shame out of it and the recovery rate climbs on its own.

4. Reach the human, not just the dunning email.

The standard setup lives entirely in one automated email that lands in a promotions folder nobody opens. We reach across more than one channel so the message gets seen, and none of it needs a rep sitting there sending it.

5. Let it run around the clock.

This is the part I love. Two of our first four recovery days were the weekend. The system doesn't keep office hours, and a big share of what came back came back while literally nobody was working.

Hope is not a retention strategy.

The payment processor will not chase those cards for you with any care, and a generic one-and-done email won't either. Build the flow once, and it quietly recovers revenue while you get on with everything else.

Everyone was calling it the SaaSpocalypse. Churn up, budgets tightening, half the timeline writing SaaS's obituary.

We  @heyreach_io were quietly having our best retention month on record. Here is what actually held the line, because it was never one heroic move.

1. We didn't make the panic moves.

When the market gets scary, the reflex is a fire-sale discount or a rushed "churn-killer" feature. We did neither. Both buy you one noisy week and cost you margin and focus for months. The accounts you rescue with a panic discount are usually the ones halfway out the door already.

2. We let the boring systems do the work.

The month didn't come from anything new. It came from systems that had been compounding for a while: dashboards that flag a wobbling account early, an onboarding flow rebuilt to get people a real win in week one, a recovery flow clawing back failed payments in the background. None of it trends on anyone's feed. All of it keeps customers.

3. We watched the leading indicators, not the headlines.

The discourse outside was loud. The only signals I cared about were ours. A drop in usage around day 7. An account that went quiet between check-ins. Those tell you about churn weeks before a cancellation does, and they do not care what the market is doing that month.

4. We made every renewal a value conversation, not a price one.

When budgets tighten, every tool gets put on trial. So we walked into renewals with proof of what we had moved for that client. A tool that can show its work keeps its seat. The ones that can't are first on the chopping block the moment the CFO comes looking.

5. We kept building while it got loud.

This part is the team, not me. The noise outside did not change the work inside. We shipped, measured, and fixed in a scary month exactly the way we do in a calm one.

The SaaSpocalypse looks less like the end of SaaS and more like a cull of the tools that stopped earning their seat. The month we had came down to a pile of unglamorous systems doing exactly what they were built to do, on the month it mattered most.

What I couldn't see at the time was that hospitality had already trained me for the rest of it. Happy guests, furious guests, the ones who just needed someone to listen. I'd handled all of it for years. I didn't have a job title that made it count yet.

In December 2021 I landed my first real role through LinkedIn. It wasn't the one I wanted. It was close enough to keep moving, so I took it and decided to outwork everyone around me. Most weeks that meant 12-hour days nobody asked me to do. I wanted to earn the seat.

From there it went to account management, then bigger clients and longer deal cycles, then building a client success department from nothing as a director. Every place I landed was missing the same thing: real systems.
No playbooks, no process, people holding it together by effort. So I built the systems. Churn reduction, onboarding, upsell, all the things the job itself never handed me, I taught myself on the side.

That road runs all the way to now, and it led me to being the Chief Client Officer at HeyReach instead, a $15M SaaS.

Hospitality taught me more about people than any course could have, and you don't realize it's training while it's happening. Strip retention back and it's the same job I had behind a front desk. Make sure the person in front of you gets what they came for, before they have to ask for it.

The version of me on Upwork in 2021 with no offers had no idea any of this was coming. If that's where you are right now, neither do you. Keep going.

You don't need twenty scripts to run a great account.

After almost ten years in client work, the same 5 conversations keep showing up across the accounts that actually retain. Get these right and most of what people call a retention problem never forms in the first place.

1. The onboarding alignment call.

This is the one that sets the ceiling for everything after. You define what success looks like for this specific client, in their words, and you write it down so nobody is guessing later. Most teams burn this call on a tour of process and tools. The accounts that churn early almost always trace back to a kickoff that skipped the part where you agree on what winning even means.

2. The early-momentum call.

Clients go quiet long before they ever go unhappy. What they lose first is the sense that they are getting somewhere, and that fade is invisible if you are only watching deliverables shipped. So this call exists to put a win in front of them, early, while the relationship is still warm. Miss the window and you spend the rest of the engagement trying to rebuild a feeling you let slip.

3. The value check-in.

The weak version is "how's everything going?" The one that works walks them through where they started, what has measurably changed, and what is coming next. This is the call that decides whether you are someone they like or someone they keep. Run it on a rhythm, not only when something breaks.

4. The risk call.

The hard one, and the one most people avoid. When engagement dips or the tone on a call shifts, the instinct is to hope it passes. I would rather raise it directly while it is still a conversation. A reset that happens early can save six months of slow drift, and the client almost always respects you more for naming it before they had to.

5. The continuation call.

Don't leave it to the week the contract ends. Raise it while the current work is still landing, walk them through what worked, what is coming next, and let the next phase feel like the obvious step. Leave it to the end and you have turned a partnership into a quote war with three other agencies the client is suddenly comparing you against.

5 conversations, run on purpose and in order.

Master those and retention stops being the thing you scramble to save at the end. It becomes something the relationship just produces on its own.

Discounts have a role in retention but not for the reason you think. When an account is on the fence about churning, the reason is rarely the invoice.

The results have slipped, or never landed clearly enough, and a discount doesn't address that. It hands the customer a smaller invoice for the same unsolved problem and quietly tells them you agree the product wasn't worth what they paid.

What actually saves accounts at our scale is adding capacity: more LinkedIn sender accounts, more campaigns running in parallel, sometimes the email channel layered in through our Instantly integration.

A lot of the accounts at the fence are agencies running outreach for their own clients, and the math is simple: If they are already seeing real results on the senders they have, doubling those senders roughly doubles the meetings booked each month, which usually means more revenue from their end-clients, which makes the spend on us pay for itself comfortably.

The conversation only lands when the underlying results are real. We can sit with the account and say: "You are already converting on your current senders. Doubling them, on the same conversion, doubles your meetings each month. Most agencies we've done this with see the new numbers well before the next decision point."

A discount delays the loss by a month. Adding value is what gives the relationship a reason to grow.

When a SaaS account is about to cancel, the default move is always the same: drop the price. But it almost never saves the account.

We do offer discounts at @heyreach_io. But for a customer that's already on the fence, a discount doesn't fix what's broken. 

Their numbers fell off, or they never really saw the wins in the first place. A smaller invoice gives them the same broken setup at a lower price.

We've saved hundreds of accounts by adding capacity instead. 

More LinkedIn senders, more campaigns running in parallel, sometimes email on top through our Instantly integration.

If an agency is already converting on the senders they have, doubling those senders roughly doubles the meetings booked each month, and the extra revenue from their clients pays our bill several times over.

This only works when the results are already real. We can sit with the account and say: 

"You're already converting on what you have. Double it, on the same conversion, and you double your meetings."
 
Most agencies we've done this with see the new numbers well before they have to renew.

A discount buys you another month on most dying accounts, but adding more capacity is what helps you grow the account in the long run.

Today @heyreach_io crossed $16M ARR. I run retention and support, so I spend most of my time with the customers who were thinking about leaving.

I joined in February. We were at $10.5M then, 9% revenue churn, thousands of customers already on board.

Everyone assumes retention is hardest at a company that's falling apart. For me it's been the opposite. Trying to hold onto customers while the whole thing grows this fast, with people signing up quicker than you can learn their names, is the harder version of the job.

Honestly I got lucky with timing.

The brutal support era here was 2024, before me, when tickets swallowed the team and a real chunk of the churn was just people tired of waiting for a reply.

Ebru from our team rebuilt support after that. So by the time I showed up the building wasn't on fire, and I got to work on keeping customers instead of apologizing to them all day.

Then March happened and it got bad in a different way.

@nikolak47's LinkedIn got restricted, our company page went down with it, and there were people online more or less announcing our funeral.

I expected churn to spike that month. It went the other way. March ended up being our best retention month on record, and that one still surprises me.

I can't pretend we cracked some code. We mostly just started looking earlier.

We built a way to spot customers going quiet, the ones who stop logging in and stop using the product, before they email us to cancel.

Catch someone at day 7 and it's a conversation. Wait until day 30 and you're doing damage control.

We stopped reaching for a discount every time someone wanted out. A lot of them didn't want a cheaper plan, they wanted to get more out of what they were already paying for. So we gave them extra seats and better use cases instead, and a surprising number of those "I want to cancel" calls ended with the account getting bigger.

And we went and collected the money that was quietly failing in the background, cards bouncing, invoices not clearing.

Unglamorous work.

We got back about 30% of it in four days, two of which were a weekend.

Churn went from 9% to 7% in my first three weeks. Lowest the company had ever run. It wasn't a masterstroke, we just paid attention sooner than we used to.

So yeah, $16M today. The word of mouth and the product are @nikolak47 and @VukConfidential to talk about. I just wanted to give a nod to the customers who almost left and stayed.

Really glad I get to be here for this one. Back to work.

How to reverse a revenue leak in your SaaS:

I took over retention at @heyreach_io earlier this year with 9% churn on the door. About ninety days in, we hit the best retention month the company had ever recorded. What changed was three moves, run in one specific order.

Move 1: build a way to see the leak.

Ship one boring alarm this week. Pick the most obvious signal your product has (a last login older than seven days, an unpaid first invoice, a core feature untouched) and turn it into a live list of accounts at risk. Add six or seven more signals over the month.

Skip this and month one becomes theater. You design save flows for accounts you cannot yet identify, you fix things that were never causing churn, and the team looks busy while the number sits exactly where it was.

Move 2: fix the first fourteen days of the product.

Sort your accounts by whether they stayed past ninety days or left inside ninety, and you'll find that customers who saw a real result in their first two weeks stayed while those who didn't, left. Define "a good first result" as a measurable number, shorten the path from signup to it, and add guidance where your usage data shows people stalling.

Skip this move and try to save accounts on the phone instead, and your best AEs end up trying to talk customers out of a decision the customer already made in week two. Most retention projects get stuck here, sharpening the save script and blaming the pricing while the number refuses to move.

Move 3: kill the discount reflex on the save call.

Rewrite the script so the first offer is more product instead of less price. Extra seats, then unused capacity, then a feature the customer has been asking about. Discount only comes out after those, if at all.

Skip Moves 1 and 2 and Move 3 collapses into a discount factory. You cannot see who is really at risk, so you throw price at everyone to be safe, and once your market notices, every renewal turns into a negotiation.

Three questions any SaaS can answer this week:

1. Can you see the leak? If not, ship one boring alarm.
2. Can new users see a real result in their first fourteen days? Define it as a number.
3. When you save, is your first offer more product or a lower price?

That's how we ran it at @heyreach_io. If your revenue is leaking somewhere, this is the order I would run before I did anything else.

I sent cancellation notices to 260 paying customers. Hundreds paid us more.

The most controversial retention move I've ever run at HeyReach.

We gave each one 3 free seats for 30 days. No strings.

Behind it, a 5-email flow segmented by behavior.

Day 1: activation nudge.

Day 3: split the list by who actually touched the seats.

Day 7: halftime check.

Day 14: results check.

Day 27: removal-notice pre-warm.

Inside the first 72 hours, 14% had activated. ~40 had connected a fresh LinkedIn account on the extra seats. By the midpoint, ~60 were still actively running on the wider seat count.

Then on day 30 we sent the email most CS teams would flinch at.

> "Your extra seats are being removed in 3 days."

Same day, 20+ came back unprompted, asking to keep them.

Every retention consultant will tell you this is aggressive. Looks like a sales trick. Looks like punishing the users who didn't upgrade. They'd tell you to close a trial with a soft "thanks for trying us out" send.

That's the worst possible way to end a trial.

For 30 straight days those customers had been building the extra seats into their workflow. New team members were plugged in. Old campaigns were quietly running on the wider seat count. Roles had been reorganized around the extra headcount.

The removal notice forced a decision they had been putting off since day 1. Revert to the old workflow, or commit to the new one.

The removal is the sale.

The welcome is not.

Every free trial and every free-feature window I run at HeyReach now ends the same way. With a removal notice.

text:
Most SaaS teams watch day 30. The customer already decided on day 14.

I call it the Day-14 Stranger Test. One question: does the new customer still feel like a stranger to me on day 14?

If yes, you already lost them. They just haven't cancelled yet.

I built the test running retention on a paid community, which is SaaS on hard mode. 

Monthly billing, one-click cancel, no procurement moat, no golden handcuffs. 

From February 2025, Julian Goldie and I grew AI Profit Boardroom from 0 to over 1,200 paying members at $49/mo by September of that year, with no paid ads, no launch, and no affiliate program. 

50 by the end of week one. 100+ by the end of week two. 158 by February 21. Then it kept compounding.

The five moves that made the test pass every cohort:

1. Own the first 24 hours. Personal DM from a human, uses their first name, references one specific thing about their business, points them at the one thread that helps them fastest. Any distance they feel on day one gets stored as regret.

2. Give them a first-week win. One binary thing to close a loop on inside 7 days. Progress in the first week quiets the buyer's remorse voice before it reaches the cancel button.

3. Check in during week two. Six words: "How's it going, where are you stuck?" No pitch, no discount. Week two is the quietest window in the customer's head and the one nobody messages them in.

4. Public shoutout the moment they win. Named, specific, short. It changes who they are in the room. Once the community publicly calls someone a winner, cancellation gets emotionally expensive.

5. Run the playbook every cohort. Batch welcome DMs or skip week-two check-ins and the churn number moves. Not that week. Six weeks later. By the time it shows in the dashboard, it is already priced in.

The dollars change, the vehicle changes, the moves do not.

$49/mo community: move 1 is a DM. $500/mo SaaS: a personal Loom from CS. $10K/mo agency retainer: a kickoff call where the account owner already knows enough about the client to skip introductions.

Same move, different vehicle.

Day 14, ask yourself: does this new customer still feel like a stranger?

If yes, you already lost them. If no, they stay for a long time.

That is the whole test.

Retention is a butterfly effect.

A choice you make on a Tuesday in February decides the dashboard for the whole month of March. You rarely trace the line back, because by the time the number posts, the day it was decided has already scrolled off your calendar.

Two days from February built our best retention month on record at @heyreach_io

Feb 16. Umer from our GTM team and I turned on the inactivity alarm. Seven days with no login, no API call, no webhook, no platform actions. The account lands on the board while day 7 is still a conversation. Day 30 is damage control.

Feb 23. We tore up first-touch onboarding. Redesigned it around one job: get the user to a real result before day 7. We defined "good first result" in specific numbers, so the team stopped guessing and started nudging on signal.

Three weeks later, March started. The dashboard did the rest. Best retention month on record.

Here's the part people don't talk about. When you saw the March number, the work was already a month behind me. What looked like a great March was a decent February with follow-through.

That's true for most milestones you scroll past. The founder posting the win is a full quarter downstream of the day it was decided. You're watching the lagging indicator. The leading indicator was a Tuesday afternoon eight weeks earlier, on someone else's calendar.

The trap is planning your own wins for the month you want them.

The move is planning them for the month that decides them.

If you want a March, do the February work. The person you envy on your feed already did.

Every big number has a small day behind it.

I joined @heyreach_io early this year when their revenue churn was 9%. Six weeks later, we’ve had the best retention month in the company history.

Here’s the step-by-step playbook that made it possible:

1. Ship one boring health signal first.

Our GTM engineer Umer and I mapped twelve candidate signals in week two. We shipped seven. Inactivity went first: seven days without a login, no API calls, no webhook activity, no platform actions.

2. Fix the first fourteen days of the product.

I read the churn data on dozens of accounts in week three.

Users who saw a real first result inside fourteen days stayed. Users who didn't, left. Nothing after week two moved the curve.

So we shortened time-to-first-launched-campaign and wrote down what a "good first result" on HeyReach looks like: an account connected, a campaign live, one reply coming back on it.

3. Call three cancelled customers every week.

Exit surveys don't tell you what happened. A phone call does.

One customer told me, "honestly, we never really figured out how to get value from it." That single sentence can reshape a quarter of the roadmap.

4. Stop discounting on save calls.

In April we ran the opposite: 280 clients got three free HeyReach seats each for thirty days, and on revocation day more than twenty of them wrote in unprompted asking to keep the extra seats at the paid rate.

Hundreds have expanded on that pattern since. Zero closed on a discount.

5. Buy the retention tool last.

We only signed a platform contract once the workflow already existed and the morning query fit in one sentence. A tool bought before the workflow has nothing to amplify.

By six weeks we were on track for the best retention month in company history, and churn down to 7%.

By end of March hundreds of accounts that would have cancelled had ended up expanding instead.

Churn is an emotion long before it becomes a decision. The clients I have lost were still getting results the month they cancelled.

Weeks earlier, without saying a word, they stopped believing it was working. That is the moment they actually left.

And this is what dashboards cannot see. Usage, logins, outcomes, your analytics tracks all of it.

What it cannot track is the moment a client starts to feel unsure, and that feeling moves them long before any number does.

So next to the usage data, I track confidence. It leaves signals.

Confidence is rising when:

- Replies get faster and more detailed
- They ask sharp, forward-looking questions
- They share context you never asked for

Confidence is dropping when:

- Replies get short
- Calls start getting pushed
- The same concern comes up more than once

You will not find any of that in your product analytics. It lives entirely in how a client talks to you.

Results make a client satisfied. Confidence makes them stay. So watch the tone, not just the usage, and you catch the churn while it is still just a feeling.

There is one number that predicts whether a customer stays, and it is probably already sitting in your data. This is how you find it

1. Pull every account from the last 6 to 12 months and split them into two piles. The ones who are still here, and the ones who churned.

2. Now find the single action the survivors took in their first week or two that the churned group never got to. There is almost always one. A first campaign launched. A first result seen. A teammate invited. Something that happened early for the ones who stayed and never happened for the ones who left.

3. That action is your activation metric. Define it as a number you can measure.

When we ran this at @heyreach_io  across dozens of accounts, the pattern was blunt. Users who saw a real result in their first two weeks stayed. Users who did not, left.

So we stopped optimizing logins and rebuilt onboarding around that one result. We defined exactly what a good first result was, shortened the path to a live campaign, and started nudging accounts before day 7 instead of after.

The outcome: the lowest churn rate we had ever recorded.

A login tells you someone showed up. Your activation metric tells you they got what they came for. Find yours, then make onboarding a race to it.

The same 5 conversations keep separating the accounts that renew from the ones that leave. Run them in order and a retention problem will never form:

1. The alignment conversation.

Have it in week one. Agree on what winning actually looks like for this specific client, in their words, and write it down. Skip it and you spend the whole engagement optimizing a goal nobody agreed on.

2. The early-momentum conversation.

Clients go quiet long before they go unhappy. Put a real win in front of them early, while the relationship is still warm.

3. The value conversation.

Skip "how's everything going?" Walk them from where they started to what has measurably changed, and what is coming next. Run it on a rhythm, not only when something breaks.

4. The risk conversation.

When engagement dips or the tone on a call shifts, the instinct is to hope it passes. Name it early, while it is still something you can steer. Clients almost always respect you more for raising it.

5. The renewal conversation.

Start it 90 days before the contract ends, not the week of. Walk them through what worked and what is next, so the next phase feels like the obvious step.

Two senior people had just left by the time I stepped in. So the easiest thing would have been to hire fast and patch the gaps. But I did not do that.

What I did instead:

1. I spent the first few weeks rebuilding Fin ( @intercom 's AI Agent) from the ground up. I rewrote its logic, expanded what it could resolve on its own, and redid our entire knowledge base so it had real depth to pull from, 30+ new articles.

2. Then I brought the team in. They mapped out what Fin should handle, what it shouldn't touch, and the exact points where a human still needs to step in. Every rule in there came from the people who run support.

3. From there they started owning real parts of the operation, knowledge base, Stripe onboarding and billing, integrations.

To show where this is heading: one day last week, 25 conversations ran at 68% automation, 85% resolution, and a 100% CX score. Small sample, and I know it. But three months ago a day like that wasn't possible.

The numbers Nick posted came out of all of that. And the team's in a completely different place than they were three months ago.

Still plenty to build here, but a solid start nonetheless.

We recovered 30% of the revenue we were about to lose to failed payments. In four days. None of those customers had chosen to leave.

A big chunk of it was never a decision.

Somewhere between 20% and 40% of SaaS churn is involuntary: expired cards, declined charges, failed renewals. Customers who still want the product and never meant to go anywhere.

That makes it the easiest revenue you will ever recover, because there is no one to convince. The payment failed. You just need a system that catches it and follows up.

This is what actually recovers it:

- Retry timing: A charge retried at the wrong moment fails again. Retry at smarter times, like the days after a payday, and a real share clears on its own.

 - A dunning sequence: Most teams send one "your payment failed" email and give up. A short, escalating sequence that makes updating a card a single click recovers far more.

- A card updater: When a card expires or gets reissued, the card networks can push the new number to you automatically, so the charge goes through without the customer doing anything.

That is the system we rebuilt at @heyreach_io. Industry data puts recovery at 60 to 80% of failed-payment churn with a setup like this.

Most teams recover almost none of it, because they are busy fighting the churn they can see: the save flows, the win-back campaigns, the exit surveys, all aimed at customers who actually chose to leave.

Discounting to save a renewal is the one piece of retention advice I will never agree with.

We tested the opposite at @heyreach_io. Instead of dropping price for accounts at risk, we gave them more features. Hundreds of them expanded.

Because discount tells the client the product was overpriced the whole time, and that lower number becomes the one you negotiate against forever.

This is one of the core principles I run retention on, and @asmartbear (𝘧𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘧 WP Engine ) gave the cleanest version of it I've heard.

A client says yes to you six times before they ever say no once.

Look at what a lead had to do to become a your client:

- Find you -> click
- Not bounce off the homepage
- Survive the pricing page
- Get the budget approved
- Buy the thing
- Sit through onboarding

Six YESES in a row. So they also wanted it to make this work. Hence the churn they do is old.

Something broke long before anyone clicked the cancel button.

Read the first 30 days if you want to find out why a customer churned, not their last 30.

A quiet support queue used to feel like a good week to me. Now it worries me.

@btaylor tells a story here about a retailer that automated their support.

Their conversation volume went up 2 to 3x instead of down. Costs barely moved. The CEO was thrilled, because his customers were finally talking to him.

Every deflection case ever built assumes the number of questions is fixed. People ask more when asking gets easy.

So all of those extra conversations already existed. The client just decided it was not worth the wait, closed the tab, and went back to wondering whether this thing works for them.

That is the state clients churn from. Doubt they never bothered to voice.

text:
Cancellation reasons are the first thing I look at every week. This made me distrust every one of them. This is also why I rebuilt the cancellation experience at @heyreach_io

@asmartbear noticed a clear top churn reason at Smart Bear and thought it might be hoax, so they randomized the order of the list. After that every option got picked about equally.

His #1 reason was just the first line on the list. The data had been noise the whole time.

His fix is one word.

"Why did you cancel" to "What made you cancel" and usable replies went from 10% to 20%.

The last thing a client tells me before leaving is the most honest data I get all year. I am not collecting that in a picklist.

The most misused number in retention is Slack's 2,000 messages.

@stewart said back in 2015 that any team which exchanged 2,000 messages in its history almost never left. 93% still on it. Great finding.

But then everyone turned it into a rule, like 2,000 was a magic line that holds in any product.

It only ever held in Slack. That number came out of Slack's own churn, built on how people actually use Slack. It was never going to mean the same thing in yours.

I ran the same exercise on ours at @heyreach_io. Split the accounts that left from the ones that stayed, looked for the one early thing only the stayers did.

The accounts that got a real result inside the first 14 days stayed. The ones that did not mostly left, and no discount pulled them back.

I wouldn't run my retention on a figure I lifted off a 2015 blog post, even if it's a great one.

Came across the most interesting table I've seen in a while yesterday. Retention numbers for the games I burned my teens on.

So now I'm nostalgic and reading a churn report at the same time, which probably tells you what I do for a living.

Two rows tell the whole story. Paper io kept 49% of players on day one, Cashman Casino only 41%. By day 30 Cashman had almost double the players left, 15% against 8%.

Week one is where that got decided. Which is why day 7 is the number I watch at @heyreach_io.

If an account goes quiet and I catch it on day 7, that's still a conversation and I can ask how the setup is going. Catch the same account on day 30 and they have already moved on in their head, so now it's damage control.

The window looks the same in a casino app, and those two products could not be further apart.

Day one flatters everybody. That's why I don't celebrate it.

A couple of years back, CrowdStrike pushed an update that took 8.5M machines down. Worst outage in IT history. The first thing I wondered was their churn number.

To my surprise, almost none of it turned into churn. Gross retention moved less than half a point.

The churn they did get sat in the very small MSP accounts, by Kurtz's own read, while the larger and midsize deals held.

I'd seen a smaller version of the same thing at @heyreach_io.

We gave 280 of our clients three free seats for 30 days. 14% activated in the first 72 hours, about 60 were active at the midpoint, so most never really picked it up.

But on the day we took the seats back, 20+ asked to keep them, inbound and unprompted. My read is those were the accounts that had already built them into how they work.

The lesson I learnt from this was retention is really the cost of leaving.

Get your users woven deep enough into the workflow with great service so that the cost of leaving is higher for them than it is for you.

The AI churn wave is the new buzzword I've seen people talk about. But tbh, it's a fancy packaging for activation problem, and @poyark data across 3,500 companies is what convinced me.

AI-native companies keep 40% of their revenue over a year. B2B SaaS keeps 82%. But it has nothing to do with AI.

AI self-serve users might be paying customers, but they see themselves as trial-ers.

That was us at @heyreach_io had long before anyone said the word AI.

People would sign up -> pay -> poke around for a week -> leave.

On paper they looked identical to our best accounts. Same plan and billing.

The difference was the good ones got results of the product early and the rest never did.

So we sat down and defined what a good first result actually looks like in our product.

It took longer than I'd like to admit and we didn't agree at first. But you can't nudge someone toward a win you've never written down.

Josh is asking the right question and I think the answer is boring.

People quit AI agents because the first couple of days does not get them a win/result they could point to.

You open one and you get a setup screen, a permissions prompt, some config, and then an output you have to go verify yourself. Homework, basically.

You are being asked to trust the thing before it has given you a single reason to.

Compare that to the moments Josh lists. 

Snapchat and Instagram stories. Uber and DoorDash. You posted a photo and three friends liked it inside a minute. You pressed a button and a car showed up outside your building.

30 seconds in you had something you could feel, and you understood nothing about how any of it worked. You did not have to.

Almost every agent I have tried is built to prove capability. Very few are built to hand you a result you can point at on day one. So people try it, nod, close the tab, and never think about it again.

Came across this in a churn playbook doing the rounds, and I have been chewing on number 2 since.

One and three are right. Two is wrong, and it is the expensive one.

They are right about the room. Nobody tells you the truth in a 30 minute call with their account manager. There is a renewal coming, a favour they might need in March, a person they like and do not want to insult. Everything gets edited on the way out of the mouth.

But there is one moment where none of that applies, and most companies treat it as a form: The cancellation flow.

By then they have already decided.

No relationship left to protect, nothing left to manage. They are the only customer you will ever speak to who has no reason to be polite about you.

Rebuilding that experience was one of the first things I did at @heyreach_io.

People edit themselves while they still have something to lose. Take that away and they get honest fast.

The most honest data you own is what people tell you on the way out.

Listening to Matthew Tharp on Churn FM, and this is the one line I would push back on.

He owned retention across nine products at LogMeIn, so when he says three weeks I take it seriously. My own data says two.

Earlier this year I went through the churn data across dozens of accounts at @heyreach_io, looking for the pattern in the ones who left. It was almost embarrassingly consistent. Users who got a real result in their first two weeks stayed. The ones who didn't were gone, and no discount or win-back email pulled them back.

Two reasons I think mine is shorter.

- One is the product.
He was measuring across nine tools including enterprise, and he says himself that enterprise runs longer because more people are involved. We are one tool with a job you can measure in days. You run a campaign and you either get replies or you don't. Fast feedback loop, fast verdict.

- The other is the decade.
He built that model back when CDPs did not exist yet. Users had fewer alternatives and switching was a project. Now switching is a Tuesday afternoon. Patience has been shrinking for ten years and I do not think our onboarding benchmarks have moved with it.

The shape he describes is right. I just think the window keeps closing, and most onboarding is still built for the old one.

You can improve a churn number without helping a single customer.

@archieabram (VP Product at Shopify) says the same thing about growth funnels on Lenny's podcast and calls it the bane of his existence.

The easiest way to lift the conversion rate of your stage is to make the stage before yours harder to reach. Fewer people get in, the ones who do are higher intent, your number looks great.

Retention works the same way, and the levers there are easier to reach.

If I wanted my churn number to look better by the end of a quarter, I would not have to improve anything:

1. I could push everyone onto annual contracts -> watch monthly churn disappear -> which really just moves the problem twelve months out into somebody else's quarter.

2. I could raise the entry price so only the most committed buyers get through the door.

3. I could discount an at risk account into staying one more cycle.

Every one of those improves the number I am measured on. None of them makes a single client more successful.

I learned this the expensive way years ago in an agency seat. I hit a delivery number that was a company record and lost the client anyway, because the number I owned was not the number that mattered to them.

So the question I keep coming back to is whether churn went down because more people succeeded, or because fewer people ever got the chance to fail.

text:
How many of you remember this email?

@sivers wrote it in twenty minutes and CD Baby sent it with every order. 

Decades later people still quote it, which says a lot about one of the most underrated places where customer retention begins: the confirmation email.

Every touchpoint with your customer is an opportunity to shape their perception of your company, and that perception follows them into every buying decision after.

We spent this year doing things you're not supposed to do to your revenue.

> We let paying accounts leave without a fight
> We gave 280 clients free seats, then took them back
> We shipped our tracking system at half its planned size
> We ran support two people short
> We stopped opening save calls with a discount

Churn dropped after every single one.

Each of these spent weeks looking like a straight mistake. 

My save rate got worse and stayed worse. Support ran thin the whole time we were rebuilding it...

The costs always hit the month they happened. The paybacks landed later, spread out, in numbers nobody connects back to decisions like these.

That's retention. Results arrive on a slower clock than reviews do, and whoever can't sit through the ugly weeks keeps the churn number they already have.

Ask a company how many customers they signed last month and you'll get the number in ten seconds. Ask how many left and people start looking at each other.

Quick math on why that second number matters.

Say you lose 5 customers out of every 100 a year. At a hundred customers that's five people. Easy to replace, nobody panics. Now run the same rate at ten thousand customers. That's five hundred gone, and your sales team has to sign five hundred just to get you back to where you started.

The rate didn't change. You got bigger, so the churn got bigger with you.

Keep going and you hit a point where a full year of new customers only covers the ones who left. That's the ceiling. Doesn't matter how good the product is.

When I joined HeyReach our revenue churn was 9%. The company was growing fast and everyone's eyes were on new signups, which is normal. That's where the good news is.

I spent my first months on churn. First thing we touched was the cancellation flow.

Then me and Umer (one of our engineers) went digging for the early signs that somebody's on their way out. We found twelve. We shipped seven. Now an account going quiet lands on a list while there's still time to do something.

Then we redesigned how we go after failed payments. Expired cards, bounced charges, the boring stuff. Four days after it went live it had recovered 30% of what was failing. Two of those days were a weekend, nobody in the office.

None of that signed a single new customer.

Churn sets that ceiling. That's the whole reason I spend my weeks on it, and it's still the number nobody asks about.
