article_title: The summer slowdown hits every SaaS, but we still collected more cash than our MRR

text:
There isn't a single new customer in this chart.

Ask anyone in SaaS about the summer slowdown and you'll hear the same thing. Numbers come down, renewals get harder, and the usual answer is to survive it and wait for September.

We crossed $17M ARR in the middle of it instead...

And here's how we did that: we went to the clients we already had with one trade. A better rate in exchange for paying upfront and staying longer.

Every step on that staircase is one of those decisions.

An existing account prepaying a quarter or a year, or taking a save offer instead of cancelling. My Success team's slice alone cleared $93,000 in those 30 days.

And the offers did something I didn't expect: they made people look at their plan again, and a few realized they'd outgrown it. So a promo that was never chasing upsells turned into one of the best upsell periods we've had.

That's the part I keep coming back to. New demand slows down every summer, but the lifetime value of an existing client doesn't follow the seasons.

Someone commits for 12 more months in the middle of the slow season, someone moves up a plan, and revenue grows without a single new signup.

I broke down the whole campaign I ran in the article below (bookmark for later)

Hot take: when the cost of acquiring new customers is super cheap, you are likely to be terrible at retaining them.

Let me explain.

Growth comes with many benefits, and also problems. One of the biggest ones being hiding churn.

You see, nobody in the building has to get good at retention while you've endless customers coming in.

Then one day acquisition isn't cheap anymore and everyone wants to talk about retention and churn. But by then, there's no solid foundation to track, sense, and retain customers.

When I joined @heyreach_io our revenue churn was 9%, and the first thing I wanted was some way to see it coming.

So me and Umer (one of our engineers) mapped twelve signals that say somebody is about to cancel, and we shipped seven of them immediately.

But generally speaking, most of it came down to watching the five things:

last login older than seven days, no API calls, no webhook activity, nothing happening in the platform, and nothing going out to their own leads.

Any one of those on its own means nothing. All five at once is a customer who already left, they just haven't cancelled yet.

We try to catch it in the first week, because by day thirty they've usually found another way to work and moved on in their head.

Then we rebuilt the cancellation flow, so when somebody does leave we find out where the value broke down for them.

And we redesigned how we chase failed payments. Expired cards, bounced charges, that kind of thing. Four days after it went live it had recovered 30% of what was failing, and two of those days were a weekend with nobody in the office.

The result?

Earlier this year, in the middle of everyone calling it the SaaSpocalypse, we were having our best retention month on record. We even crossed 17M ARR during one of the slowest months for SaaS.

Amazon once wrote a six-word button so shamelessly clever that the FTC banned it when announcing a $2.5B settlement:

“No, I don’t want Free Shipping.”

I hate how good this sentence is.

Let me explain.

Amazon wanted fewer people declining Prime. Fair enough.

A normal decline button might say, “No thanks.”

Amazon’s button made you announce that you did not want free shipping.

That was the trick at signup. Then the FTC looked at what happened when people tried to cancel.

The agency alleged that the main purpose of Amazon’s Prime cancellation process was to stop people from cancelling.

Internal Amazon documents quoted by the FTC called subscription-driving “a bit of a shady world.”

Now for the part I care about.

When I rebuilt our cancellation flow (at @heyreach_io) this year, I gave it a slightly embarrassing job:

Tell us what we messed up.

We ask what the customer was trying to solve, where the value broke, and what they are moving to. Then I call three cancelled customers every week because the form rarely tells me the full story.

One former client told me:

“Honestly… we never really figured out how to get value from it.”

That answer sent me back to onboarding, product and CS. Turns out, we had lost them long before they clicked cancel.

If I rebuilt the flow from scratch all over again, I’d do the same:

> Let people cancel without a fight.
> Ask what they were trying to solve, where the value broke, and what they are moving to.
> Call a few of them every week.
> Send every repeated answer back to onboarding, product and CS. Then fix that part of the experience.

My rule is simple:

The exit flow cannot make customers feel stupid for leaving.

It has to show us where we were stupid before they did.

Duolingo got more users to come back by asking less of them.

I love how backwards that sounds.

You see...Duolingo’s streak used to be strict.

You chose a daily goal. Hit it and your streak survived. Miss it once and the counter went back to zero.

Great system when life behaves. Terrible system when weekends happen.

Duolingo saw daily activity fall by as much as 5-10% on weekends, so the team tested something called the Weekend Amulet.

Equip it on Friday and you could skip Duolingo for the weekend without losing your streak.

That sounds like a strange retention feature. They were rewarding people for not opening the product.

It worked.

Users offered the Weekend Amulet were 4% more likely to return a week later and 5% less likely to lose their streak.

So Duolingo went further.

It separated the streak from the daily goal. One completed lesson kept the streak alive. Everything beyond that still counted toward the larger goal.

Day-14 retention increased 3.3%. Overall daily active users increased 1%. Within 20 days, the share of daily learners with a streak increased 10.5%.

All relative changes. All from making the minimum action smaller.

Years later, the streak has become enormous.

By the end of 2025, about 43 million daily users had a streak of at least seven days. Around 15 million had kept one for at least a year.

I keep coming back to this story because we made a similar decision while rebuilding onboarding at HeyReach.

We shortened the path to a first launched campaign and wrote down what a good first result actually means:

Connect an account, launch a campaign, get one reply.

A new customer can learn the rest of the product later. First, I want them to close one useful loop before life interrupts.

That small win gives them something to come back to.

After the rebuild, we recorded our lowest churn on record.

The questions I kept asking during that rebuild were painfully simple:

What is the smallest action that proves value?

Can a customer complete it on a bad day?

If they disappear once, how easy is the way back?

Customers have bad days.

Somebody will miss a day.

Since then, I check the path back before I add another reminder.

Support tickets contain some of the best growth advice your SaaS will ever get.

Most teams throw that advice away the moment they mark the ticket solved.

I run both Success and Support at @heyreach_io. And when a ticket comes in, the question I care about most sits one level below the issue:

What was the customer trying to do?

That answer changes how I read the ticket.

An integration question can carry product demand. Someone asking how to add teammates can be ready to expand. And the same setup question showing up again points straight at onboarding.

The problem is that most support reporting records the issue. Billing. Integration. Setup. Those labels help the team answer faster, but they do not capture the outcome the customer wanted.

So Support can answer the question perfectly and still lose the useful part when somebody hits “solve.”

The first change I would make tomorrow is adding one sentence to every ticket: “The customer is trying to ___.”

Then every week I would group tickets by that field instead of the issue tag. Five completely different questions may be hiding the same customer goal.

For every repeated outcome, I would name one owner and one next action. A confusing path goes back to onboarding. A missing capability becomes a Product decision, while customers trying to do more get a Success follow-up.

Then I would check the following week for the same outcome. If it keeps appearing, the fix did not work.

If I needed the next growth move for a SaaS, this is where I would start.

Most people will read this as a growth story.

I read it as a story about how long a company can keep growing after the customer experience has already started breaking.

Long before I joined @heyreach_io, revenue was still climbing while Support had 200+ tickets coming in every day, first response reached 10 hours, and churn crossed 15%.

If you only watched ARR, the company looked healthy.
If you listened to customers, the warning was everywhere.

This is the uncomfortable part about churn. The cancellation is usually the last event. The first happened weeks earlier.

The first event might be a user who never gets their first result. A setup question that keeps returning. A customer who replies with less detail every week. A support issue that gets closed, while the reason behind it stays.

By the time those problems reach the churn report, the customer has already spent weeks losing confidence that the product will work for them.

That is why I don't see Support and Customer Success as departments that sit after growth.

They are the part of the growth system that tells you if growth is real.

When I joined, my mission was retention. In my first three weeks, we shipped three new systems. One of them worked at a 30% success rate.

Perfect? No.

But imperfect visibility while there is still time to act is far more useful than a clean churn report after the customer has left.

The most important part of Nick's article comes after the company nearly broke.

Growth took off again once reliability, support, billing, and customers getting the outcome they paid for became the work.

Acquisition can keep the chart moving for a while.

Customer Success and retention are what make that movement compound. Otherwise the next month of acquisition is spent replacing what leaked out before it.

Saving more customers can hide worse retention.

In my first month at HeyReach, we rebuilt the cancellation experience and defined new retention KPIs. I wouldn't judge that work solely by how many cancellations we reverse.

Here's a hypothetical month. Two SaaS companies start with 1,000 customers each.

At the first, 100 ask to cancel. The team saves 80. Twenty leave.

At the second, 20 ask to cancel. The team saves 5. Fifteen leave.

The first team has an 80% save rate. The second has 25%.

I'd take the second company's retention. It lost fewer customers, and far fewer wanted out in the first place.

But if I'm judging the work by cancellation saves, the first team looks incredible.

This is what bothers me about making saves the headline KPI. A customer has to ask to cancel before that metric gives us credit for keeping them.

Help that same customer earlier, and there's no save to report. They just renew. It looks like nothing happened.

I'd still want the team to save an account they can genuinely help. That work matters. But I'd want to know why so many customers needed rescuing.

I'd put cancellation requests as a share of the customer base beside the save rate. Then I'd check whether the saved accounts are still using the product and paying after the offer ends.

If the same setup problem keeps coming up on save calls, I'd give someone ownership of fixing that step for everyone who signs up next. I'd want to see fewer customers reaching cancellation with that problem, even if it means fewer saves to report.

We rebuilt one failed-payment flow at @heyreach_io and recovered 30% of what was failing in four days.

Two of those days were the weekend, with nobody in the office.

The operating rule I took from it now shapes how I look at every customer problem: get them unstuck, then give someone ownership of why they got stuck.

Those customers had not decided to leave. A card expired or hit a limit, and silence would have finished the job.

We rebuilt the flow around that moment. We changed when charges were retried, rewrote the message so it felt like help instead of a payment demand, and reached the customer in more than one place.

That is how I make Nick’s point about Support operational.

If I were building Customer Success from zero, I would make root-cause review a weekly habit. The moment the same customer outcome gets blocked again, it enters that week’s review.

I would group the issues by the outcome they blocked, rather than the tag sitting on the ticket.

Every issue would leave that review with three things: an owner, one change to make, and a check for the following week.

Did the same issue return? Did the affected customers reach the outcome they originally came for?

The owner cannot always be Support. 

> A billing problem belongs with billing. 
> Repeated setup confusion belongs in onboarding. > Product friction belongs with Product.

If Support keeps absorbing the same problem every week, the company is paying people to carry friction it should have removed.

Say your sales team signs 100 new customers a month. 

And every month, 5% of the customers you already have walk out.

For a while, this might look great.

But when you reach, say, 1,000 customers... you're losing 50 a month and signing 100, so you're up 50. 

At 1,500 you're losing 75, so you're up 25. Still growing, just slower.

At 2,000 you're losing 100 a month and signing 100 a month.

That's the wall. Every deal your team closes after that only replaces somebody who left.

There are two ways past it, and they end up in exactly the same place.

Double the sales team so it signs 200 a month. You stop at 4,000 instead.

Or leave sales completely alone, get churn from 5% down to 2.5%, and you stop at 4,000.

Same number, either way.

They cost completely different things though. 

Doubling the team means headcount you pay for every month, and the ceiling drops back the day you stop paying. 

The churn work, on the other hand, is a handful of systems you build once, and they keep running on autopilot. 

When I joined @heyreach_io in February, revenue churn was 9%. Three weeks later we were at 7%. That did the same thing to our ceiling as adding 29% more sales.

ChurnZero’s new AI agent reads a churned account’s history, assigns a reason, and adds a confidence score.

If I plugged this into my team tomorrow, I’d audit our churn-reason list before reading a single summary.

AI will make whatever taxonomy we give it more consistent. Honesty still depends on the questions the team chose before the agent arrived.

For every “too expensive,” I’d ask what value the customer reached first.

For every “missing feature,” I’d ask whether the feature was truly missing or the customer never found the workflow.

For every “went with a competitor,” I’d ask when their confidence shifted and whether we saw it happening.

The risk is a clean dashboard full of symptoms.
The real impact comes when those summaries expose weak assumptions in the retention system itself. Faster notes are the easy part.

Hot take: distribution gets too much credit for growth.

A company can add channels, spend more, and keep the signup chart moving, but if customers never reach the result they bought the product for, distribution only sends more names toward the cancellation queue.

I saw this when I went through churn data across dozens of HeyReach accounts. The pattern was almost embarrassingly consistent. 

Users who got a real result in their first two weeks stayed. Users who did not, left. No discount or win-back flow could manufacture the value they never felt.

That is why I agree with Nick that the CEO should be the CPO.

Product decisions do not end when a feature ships. They surface later as support tickets, quiet accounts and cancellation reasons. 

My team (customer success) can catch an account going quiet on day 7 and help before day 30. But if the same friction keeps appearing across accounts, it goes back into the product roadmap. 

And the CEO has to decide whether it gets fixed, because support and customer success cannot keep saving the same product problem forever.

Yesterday I was reading our new guide on semantic deduplication.

It explains how the same person can appear in your systems with a different email, LinkedIn URL, or company record.

Each entry looks unique, so separate campaigns can enroll the same person without realizing it.

The system sees several leads. The prospect sees the same company messaging them again and again.

If this reaches my team, this is how I’d handle it:

1. Support contains it

Pause the overlapping campaigns and make sure another message cannot go out.

2. Ops traces it

Find where the duplicate records entered, which identity check missed them, and whether anyone else was affected.

3. Ops prevents it

Create one shared identity check and suppression list that every campaign uses before enrollment.

4. Success closes the loop

Explain what happened, show what changed, and monitor the next live campaign with the customer.

A Support ticket closes when the duplicate messages stop.

A retention risk closes when the customer trusts their next campaign.

There is a number that caps how big your company can get:

New customers divided by churn rate.

Let's say you add 100 customers a month and lose 5% of your base every month, and you climb to 2,000 and stop there.

At 2,000, five percent is 100 people. Exactly what you signed that month. The chart flattens with the pipeline still full underneath it.

Now walk the churn down one point at a time.

5% caps you at 2,000.
4% caps you at 2,500.
3% caps you at 3,333.
2% caps you at 5,000.

Same team. Same spend. Same 100 a month.

The first point you take off buys you 500 customers. The last one buys you 1,667. Every point is worth more than the one before it.

So the best time to work on churn is when it already looks fine.

Run yours. New customers a month divided by your monthly churn rate, and that's the biggest you get on the setup you have today.

I keep seeing this chart posted as a growth win. And this is where most founders will loose customers.

Adobe published the number in June, across more than a trillion visits to US retail sites.

AI referred means chatgpt/claude gave them a reco. They measured those sessions against everything else, search and ads and direct.

I run retention at @heyreach, so a conversion chart is never where my eye stops.

A conversion rate is a same-session number. It says somebody finished a task. Whether they chose you is a separate question, and it is the one that matters at renewal.

When an agent compares the options and completes the checkout, no human sat with the decision. Preference is what carries someone through the week your product annoys them.

So here is what I would run before calling it a win. Tag the AI-referred cohort at signup. Leave it tagged.

Compare its month-3 retention and its expansion rate against your blended base, and give it two full renewal cycles before you decide anything.

Seven months in at @heyreach_io and this is the launch I was waiting for.

Huge shoutout to Nick, Stefan and the whole product team. 

From where I sit in customer success and retention, the thing new accounts get stuck on is getting that first campaign live, and this update goes straight at it.

Proud to be on this team. Go watch the video.

Close to 100,000 campaigns have run through @heyreach_io. I run support and success here, so I see the broken ones, the ones that make the same mistakes which leads them loosing their first month.

Starting this week I'm running a live session every week free.

The first one is how to build from zero to your first campaign that gives you a predictable pipeline, start to finish.

I'm doing this because everyone talks about copy and targeting, and almost nobody walks you through connecting an account properly, setting your limits, or whether you need a warm-up at all.

What we're covering:
1. How to connect your first account without breaking anything on day one
2. The sending limits users get wrong, and what it costs them
3. When a warm-up is worth it, and when it's a wasted week
4. Launching your first campaign, live
5. Where to find your reporting, which numbers I check in week one, and the ones I ignore
6. What it takes to go from 0 to 20+ meetings in a month, from the accounts I watch every day

See you there....

A percentage point of revenue churn is worth about $14,100 a month to us.

At @heyreach_io, we’re at $17M ARR, roughly $1.41M in MRR, with over 7,000 accounts. That gives me a useful way to put a dollar value on the retention work.

At that revenue base, reducing monthly revenue churn by one percentage point means roughly $14,100 less MRR lost that month. Our churn rate has averaged 7.3% over the past 6 months.

Whether we keep that revenue depends on what those clients do next.

It changes how I look at the smaller fixes.
- A better email
- A failed-payment recovery flow
- A cancellation experience that gives us a chance to address why someone wants to leave.

Each can look minor when I’m looking at one account.

In July, our rebuilt cancellation flow saved approximately $17,300 in MRR. That came from a system running throughout the month, helping retain clients who were on their way out.

Sure, the big saves still matter. I’m glad when we get a client on the phone and work through the problem.

But across this many accounts, I also need the everyday flows to do their job without relying on someone stepping in every time.

Putting a dollar amount against a percentage point made that work easier to prioritize. Now when I’m deciding what to improve next, I have something more useful than “this might help retention” to work with.

A client told me they were going to try building something similar to HeyReach in-house, using AI.

That was a few months ago. I’ve been hearing versions of it more often since.

It adds another question to a renewal conversation. Alongside comparing tools, the client is working out whether they need to pay for one at all.

I’ve found it more useful to ask what they actually want to build before trying to convince them to stay.

> Is there a feature missing?
> Does the price feel wrong for how much they use it?
> Or do they need something that fits their workflow differently?

Often, that gets us into an expectations gap we hadn’t talked about. I can work with that. I can’t do much with a debate about whether AI can build software.

It also makes me look harder at how we fit into their day.

Some clients do try building it themselves and come back. I always ask why.

What looked straightforward at the start?
What turned out to be harder than they expected?

Those conversations help me understand why they came back and what they need from us now.

That’s useful feedback for the next renewal conversation, and for how we explain the product much earlier. I’d rather understand what they value while they’re still using us.

If you're running a SaaS, I beg you to not send the same reactivation email to every inactive user.

A trial user who never got started and a power user who suddenly stopped can look identical on an inactivity list. The reason they’re there should change what you send.

1. Help the trial user finish getting started.

Find out what they signed up to do and the last step they completed. If they connected an account but never launched a campaign, help them launch it.

This user may never have experienced the thing they signed up for. Asking them to come back leaves the original obstacle in place. Give them help with that specific obstacle.

And if they were only exploring, find out when they’ll actually need the product. Another reminder won’t create a project for them.

2. Find out what changed for the power user.

Check their previous usage and recent support conversations before reaching out. They’ve already figured out the basics. Something has interrupted their normal use.

A broken integration needs a fix. A change of account owner needs a handover. A finished project needs a conversation about when the next one starts.

Those require different follow-ups. Looking at the account history gives you a useful starting point and saves the customer from explaining everything again.

3. Check whether your help solved the problem.

For the trial user, confirm they completed the task they were stuck on. For the power user, check that their workflow is running again. If they’re deliberately taking a break, agree on a sensible time to follow up.

This matters because a customer can open your email, reply politely and still be stuck. Keep the follow-up open until you know what happened after the reply.

Some renewals should be smaller.

If a customer's team has shrunk, asking them to renew every seat needs a better explanation than last year's seat count. The people still using your product can be happy with it and the bill can still be too big for what the team needs.

Slack does part of this automatically. 

On eligible self-service plans, it gives the customer a credit when a paid member hasn't used Slack in over 28 days. That credit covers the unused part of the billing period and goes toward future bills.

If you run a SaaS, before your next renewals, you might want to check these: 

1. Check which seats are being used.

Pull the paid-seat count and recent activity. Look at the work getting done, because a monthly reporting tool won't show the same pattern as something people use every day.

2. Ask the customer what changed.

Did their team shrink? Did a project finish? Or did they buy seats for people who never got through setup?

Those answers change what you recommend. Help the people who got stuck get started. If the work has gone away, another training session won't create a reason to keep the seats.

3. Be willing to send a smaller quote.

At HeyReach, admins can reduce their paid seat count themselves, with the change taking effect at the next billing cycle. That's one option to raise when a customer needs less.

If you need to justify the smaller renewal internally, bring the usage data and the customer's reason for reducing seats.

But the customer shouldn't have to threaten to cancel before someone helps them work out how much they actually need.

A few weeks ago I was in Bali with our leadership team, planning 2027 for @heyreach_io.

Around the table were @nikolak47 , Ilija, Umer and Bojan. Everyone owned a different piece of the future, and mine was client success and support. Nobody talked about what was broken or what was on fire. We talked about what we want to build and where we want to take this.

At some point I did the math on where we actually are. Nearly $17M ARR. Over 7,000 active clients. Hundreds of thousands of accounts connected to the platform. And a support team running smoothly back home while we sat 8,000 kilometers away talking about 2027.

Then I thought about 2021.

COVID had taken the whole industry I knew, so I was scrolling freelance gigs at night trying to work out what came next. I did months of interviews with nothing to show for them, and I still had this stubborn belief that working with people was what I was built for, with almost no evidence to back it up.

That version of me couldn't have pictured being trusted to help shape what a $17M company becomes next.

None of it was easy or inevitable. I'm sharing it because the gap between where you are and where you want to be is mostly patience, and I had to sit in Bali to see that clearly.

We were looking at software to help us retain clients who were about to cancel HeyReach.

I wanted to change what we offered someone based on how they used the product, try different offers, and see whether any of them convinced that client to stay.

But the more I asked, the less room we had to do that. Some changes weren't supported, testing was limited, and seeing which offers worked required a more expensive plan.

We ended up building it ourselves, starting with what happens when a client's payment fails.

Someone who has been with us for years has a different relationship with us than someone who just signed up. I wanted our messages to take that into account.

We then built the cancellation process so we could see why someone wanted to leave, what we offered them, and whether they stayed.

When clients respond differently, we can change the messages or offers ourselves and test them again. That takes time from our team, but we can make those changes without waiting for a vendor to support them.

At @heyreach_io we built our own reactivation flow to bring churned clients back. It targets clients who left 40 to 90 days ago, a window most retention tools ignore. Here is how it runs, from the exit to the return (you might want to copy this for your SaaS):

1. The flow starts with the exit data, so we collect it properly.

When someone cancels we ask what made them cancel in their own words, what they were trying to solve, where the value broke, and what they are moving to.

We log what they were offered on the way out and whether it changed their mind.

Then I call 3 cancelled clients every week, because the form rarely tells the full story. That is the raw material for everything below.

2. Every reason someone gave for leaving is a roadmap for winning them back, once we have addressed it.

That is the whole principle. We go back through the reasons people gave, and when we have fixed one, the people who gave it are the ones who hear about it.

A former client already knows the product, so the message is about the thing that pushed them out and what is different now.

When the fix is real, it is one of the easier sales we run, because there is nothing to convince them of except that the thing they named is fixed.

3. Failed payments go through a different flow.

A card that bounced is a client who never decided to leave.

That is delinquent recovery, with its own timing and its own tone, and mixing the two would mean sending win-back copy to someone who just needs to update a card.

4. It runs automated and consistent, with attribution on every send.

Doing this manually, one email at a time, hoping you remember to follow up, is how reactivation dies at most companies.

We track which clients got which message and which offer, and whether anyone came back on it, so we can test offers against each other. That attribution is part of why we built the flow ourselves instead of renting one.

Saving your biggest customer can mean committing your team to another year of work nobody priced.

If the offer includes weekly calls, custom reporting or hands-on help, put a cost against those commitments alongside any discount.

Before you agree to more:

1. Count everyone involved in serving the account.

Ask the CSM, support and engineering what they spent on the account in a typical month. Include internal investigations and coordination. A quiet customer can still keep several people busy behind the scenes.

Cost that time before adding more to it.

2. Work out which costs will repeat.

A difficult onboarding month can settle down once the customer is running. A product bug needs fixing, especially if other customers are hitting it too.

But if someone on your team has to build the same custom report every Friday, keeping the account means keeping that work. Check whether it can be automated, simplified with the customer, or included in a paid service.

Don't label a customer expensive before checking how much of the work your own product is creating.

3. Make the service commitment explicit.

At @heyreach_io, our Agency plan explicitly includes done-for-you onboarding and a dedicated Slack channel.

When you offer extra help to retain an account, spell out the work, its recurring cost, who will deliver it and when you'll review it. If it becomes an ongoing service, discuss the scope and price with the customer while honoring what you've already promised.

You may still decide the extra investment is worth it. Then be specific about what you expect to change: less support after setup, a larger contract, or a fix that helps other accounts too.

Before you promise more to save the renewal, bring the people who will deliver it into the decision. They should have a say before another weekly commitment lands on their calendar.

Please don't make your customers test your AI support bot for you.

SpaceXAI started by keeping Grok's work inside the support team, where people could check it before customers saw it.

Our Fin rebuild at @heyreach_io included changes to its logic and more than 30 new help articles. The support team also defined what it should handle and where a person needed to take over.

Here's a good framework to integrate AI into your support..

Start with one recurring problem:

1. Test whether it can find the cause without seeing the answer.

Take a batch of solved tickets the bot hasn't seen. Give it the information available when each ticket arrived, then ask for the likely cause, supporting evidence and next step. Keep the solved conversation out of both its input and searchable history.

Have someone who handles those tickets compare its findings with what actually solved the problem.

2. Make your support team own the corrections.

Record whether the person could use the bot's findings, had to find missing information, or had to start again. Keep wording edits separate from a wrong diagnosis.

If the answer is missing from your help content, add it. If the instructions are wrong, correct them. Then test the change on other tickets with the same problem.

3. Define where it must stop before you switch on replies.

Write down what the bot can handle, what requires approval and who takes over when it can't establish the cause. Include what it checked and what is still unknown in that handoff.

If the bot keeps getting the cause wrong, keep that ticket type on internal notes.

For ticket types that pass review, test direct replies and compare reopened tickets and repeated questions with the same category when people handled it. Read the conversations too. A customer going quiet doesn't always mean the problem is solved.

Repeat that review before adding the next ticket type. Getting account access right tells you very little about whether it can handle a disputed charge.

text:
Back in February, 9 of every 100 dollars we earned at @heyreach_io were walking out the door, and part of every new signup went to replacing them.

Plug the leak and the same signups start to compound. That makes retention the cheapest growth lever. 

And since then our success and support took that 9% down to 7% and got us our best retention month on record. 

Here are some of the retention and customer success motions we've run along the way: 

1. Failed payments (the cheapest revenue you'll ever win back)

We built an in-house delinquent recovery flow instead of waiting for cards to update themselves.

4 days after it went live, it had recovered 30% of what was failing. 2 of those days were the weekend, with nobody in the office.

2. Health signals (catch them before they tell you)

We listed more than a dozen possible signals and shipped 7. Inactivity came first: last login older than 7 days, no API usage, no webhook activity, no actions in the platform, no outward engagement.

At day 7 a silent account is a conversation. At day 30 it's damage control.

3. Onboarding (where churn starts)

The pattern in our churn data was almost embarrassingly consistent. Users who get a real result in their first 2 weeks stay, and the ones who don't leave, whatever discount you offer them later.

So we redesigned the first-touch guidance, cut the time to a first campaign, defined what a good first result looks like, and started nudging people before day 7. That gave us our lowest churn rate on record.

4. Cancellation and reactivation

We reworked the cancellation experience (in July it saved about $17,300 in MRR on its own) and built a reactivation flow for clients who left 40 to 90 days ago, because sometimes churn just means "not right now."

5. Value over discounts

In March, when everyone was calling it the SaaSpocalypse, we kept prices where they were and added value: extra seats, more usage.

100s of users expanded, and it was our best retention month on record. It's the main reason I think the room to grow is already inside our own accounts.

Of David's 5 numbers, the one I'd fight for is DAU/MAU. In my opinion, it's of more importance than gross retention.

Gross retention tells you what already happened. By the time it drops, the customer made the decision weeks earlier, and that's the difference between a check-in call with someone who still wants to make it work and a cancellation call with someone who has already moved on.

DAU/MAU is where you see the slipping first. But it's a company-wide number, and it can't tell you which customer is slipping. So at @heyreach_io we track the same thing account by account.

It was one of the first things I built here: a health-signal system, with inactivity shipped first. An account gets flagged when it goes quiet across the board. No API usage or actions in the platform, basically no outward engagement.

When all of that goes silent at once, the account is on its way out. It just hasn't cancelled yet.

Gross retention is the number I get judged on. Usage is the one I can still act on before they leave.

text:
Figma grew revenue by 48% in a year, and its growth sped up for the 3rd quarter in a row.

About half of that growth came from customers Figma already had. The rough math:

→ A year ago, customers paying $10K+ a year made up about 64% of Figma's recurring revenue.

→ Those same customers pay 36% more today. For every $100 they paid then, they pay $136 now.

1,635 companies now pay Figma more than $100K a year, up from 1,119 a year earlier.

I went through Figma's IPO filing, every earnings call since and its pricing changes.

It comes down to 5 steps, in this order:

1. Let 1 person start for free.

Anyone can use Figma for free, and 1 user can upgrade their team with a card. Every file lives in the browser and gets shared with a link, so the first user pulls colleagues in.

By early 2025, 13 million people used Figma every month, 2/3 of them weren't designers, and 95% of the Fortune 500 used it.

About 70% of new Organization and Enterprise customers included someone who had been on a Professional plan before.

How I'd run it: find your customer's first result and put your onboarding effort there.

At HeyReach that's the first campaign going live, so I run a free weekly live session just on getting it launched. Then make sharing easy, so that first user brings the next one in.

2. Map everyone already inside the account.

Engineers open Figma files to copy specs, PMs leave comments and marketing teams pull assets. Until March 2025, Figma sold a separate seat for each product, so a team lead had to work out who needed which one.

3. Give each person a seat that fits their job.

In March 2025, Figma moved to 1 seat per person. On the Organization plan:

→ Full seat for designers, $55 a month
→ Dev seat for engineers, $25
→ Collab seat for people who comment and present, $5
→ View seat, free

Full seats went up 20% to 33% in the change. Admins now approve every paid upgrade, and the user gets the new seat's features for up to 3 days while the request waits.

4. Move customers over at renewal.

Annual customers stayed on their old plan until their first renewal, so Figma spent a full year moving everyone across. From March 2025 to last quarter, net dollar retention went 132%, 129%, 131%, 136%, 139% and 136%.

By last quarter, about 2/3 of customers paying $10K+ a year had added Full seats since their last renewal. Gross retention stayed in the mid-to-high 90s the whole time.

5. Sell usage on top of seats.

Every Figma seat comes with a monthly allowance of AI credits, and since March 2026, people who need more buy an add-on.

Of the Organization and Enterprise users who went over their limit, more than 75% kept using AI credits, and over 95% of those stayed active on Figma. Over 80% of customers paying $10K+ a year now use AI credits every week.

Every extra dollar in Figma's 136% came from a customer it already had. That's why I think retention is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS.

A hill I'll die on: retention matters more than any revenue number.

Higgsfield hit $1B in revenue, and that's the number everyone's sharing. The one I'd look at is further down, 300% net revenue retention.

Revenue almost always gets the limelight. The question I always have is how much of it shows up again next year, and that's exactly what the 300% answers.

In simple words, the customers they had a year ago now pay them about 3x as much, all together. They could've signed zero new customers all year and still 3xed the revenue from that group.

Flip it around and you get big revenue with bad retention, which just means your sales team spends the whole of next year replacing the customers who left.

Congrats to the Higgsfield team, what a year.

We brought back more than $10,000 in MRR in the last couple of months at @heyreach_io, from customers who had already cancelled.

That number matters more now, because a lot of customers think they can rebuild your product with AI, and some of them will cancel to try.

I call our system A.R.R., for Ask, Root and Return, and the whole thing is in the article below. These are the parts you can set up this week:

1. Ask

When a customer cancels and mentions building it in-house, AI, or "doing it ourselves," a person calls them. We ask 3 questions before we offer anything:

> is a feature missing 
> does the price feel wrong for how much they use it 
> does the product fit how they work. Then we log which one it was.

2. Root

I'd start by listing what a typical account has connected after a few months: teammates, integrations, workflows.

Then I'd find the accounts that use one feature and nothing else. Those are the customers who'd find it cheapest to rebuild you with AI, so point your expansion offers at them first.

We collected more than $100,000 in cash from upsells in July and August, our hardest season, all from customers we already had.

3. Return

We reach out again 40 to 90 days after a customer cancels. When we fix something customers named as their reason for leaving, we tell every customer who named it. 

And when someone who left to build comes back, we ask what looked simple at the start, what turned out harder, and what changed their mind.

If a customer still wants to leave after the first call, we let them go without a fight. My save rate dropped when we started doing that, and I'd make that trade again, because some of them come back.

The article has all 3 steps in full, plus the 4-question audit I'd run on any SaaS cancel flow.

If a customer says they love your product and they're still leaving to build their own, go look at their first 14 days. That's usually where they left, and the rebuild just gave them a good reason to say it.

This is where I disagree with the "one papercut and you're out" part.

Our customers put up with a papercut if the product did something for them the week before. The ones who leave over a papercut almost always had a first month where nothing happened.

I've watched a discount fail on that second group every time. A result in week 1 is the only thing that has worked.

So I'd take every hour you're spending on retention pricing and put it into the first week.

Here's what we changed:

> first-touch guidance for every new account
> a shorter path to the first campaign
> nudges before day 7
> a written definition of what a good first result looks like

That redesign gave us our lowest churn rate on record.

It hasn't stopped every rebuild, and I don't expect it to. But the customers we lose to it now had a working product in their hands when they left, and those people come back. The ones who never got to a result don't.

I got hired at @heyreach_io on February 2nd with 9% revenue churn. 6 weeks later it was 7%, March was the best retention month in company history, and hundreds of accounts that were about to cancel expanded instead.

Here's what I did to bring down churn (and what you can copy):

1. I read the first 30 days of every churned account instead of the last 30.

- The pattern was almost embarrassingly consistent. People who got a result in their first 2 weeks stayed. People who didn't left, and no discount brought them back.
- So we wrote down what a good first result looks like: account connected, campaign live, 1 reply back.
- We cut the path from signup to that, and added a nudge everywhere the usage data showed people stalling.
- Lowest churn rate on record came from this one.

2. I built an alarm for accounts going quiet.

- We mapped 12 health signals and shipped 7.
- The first one is inactivity: no login in 7 days, no API calls, no webhooks, no actions in the platform, no engagement anywhere.
- Any one of those means nothing. All 5 together means they've already decided to leave.
- If I catch it on day 7 I can still ask how the setup is going. On day 30 I'm doing damage control.

3. I went after failed payments before anything else.

- It's the cheapest churn to win back, and most teams ignore it because they're busy fighting the churn they can see.
- We built our own delinquent recovery flow.
- 4 days after it went live it had recovered 30% of what was failing. 2 of those days were a weekend with nobody in the office.

4. I stopped discounting on save calls.

- Most people who say they want to cancel don't want it cheaper. They want more out of what they're already paying for.
- So we offered at-risk accounts extra seats and better use cases instead of a lower price.
- A surprising number of those calls ended with the account getting bigger. That's where the hundreds of expansions came from.

5. I rebuilt the cancellation flow so it actually tells me something.

- I stopped trusting the dropdown reasons.
- We rebuilt the flow to get a real answer in the customer's own words.
- I also call 3 cancelled customers every week. The dashboard tells me what happened. Those calls tell me why.

If you only do one of them, do the first. Everything else is cleanup for accounts you already lost in week 2.

I happened to stumble upon this super viral tweet and clicked to watch two AIs haggle over an internet bill. By the end it looked to me like reading a retention story.

What works way better for us is giving them more of what's already working, so more senders and more campaigns running at once. If they're already booking meetings on what they have, doubling it roughly doubles the meetings.

A surprising number of those "I want to cancel" calls end with the account getting bigger. I'll take that over a discount any day.

My Success team at @heyreach_io brought in $93,000 in 30 days this summer without a single new signup.

All we did was give the clients we already had the kind of deal that usually only goes to new customers.

Here's the 5-minute test to check if you're doing the opposite, and exactly how we ran it.

Your phone company runs it the other way. Switch carriers and you get the promo. Stay for years and you get the same bill.

SaaS does it too:
- The new signup gets the launch discount, the free setup and a senior onboarding call
- The client who never missed an invoice gets a renewal email

So your best clients learn that the one way to get a better deal is to threaten to leave. Some of them try it, and a few don't come back.

The test:
1. Write down the best offer a brand-new client can get from you today
2. Next to it, write what your longest-standing client gets for staying
3. If the new client comes out ahead, you have a loyalty gap, even if your churn looks fine

How we ran it:
- We took our best offer to the clients we already had: a better rate for paying upfront and committing longer
- On those calls, a few clients realized they'd outgrown their plan and upgraded
- When clients wanted to cancel, my team offered more before anyone mentioned price: extra seats, more capacity
- Hundreds of accounts that were about to cancel expanded instead

A discount would have bought us one more month and taught them to wait for the next sale.

Your newest client chose you once. Your oldest client chooses you every month.

10 rules for keeping customers, from someone whose team brought in $93,000 in 30 days this summer without a single new signup:

1. Give people what they came for before they have to ask. That's most of the job.

2. Message every new client by first name in the first 24 hours, and mention 1 thing about their business.

3. In week 2, ask "How's it going, where are you stuck?" Nobody else messages them that week.

4. How a client feels in the first month sets the tone for the whole relationship.

5. Watch for shorter replies, pushed calls and the same concern coming up twice. A quiet support queue used to feel like a good week to me. Now it worries me.

6. Ship the system before it's perfect. 1 of our first 3 ran at a 30% success rate.

7. A record month for you can still be a bad month for the client. I once booked a client 21 meetings in a month, and they walked because none of them turned into a deal.

8. They said yes to you 6 times before they ever said no (h/t @asmartbear). If they leave, something broke long before the cancel button.

9. Start the renewal talk 90 days before the contract ends, so renewing feels like the obvious next step.

10. Churn will always exist. Sometimes it just means "not right now," and that's OK.

That's why I believe retention matters a lot more than distribution now. ad it can defintely be the next MOAT.

2. What were you trying to solve?

In 3 months, our AI agent at @heyreach_io went from answering 19% of support conversations to 45%, and we still hired 5 more people.

Resolution and CX scores went up in the same 3 months too.

A smaller team can be the right call if you start with more people than the work needs.

But if I had hired first, I think we'd have 7 people today answering the same questions the first 2 were stuck on.

If you sign 100 new customers a month and lose 5% of your customers every month, you’ll stop growing at 2,000.

At 2,000 customers, 5% is 100 people. So every month you sign 100 and lose 100, and the total stops moving.

To find where you’ll stop, divide the new customers you sign each month by your monthly churn. It works the same with MRR.

Keep signing 100 a month and lower churn 1 point at a time:

5% caps you at 2,000
4% caps you at 2,500
3% caps you at 3,333
2% caps you at 5,000

To reach 5,000 at 5% churn, you’d need 250 new customers a month. That’s 2.5 times as many.

At @heyreach_io’s $19M ARR, 1 point of monthly revenue churn is about $15,800 a month. That’s why I read our cancellation reasons every week, and why my team calls the same day an account has gone silent for a week.

Warren Buffett wrote a 1-line test for moats back in 2007, and distribution fails it.

But every month a client stays, more builds up in their account: the workflow, the fixes made for their account, the history, and the people who already know it. Any new tool would start them at zero, so keeping them gets a little easier each month.

Buffett even names Costco in the same letter.

He picked it for its low prices, and it also shows that a moat you earn again every year can last. Nobody is trapped at Costco. Every member decides once a year whether to pay the fee again and last year 92.3% of members in the US and Canada renewed.

We try to run cancelling the same way.

Anyone who wants to cancel with us answers 4 questions and they're done. We've lost some clients we might have talked into staying because of that.

That's why I think retention is the new moat. Nobody can see what builds up inside a client's account from the outside, so nobody can copy it the way they copy a channel.

I spent my first 2 weeks at @heyreach_io writing a personal email to every client whose card failed because failed-payment churn is the cheapest revenue you will ever win back, so every client needed that email, including the ones I didn't get to that day.

2. It says what failed.
3. Fixing it takes 1 click.

We built that into our delinquent recovery flow and kept it separate from cancellations and win-backs. A client whose card failed hasn't chosen to leave, so they need a different message.

I manage $200K/month in ad spend through Claude Code... so I obviously had to build a monitoring system that tells me how these ads are performing.

I wrote up the whole build in this article. Here is the short version you can copy this week to see if these ads are generating your expected ROI.

THE 3 DRIFTS TO WATCH:

1. Creative fatigue: Your ad will lose attention. 

Look at CTR against the last few weeks, plus +frequency and reach. If the creative is weak, you need a new angle. 

If the same people have just seen it too many times, you need more reach or a different split. Don't pause the ad before you know which one it is. You'll hide the real problem.

2. Bid drift. 

Spend looks normal while the auction under it moves. 

Check CPM and CPC against the last comparable window. Then ask: did my budget buy the same opportunity as last time?

3. Audience decay. 

This one fools you because CPL improves. The platform finds cheaper people. CTR goes up. CPL goes down. Then sales opens the leads and the companies are too small.

So check who the ads actually reached against who you wanted to reach. And check platform conversions against what entered pipeline. A cheaper lead means nothing if pipeline does not move with it.

HOW TO BUILD IT (do it in this order)

1. Start with 1 alert. Skip the dashboard for now. Pick the decision the alert protects: budget, creative or audience. A pretty report nobody acts on is just another tab.

2. Then work backward. What is the earliest signal you can trust? What window do you compare it against? What would prove the alert wrong? Who makes the call when it fires?

3. Start with 1 account and 1 failure mode. Creative fatigue is the easiest one. You already know the question: did the ad die, or did the audience run out?

4. Keep the platform's original IDs. Every flag needs to trace back to the exact campaign. Field names, time zones and duplicate creatives will break your analysis. A lot of my 300+ hours went into exactly this. 

Get these details wrong and the analysis sounds confident while it points you at the wrong campaign.

5. Ask the same 5 questions on every platform:
- Where did the money go?
- Who saw the ads?
- What changed in the auction?
- Which creative lost attention?
- What reached pipeline?

A good alert tells you 4 things: what moved, when it started, what stayed stable, and which decision it affects. Anything less is just another red metric.

80% of the ad budget on our best ABM campaign went behind founder, team and creator content. Product ads got the last 20%.

On that account we scaled spend 20x and kept ROI positive. 15x on pipeline. 164 deals, 30 closed.

Here's how we did it:

MAKE THE CLICKS CHEAP

2026 benchmarks put ads run off a personal profile at $2.29 a click. The rest of B2B LinkedIn sits at $5.50 to $8.00, and C-suite targeting runs $10 to $24 and up.

Hence if you gotta run ads off someone's profile, you need an employee who already posts. Most companies do not have one, so most companies cannot bid in this auction at all.

If nobody on your team posts, you have about 6 months of work ahead of you before any of this runs.

THE 3 THINGS THAT DECIDE IF IT WORKS

1. Whose account it runs from. Your own team costs the least and takes the longest to build up. Your customers are the most believable, and you can pay for a 60 to 90 second post with a fee, a credit or a perk. Creators your buyers already follow work immediately and cost the most. I run all 3 against the same account list.

2. Whether they post enough to give you winners. You want to sponsor posts that already earned engagement on their own. Someone posting once a month will not produce enough of those to spend against.

3. Frequency across a capped list. On the accounts I care about I run 12+ impressions a head across the buying committee. People will sit through the same person 12 times. They will not sit through the same company ad 12 times. That is why this format works on a named list and wastes money on a broad audience.

HOW TO BUILD IT (do it in this order)

1. Build the list, then cap it. 500 to 3,000 accounts, pulled from closed lost, stalled pipeline and old MQLs. Every step after this points at that list.

2. Pick the people before the creative. Pick whoever will still be posting every week in 6 months. Title does not matter here. LinkedIn calls the format Thought Leader Ads, and it needs a real account behind it.

3. Let them post for a few weeks before you spend anything. Then sponsor the posts that got engagement from your buyers rather than from your own team.

4. Split the budget by stage. My rule here has not changed. Cold buys attention. Warm buys proof. Hot buys the offer. The person covers cold and warm. Bottom of funnel goes back to the brand, because by then the buyer needs a clear offer and a personal post is too soft for that.

5. Send closed won back into targeting. Check whose ads that account saw before the deal opened. That is how you work out which person to put more budget behind.

WHAT I WATCH INSTEAD OF CTR

Frequency, engagement rate and audience penetration. Penetration is the one almost nobody checks. It is the share of accounts on your list that have actually seen the person. A great CTR does not mean much if most of your list has not seen the ads yet.

WHERE IT BREAKS

The person leaves. Everything you paid to build sits on their name, and the next hire does not inherit it. I have not solved that one. The best I have is running 3 people from the start instead of the founder alone.

If I had to rebuild from zero, I would line up those 3 people before writing a single ad. Finding people who will keep posting takes longer than making the ads.

- What you would change.

- What we would do.
- What that would look like for your team.

Have the agent build the pages in draft.

6. Give sales the same research

Save the page against the account in your CRM.

The rep should know what you showed the buyer before starting a conversation.

Their next message can pick up on the finding, with a useful question or more detail.

Now the ad, the page and the sales conversation all have something specific to say about the account.

If your outbound isn't booking meetings and you've decided the copy is the problem, stop. Rewriting it won't fix anything.

The copy is almost never what's broken. It's one of the 7 steps underneath it, and they only work in one order.

Here's the system I'd rebuild from zero, in the exact sequence I'd build it:

1. Infrastructure
Nobody wants to start here. 20 secondary domains, 40 mailboxes, a two-week warm-up before a single cold send. The primary never sends, because reputation attaches to the domain and it's the one asset you can't replace. This caps your volume at ~1,000 sends a day. Write that number down. It sizes every decision that follows.

2. Data
Almost everyone lives in three sources: LinkedIn, ZoomInfo, Apollo.
Same filters + list every competitor is emailing this week. I mapped 60+. The base I'd run is 6 providers, because each one is strong exactly where another is thin. I'd rather email 400 rows that each have a reason than 4,000 that don't. The reason is what you open with.

3. Enrichment
One provider always reports a coverage number that looks fine. What it can't tell you is who it never had a shot at. A real run inside Claude Code: Apollo returned 153 contacts, a second pass ended at 149 verified. Four were invisible on one provider alone. Order the waterfall cheapest-first, and only pay the expensive one for the rows the cheap ones missed.

4. Scoring
This step exists to make the list smaller. Tier three gets nothing. No sequence, no touches, no capacity. Every send into a bad-fit account is one that never reached a good one, and you only have 1,000.

5. Signals
Fit just narrows the list. A signal is the thing that tells you to send this week instead of next quarter. A company posting three SDR roles just told you its pipeline problem in public. If you can't write the first line of the email straight off the signal, it isn't a signal yet.

6. Copy
Only now does anything get written. I ran reply data across 11K campaigns and 132K snapshots. Three frameworks keep coming back: open with their number, reference the hire, name the mutual connection. One variable per variant, or the result tells you nothing you can use.

7. Send and measure
Four touches, and the fourth is the last. Campaign level only says the campaign worked. Break it to the framework and you find out what to actually write next Tuesday.

Find your broken step:

landing in spam, copy unchanged = step 1
same list your competitors email = step 2
coverage looks fine, reach is thin = step 3
reply rate low on good copy = step 4, you're emailing the wrong accounts
can't write a true first line = step 5
great targeting, weak replies = step 6
something worked, nobody knows what = step 7

Every step caps the next one. Fix the earliest broken one first.

If it all feels random, you're starting at step 6. Go back to step 1.

Our team puts out 200+ LinkedIn posts a month across 150,000+ followers.

So I put together a cheatsheet on how to build pipeline with LinkedIn.

 1. Your Profile

Every section has one job.

 >Picture: 80% face, clean background
 > Headline: "I help X do Y." Mobile crops it around 40 characters
 >Banner: social proof + one clear offer.
 > About: hook, then proof, then the problem you solve, then a CTA.
 >Featured: one gated resource that captures the email, for great value

2. Anatomy of a Post

Every post that works has 4 parts:

 → Hook (stops the scroll)
 → Re-hook (earns the "see more" click)
 → Value (the reason they stay)
 → CTA (the reason they act)

Frameworks I lean on when I'm stuck: PAS (Problem, Agitate, Solution), AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action), BAB (Before, After, Bridge).

3. Hooks

Keep them 40 to 70 characters. One idea with a curiosity gap.

My best-performing hooks do one of two things:

 → Lead with a number ("These are the 6 AI agents we deploy across our         >$10M ARR clients")
 → Lead with an authority anchor ("Across 100 outreach sequences, these 4 signals won")

Numbers are usually the winning formula for us.

 4. Your Content system

They say best practices are to post across a funnel:

 → 50% reach (broad, relatable, top of funnel)
 → 25% authority (frameworks, breakdowns, proof)
 → 25% convert (offers, lead magnets, case studies)

I find this still works.  Two other core concepts:

→ Design is 80% of the post.
→ Post 3 to 5 times a week. Consistency compounds.

5. The Best Part

This is where 99% of "LinkedIn advice" stops.  3 plays we run every single week:

 → Your engagers: capture everyone who reacts and comments on your posts, enrich them, then retarget. They already raised their hand.

 → Competitor engagers: capture who's engaging with your competitors' content. They are potentially shopping your category.

 → Social listening: find people literally asking for what you sell ("anyone know a good X?") and reach out while the intent is actually hot. Surprisingly you might be able to find 2-3 of these per month. But you have a much higher likelihood of closing them.

I run outbound for 15 clients from one terminal, 23M+ emails and counting. My most-used lever is the delete key.

Every vendor in this space sells you more. More inboxes + enrichment + touches, a bigger list. That advice made sense when inboxes were open and domains were cheap to burn.

The clients of mine who broke their revenue ceiling did the opposite. They cut the motion down. Here are the 5 things I delete first, in order.

1. The list

A one-filter list is a phone book with a logo on it. Before a single send I score every account on four dimensions:

- funding
- firmographics
- tech stack
- growth signals.

Score the whole list on fit and timing, and send to the top slice only.

2. The redundant tool.

Most stacks run the same job through two tools, and one is failing without ever throwing an error. A tool should keep its slot only if it answers in seconds, errors loudly, and returns clean data.

Collapse the rest into one waterfall: Wiza, then FullEnrich across 20+ providers, then Prospeo for the gaps.

List every tool and the one job it owns.

3. The volume per inbox.

Sending harder from the same inboxes is how domains die. When a domain's reputation collapses, it takes every queued email with it. The fix is lower volume spread across more warmed inboxes.

The inbox policy I run:
- Warm-up: two weeks before a single cold send.
- Auth: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on day one.
- Cap: 20 to 25 sends per inbox per day.
- Complaints: under 0.1%, one or two per thousand, or the domain is done.

It is boring, and it is why we land 95%+ in the primary inbox. Audit sends per inbox. Any inbox over 25 a day, redistribute the volume or add inboxes.

4. The human doing robot work.

If a model does the task at 90% of your quality in a fraction of the time, it is no longer a human task. Keeping a person on it is a tax you pay every week.

The split is simple:
- Give the model: list building, enrichment, scoring, sequence drafts, pre-call research.
Keep the human: the offer, the targeting call, the one reply that closes a deal.

5. The vanity metric.

I do not care how many meetings you booked. Meetings are the easiest number in outbound to inflate. Pipeline by source is the only board I trust. Tag every opportunity to the campaign or signal that made it, wire RB2B or Vector into the CRM, and kill any source under your bar.

I rescore accounts daily, and 20% of my pipeline comes from ones marked cold. Rebuild your dashboard on pipeline by source. Delete every vanity tile.

One more: kill the ask-first email. "Hop on a 15-minute call?" is why reply rates cratered.

Give something usable before you ask for anything.

Before you add a tool, a channel, or a follow-up, ask what you could delete instead.

text:
If you're doing GTM, you might want to save this...

(these are the insights we gathered from building GTM systems for 275+ companies)

ICP & targeting

1. One ICP. Nail it, then expand. 3 ICPs on day one is 3 half-built campaigns.
2. Define by pain, not job title. A title and a headcount band is a filter.
3. Stack intent signals before you send. Signal-triggered lists reply at 15-25%. Static lists, 3.4%.
4. Build the list in Clay.
5. Job changes are a buying trigger. A champion who moves takes the problem with them.
6. Track tech stack. If they run your competitor, they already believe in the problem. You're selling a switch.
7. Watch hiring. A company posting 3 SDR roles just told you they're investing in outbound.
8. Layer funding on top. Recently raised means budget and a deadline.
9. Score by signal density. A 20-person startup firing 5 signals outranks a Fortune 500 firing none.
10. Re-cut the ICP every quarter. Pull the last 30-50 closed-won domains and rebuild the filters from those.

Outbound setup

11. Never cold email from your primary domain. Buy separate ones.
12. Buy 15-20 sending domains and 40 mailboxes, each on its own IP. Cap it at 2-3 mailboxes per domain and split them 50/50 across Google Workspace and Microsoft 365.
13. Warm for 2 weeks minimum. Don't send a prospect anything from a new domain for its first 14 days live.
14. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on day one. p=none is enough to clear Google, Yahoo, and Outlook. Skip it and you're in spam before the first send.
15. Scale by mailbox count. 20-25 sends a day per mailbox is the ceiling, so spread it across 40 inboxes instead of overloading a few.
16. Pick one sending tool and stay. Switching mid-campaign resets your reputation.
17. Verify EVERY address before it goes out. Under 2% bounce is the safe zone. Above it you're burning the domain.
18. Check domain health weekly in Postmaster v2. It's a pass or a needs-work, nothing in between.
19. Split inbound and outbound infrastructure. Different tools, different domains, different rules.
20. Keep backup domains warming in the background. Domains have a shelf life, replace them every 9-12 months.

Cold email

21. Relevance beats personalization. One accurate line on why you're writing proves you did the homework.
22. 3 words get the subject opened. The body sells.
23. Under 80 words.
24. One CTA. "Worth a conversation?" is enough.
25. Lead with their problem. "Struggling with X" beats "We do Y".
26. Plan 4-7 touches, then stop. 58% of replies still land on step one.
27. A/B test the offer. "Free audit" against "strategy call" is a word tweak. Change what you're actually offering.
28. Write like a human. Human-edited emails reply at 5.1%, pure AI at 2.4%. The edit is the whole difference.
29. Fix the list before you touch send time. "Best time to send" is what people optimize when the list is bad.
30. Replies are the metric. Opens are unreliable and replies are pipeline.

LinkedIn content

31. Post from the founder. Company page organic reach fell 66% in 2 years.
32. Post 3-5x a week. More frequency still lifts reach. There's no penalty in the data.
33. Narrate the work. Real numbers, real workflows, real outcomes. Manufactured takes get scrolled.
34. Your hook has under 3 seconds. Put the number in the first line.
35. Gate lead magnets by hand. LinkedIn now limits comments made by automation.
36. Documents out-reach everything. Docs 1.39x, video 0.86x and falling.
37. Repurpose everything.
38. Engage 15 minutes before and after you post. The first hour decides distribution.
39. Content is top of funnel for outbound. Prospects who've seen your posts reply at 3x the rate.
40. Specificity beats polish. "47 meetings from one workflow" is the whole post. A vague promise about your pipeline is nothing.

LinkedIn ads

41. Ads buy familiarity. Warm them up before the cold email hits.
42. Upload your target account list.
43. Retarget website visitors. The pricing-page visit is a signal. Put the ad in front of them before the email goes out.
44. Ads from a person's profile pull about 2x the CTR of company ads. No lead gen forms on them, so no direct conversions either.
45. $10 a day is the floor. $3-5K a month is the reality.
46. Make the ad look like your organic posts. Anything that reads as an ad gets scrolled.
47. Chase penetration over frequency. Past 8 exposures, click probability starts falling.
48. Promote your best organic posts.
49. Lead gen forms for bottom of funnel only. Leads expire after 90 days now, so sync them to CRM the same day.
50. Measure influenced pipeline. Revenue attribution reports at company level now. Use it.

The flywheel

51. Outbound alone is a treadmill. The list gets worked once, then next month starts from zero.
52. Content is air cover for outbound. 68% of buyers have a front-runner before they start looking.
53. Ads build familiarity before the email lands. 5 impressions in, a cold email feels warm.
54. Outbound generates your content. Every objection, win, and lost deal is a post.
55. Point all 3 channels at the same account list. Same rows, same week, or nothing compounds.
56. Build in the order above: list, domains, email, content, ads. One layer at a time.
57. The flywheel compounds monthly. Month 1 is a list and 3 posts. Month 6 is replies from people who saw the posts.
58. Warm outbound is where this is going. Pull the post engagers into Clay and sequence them first.
59. Content engagers are your best targets. 3 post likes beat any third-party intent signal.
60. Every channel feeds the others. The post builds the ad audience, the ad drives the site visit, and outbound closes.

AI in GTM

61. AI replaces tasks, not judgment. Vercel's lead agent took over inbound qualification and 9 SDRs moved to outbound.
62. AI writes bad outbound by default. Give it your voice, your ICP, and your real signals or it writes for nobody.
63. Clay plus AI is an unfair advantage. Enrichment and signal scoring at a scale no SDR team matches.
64. Build AI workflows before you buy AI tools. An n8n flow built once runs on every client after that. A rented tool bills you again for every seat.
65. AI SDRs work best as augmentation. 11x's own CEO: "I don't think AI SDRs work."
66. Use LLMs to score and prioritize signals. Ours runs every account through a classification prompt with closed-won plus signal data as the rubric. 110 companies tiered in under a minute.
67. Automate the first mile. Keep the last mile human. Claude pulls and scores the list. The Tier 1 message still goes out by hand.
68. Let AI do 70% of the draft. You own the last 30%, and that's the part that ships.
69. Connect the stack with MCP. I run 18 of these daily in Claude Code: Clay, Apollo, Instantly, Attio, Supabase.
70. Small teams are pulling ahead, slowly. Revenue per employee moved 9-17%.

Tech stack

71. CRM is the foundation. Pick one and commit. Watch the bill. Everyone is repricing to credits.
72. Clay for enrichment and signal stacking.
73. Apollo for prospecting data on a budget. Best value per valid email. Database size is the wrong number to shop on.
74. Layer enrichment tools. Cheapest and cleanest first, escalate only on a miss. With a full waterfall (Wiza, FullEnrich, Prospeo) coverage can push past 90%.
75. One sequencing tool. Instantly for volume, lemlist when the sequence spans channels.
76. Split your LinkedIn tool from your email tool. One suspension shouldn't take both channels down.
77. Taplio for scheduling. Never for auto-commenting.

Day 1
→ Buy 15 to 20 sending domains and 40 mailboxes, and start the warm-up.
→ Switch on 7 triggers to start. A trigger is a recent change that gives you a reason to email, like a funding round. Give each one an age limit, so a company doesn't rank higher for a round it raised 4 months ago.

Week 1
→ Pull your last 30 to 50 customers from the CRM, and use CompanyEnrich to find 50 similar companies for each one.

→ Have Claude sort every company into 3 tiers, best fit first. If it isn't sure about one, it goes down a tier.
→ Write down why every removed company was removed. Without the reason, Claude adds them back on the next run.

Week 2
→ Write 1 first line per trigger, before you have a single name to send it to. Nobody wants to hear "saw you raised a round", so say what the change means for them in that same line.
→ Run the whole setup on 5 companies where you already know the right answer. Make 1 of them a current customer. It should never get an email.

Last days of warm-up
→ Pull the 3 people you want at each company and verify every address that same day. Above a 2% bounce rate, you're burning the domains you just spent 2 weeks warming.

Day 15
→ The first campaign goes out, best-fit companies first.

After launch
→ Re-score every company every day. In Q2, 20% of our pipeline came from companies our CRM had marked cold 30 days earlier.
→ Start from the 3 email frameworks in the article until you've sent 10,000+ emails. After that, write from your own winners.

→ Use Warmly or RB2B to see which company visited, and the person when the tool can tell.

5. Find buyers in your competitors' comment sections
→ Every day, scrape everyone who reacts to or comments on a competitor's LinkedIn posts.
→ Anyone who fits gets a LinkedIn message about the post's topic. 3 days later, their colleagues get the same angle by email. Never mention that you saw them engage.

Rung 3 is where a voice shows up. The framework is still there, only now there is a real client sitting inside it, a real number from the business, a way of phrasing things you would know even with the headshot cropped out.

Rung 4 is authority. You are teaching from something you did last quarter, with an opinion you paid for by doing the work instead of reading about it.

People start trusting you at rung 3. Rung 4 is where that trust starts turning into pipeline.

Almost every call I've booked on LinkedIn started in someone else's comment section.

Posting is what makes people warm to you, but the real conversations tend to start earlier than that, down in the comments, weeks before I have pitched anyone anything.

There is a system underneath it all. Fifteen comments a day, spread across three tiers.

1. Your ICPs, the people you want as clients. Open one prospect's profile, look at who they reply to, and go find those people too. They will have seen your name around long before you reach out.

2. Your peers, same niche, competitors included. Their feed doubles as a live readout of what is landing this week.

3. And the big accounts, where one insightful comment in the first half hour can put you in front of thousands of exactly the right readers.

How you comment is the part that decides everything.

Also, don’t hesitate from disagreeing or sharing a contrarian viewpoint.

A like or a supportive comment is generally forgettable and lost in a sea of other affirmative comments. But a disagreement or a no can end up earning you actual replies.

Publish a LinkedIn post, glance at it once, close the app, and you just threw away 70% of its reach. Almost everyone does exactly that.

LinkedIn tries every post out on a small crowd first. Get some traction in the opening 60 to 90 minutes and it opens the doors wider, get nothing and it lets the post slip away. That single window decides about 70% of the reach a post will ever see.

The actions inside it carry different weight, too. A comment is worth 15x a like, a share 5x, a save 3x.

Which means the moment you publish, the work has barely started. Reply to every comment in that first hour and you earn 50% more engagement across the whole life of the post.
