text:
LinkedIn changed its algorithm in March. Eight things that worked in 2023 now actively cost you reach.

The four that trip people up the most:

1. Length. The old sweet spot was short and punchy, and now it is the opposite. Long posts win, 1,250 to 3,000 characters, for +227% reach.

2. Links. They used to bury a post, and now they lift it. One to three links, +43%. More than three, +441%. As long as you are sending people somewhere worth the click.

3. Format. Carousels fell off a cliff, down to 6% of top posts. Infographics, video and quotes carry 79% between them now.

4. Replies. The strongest creators answer their comments 255% more than everyone else, because the conversation is what keeps a post alive.

Reach is already down 68% since 2023. Running the old rules just gets you there faster.

I put together an in-depth breakdown of everything I know about growing on the platform (coming from someone that has scaled multiple LinkedIn accounts that generated millions in recurring revenue):
still can't believe people pay thousands a month for lead lists

Your AI writes like a robot because you talk to it like a human. It doesn't fill in what you left out, and it never will.

Tell a friend you are thirsty and they hand you a glass of water. Say the same thing to AI and it takes the words at face value, because it has none of the context you carry around without noticing. You have to hand that context over on purpose.

Two fixes I run on every draft.

The first is to brief it like a new hire, with a role, a task, constraints and a style. "You are a content strategist for B2B SaaS, 300 words, no bullet points, write like you're explaining it to a colleague." That will always beat "write me a post."

The second is to show it instead of describing it. Paste three things you have written yourself, point out what makes them sound like you, and ask it to match that pattern. AI is hopeless at following a description of your voice and surprisingly good at copying a real example.

I have a content twin. It runs inside Claude Code, it writes like me, and I do not start from a blank page anymore 🙂

If you are still typing "write me a LinkedIn post" into an empty chat, you will keep producing the kind of thing people have read a hundred times, written by a hundred people who all sound the same.

What turned it around was one file: 25 questions about how I actually talk. My beliefs, my humor, the words I reach for, the ones I would never use.

Everything else stacks on top:

→ It learned who I write for and the few themes I keep coming back to.
→ Research pulls from five places at once, so I write about what my audience cares about.
→ Ideas arrive already ranked. Monday never starts empty.
→ 20+ hooks per idea, I keep the one that pulls.
→ It drafts in my voice, then I trim and drop in the real story.
→ It grades itself before I see anything. Five dimensions, out of 50. Below 38 goes back.
→ What faded gets dropped, so the next cycle starts sharper.

Save it for the day you open Claude and feel the blank page panic.

My first viral post passed 50K impressions. I sat there near midnight refreshing, watching the number climb, feeling like I had finally won something.

The next morning my inbox was still empty. 🥲

That is all a loud post is, sometimes. A lot of strangers clapping in a room they will walk out of and won't remember.

Months later a she-EO messaged me. "I've been reading you for a while, can I hire you to help with my LinkedIn profile." I went back to find which post had brought her. It wasn't the viral one.

That was the day I understood these 3 things:

1. Reach is a crowd walking past a street singer.
2. Resonance is the one person who stops and writes the name down.
3. Revenue arrives months later, when she comes back and asks for you by that name.

Almost all the energy goes into gathering the crowd, and the business is sitting with the one person who stopped.

So before you chase the next viral post: how many of today's readers will remember you tomorrow?

you liked something of ours thirty days ago. you've forgotten.

we have not.

you'll reach out eventually and think you found us. https://t.co/UiZUqcQCnQ

We run content for an ads team, so I keep getting asked to point at the post that booked the call.

The instruction underneath: find the winner, do more of that. In their world that is correct. In mine the instruction has nowhere to go.

Ads rent a new audience every time you pay. The winner goes out to 10K strangers who have never seen it, so you scale it by running it again, wider. Repeating with variations is the whole point.

Content doesn't work that way. You live in the same room. The same people see you post after post, so when you repeat your winner they have already heard it.

You can't strip-mine a good post the way you strip-mine a good ad.

That one thing, renting strangers versus living in the same room, changes the sequence:

→ The winner stops being a post and becomes a lesson. You never run it again. You take whatever made it good and pour it into a new idea next week, for the same people.

→ So the job is a new idea every week. I used to think that meant I was scattered 🙃

→ Ads get narrower over time, down to the one thing that works. Content keeps getting wider, because you learn what kind of ideas land and then keep inventing new ones.

The method is same: test, measure, learn.

I drew the whole thing into a map 👇

I build AI content systems for a living, and I keep going back to rules written before any of these tools existed.

Hundreds of posts and dozens of AI writing tools later, these nine rules are the ones I swear by:

1. Sweat the headline.

5x more people read your first line than everything under it. A weak one wastes the whole post.

2. Be specific.

"Cuts onboarding from 3 weeks to 3 days" gets believed. "Improves onboarding" gets scrolled past. Exact claims are hard to fake, so people trust them.

3. Write the way you talk.

Boomerang read 40 million emails. The ones written at a third grade reading level got 36% more replies than the ones dressed up in big words.

4. Lead with the benefit.

Turn every spec into what the reader actually gets. "1,000 songs in your pocket" beat "5GB MP3 player."

5. Cut every word you can.

The first draft is you working out what you mean. The edit is where it becomes worth reading.

6. Earn the next line.

No one owes you the whole post. Each line has one job: make the next line get read.

7. Show proof, skip adjectives.

One real number does more work than a paragraph of "trusted" and "leading."

8. Test, don't guess.

Your favorite line is rarely the reader's favorite. Change one thing, keep what wins.

9. Keep one voice.

Say the same true thing, the same way, long enough that people recognize you before they see your name.

None of it is a hack and none of it is about the tool. That is why it stays timeless.

I've been the solo content team for 24 people. Those posts signed 27 new clients and $153,000 in new MRR in a single quarter.

I also built the system underneath it, the whole content operation running inside Claude Code. 

Here's everything I know about making LinkedIn produce pipeline:

Foundation

1. Pick one person to write for. A vague audience gives you vague posts.
2. Name the one outcome the account exists to create, in plain words.
3. Positioning in one line: I help [who] do [outcome] without [pain]. Test it on a stranger.
4. Three topics per account, maximum. Anything past that dilutes the signal.
5. Write the no-go list. What you never post about is worth more than your topic list.
6. Three to five content pillars, each with a goal and a funnel stage.
7. No random acts of content. If a post traces back to no pillar, it doesn't get written.
8. Split the buyers into three tiers: decision-makers, champions, practitioners.
9. Per tier, write their pain in their words, the language they search, the signals that mean they are buying.
10. The About section opens on the reader's problem. Profile photo is roughly a 21x multiplier.

The voice profile

11. Capture voice from speech. Record them explaining their work, then transcribe it.
12. Twenty-five questions, in conversation. Nobody's ever answered "what is your tone?" honestly in a form.
13. Capture their beliefs, their humor, their rhythm, their hard-nos.
14. Keep an anti-voice file beside it, listing the exact words they reject.
15. Without a voice profile, every account you run slides into the same beige.
16. Read it out loud. If they wouldn't say it in a meeting, it isn't their voice yet.
17. Steal the reader's own phrasing from their Slack threads, podcasts, comments.
18. Delete jargon instead of defining it. A plain sentence does the same job.
19. The foundation docs are living. Someone raises a round, you change the file.
20. Refresh the voice profile monthly. Voice drifts without announcing itself.

Research

21. The research runs in parallel, never one source at a time. Apify first, for what's performing in that niche right now.
22. Reddit for how buyers describe pain when no vendor is listening.
23. YouTube for frameworks worth adapting.
24. X for the live debates, because the argument always lands here first.
25. Fireflies transcripts. One 30-minute call carries 3 to 5 points the client never knew they made.
26. Your own archive, read for gaps. What an account never covered is as useful as what is trending.
27. One keyword string triggers all of them, once a week. Research is a batch job. Redo it per post and the week disappears.
28. Mine your DMs and your voice notes. A question you've answered twice is a post.
29. Every "but what about X" from a prospect is a post already half written.
30. Steal the angle and leave the words. Save 20 winners a week, map their structure.

Ideation and hooks

31. Run one idea session a week. Score every idea against the buyer tiers, then keep only as many as you can actually publish.
32. Keep a 50-idea backlog. I no longer start from a blank page, and I never will again.
33. Document, don't ideate. Write what you did on Tuesday.
34. New account to first post in 48 hours. Foundation on day one, full draft by day two.
35. The first two lines decide everything. They sit above the "see more".
36. Cap hooks at 8 to 12 words. Mobile cuts the rest.
37. Open with a number, a name or a claim, and put the verb first.
38. Be uncomfortably specific. "Lost on slide 14" beats "I lost a big deal".
39. Twenty-plus hook variations per idea, from 59 templates sorted by trigger: desire, curiosity, fear. One ships.
40. Don't tease. Pay off in line one, because "here's what I learned" loses them.

Drafting

41. Brief it like a new hire: role, task, constraints, style. "Write me a post" gets you a robot.
42. Claude writes like a robot because you talk to it like a human. It never fills in what you left out.
43. Show it, don't describe it. Paste the example in.
44. One idea per post. Three insights stacked is three posts nobody finished reading.
45. Cut your first paragraph. It's almost always warmup.
46. Show the example before you name the principle.
47. Numbers beat adjectives. "From 12% to 41% reply rate" beats "big improvement".
48. Cut every word doing no work: just, really, actually.
49. Give the designer a brief. Layout, exact copy placement, reference images.
50. The last line is the second hook. It earns the comment.

The grading system

51. Nothing ships unchecked. Four gates: a de-AI pass, a quality score, a rule check against that client's own law, then delivery.
52. The quality score is five dimensions out of 50. Below 38 it goes back with the fixes named, no vague "make it better".
53. Two loops maximum. Still failing, a human reads it, and the human is me.
54. That loop is why 24 accounts don't need 24 editors.
55. Revision asks why it chose this angle and where the argument is weakest.
56. Smoothing sentences is approving a thinking process you never went through.
57. The deskilling spiral: better output, less practice, weaker judgment, more dependence. It feels like productivity all the way down.
58. Design the workflow before you pick the model. If nobody has to decide anything, the model is just typing faster.
59. Before anyone automates, make them write the hook by hand once.
60. Claude will tell you, very confidently, that it can do a job it can't. I let it try once. It was wrong, and it admitted it in the end. Confidence sells heaters in the desert.

Writing for pipeline

61. "Interesting" is a compliment that books nothing. Write until the comment says "they get my problem".
62. Audience content is fine. Trouble starts when it is all you make.
63. Build the resource before you gate it. The post is only the promotion.
64. Reach, trust or conversion. Pick one, because a post chasing all three lands none of them.
65. Write toward what the reader does next. A post with no next step gets one good day and then nothing.
66. If a post can't run as an ad or carry outbound, it doesn't scale.
67. The buyer often isn't the engager. That's fine, as long as a path back exists.
68. If the content educates your competitors, it is noise.
69. "What would you add?" outperforms "book a call".
70. Posts build trust, DMs close, and one post can't do both.

Running many accounts

71. Three voices in parallel. Founders carry positioning, operators carry proof, customers carry the intro.
72. Only the founder posting smells like a brand exercise, and everyone can smell it.
73. Only operators posting means the company has no point of view.
74. Once all three post on their own rhythm, the account stops depending on any one of them.
75. Followers and DMs belong to the employee, or nobody lasts past week six.
76. One editor, twenty minutes. A draft sitting three days dies in the doc.
77. One folder per account: profile, voice, ICP, pillars, CTAs, brand, transcripts, learning log.
78. Claude reads those files every run. Better files, better output.
79. A skill is a saved API call. Checkpoint the good ones so nothing starts from scratch.
80. Log every session: what shipped, what changed, what got rejected. Read five of those logs back and you can see which sentences keep getting rewritten, which is where the voice is drifting.

Distribution

81. The post is half the result on its very best day. Everything after it decides the other half.
82. Three things have to run together: the post has to be something only they could say, it has to land in feeds beyond their connections, and the readers have to end up in a conversation. Run one and you plateau.
83. Feed the engagement data back into the system every week. Recycle what worked, flag what died.
84. The first 60 to 90 minutes decide roughly 70% of a post's lifetime reach.
85. Reply inside the first hour. Worth around 50% more engagement across the post's life.
86. For reach, a comment is worth about 15x a like, a share 5x, a save 3x.
87. A post with fifty comments is 51 pieces of content. Write your replies like posts.
88. Almost every call I have booked started in someone else's comment section.
89. Leave fifteen comments a day, split across your ICPs, your peers, and the big accounts.
90. Comments under 15 words barely register, and engagement pods get caught around 97% of the time.

What compounds

91. LinkedIn changed its algorithm in March. Reach coming from your own connections fell from 70% to 10%, and reach coming from strangers who follow the topic rose from 5% to 50%. (All the platform numbers in this section: Richard van der Blom, Algorithm Report 2026.)
92. So most people seeing a post have never heard of the person who wrote it. Write for the stranger who just found you.
93. Long posts win now. Somewhere between 1,250 and 3,000 characters earns +227% more reach than the short punchy style that worked in 2023.
94. Carousels collapsed to 6% of top-performing posts. Infographics, video and quotes now make up 79% of them.
95. One post that performed becomes five pieces rebuilt for five platforms. Copy-paste it instead and you get it ignored five times.
96. Dwell time is the metric that matters. A post people read for 61 seconds or more earns roughly 13x the engagement of one they skim past.
97. Resurface an evergreen post after 30 days. The algorithm keeps dragging old winners back up.
98. Saves, sends and profile views tell you more than likes. A profile view means somebody is sizing you up.
99. Audit the strategy monthly and the posts quarterly, reading your bottom 10 as closely as your top 10. A format that underperforms three times running gets retired for 30 days.
100. And the only metric that ever mattered: did the right person reach out?

All the system really buys me is that the writing still happens on the Tuesdays when nobody feels inspired. It can't make anyone care.

That part is still people. A save means someone wants to keep thinking about it later. A comment is more public than that, they want to be seen having the take. A share is somebody putting your idea next to their own name. The algorithm is just the residue of all that.

Anyway. Which section did you skip while reading this? That's the one 🙂

I almost let Claude sell me a heater in the desert last week.

I wanted an iceberg infographic. And I knew one thing going in: clean shapes are not what Claude does well. We had produced some really ugly visuals before I learned that.

So I came with a plan.

Gemini makes the shape first, then Claude builds the CSS and HTML on top of that layer.

Then Claude told me (very confidently) that it could do the whole job on its own. No Gemini needed.

I was sure about my decision before that. But hearing the confidence, I opened the door to listen.

So I said, ok, try it, then tell me.

And it tried every possible way, (it wanted to) prove me wrong.

Unfortunately for Claude, and fortunately for my self-esteem 😂 it was wrong. I was right. In the end it told me my instinct was correct and that we should do it the way I suggested from the start.

The moral of the story is that I won an argument with a machine 🤪

Jokes apart, I think the real lesson is that if I did not know my stuff, I would have believed the confident voice & shipped out something ugly then blamed the system didn't work.

So know your stuff first before letting AI takes over. That's why you should develop a taste.

I create LinkedIn content that grows pipeline, and I help teams at a lot of other B2B companies do the same.

So when people tell me reach is dead, I go and look at the numbers first.

It did drop, 68% since 2023, and it lines up with what I've watched across client accounts.

Then I came across a study that put a number on it: across a 1,000+ creator sample over the last 90 days, split by follower size.

At 10,000 followers you'd expect around 26,000 impressions and 540 new followers. I stopped reading halfway through to go open my own 😅

I have 12,865 followers.
Same 90 days: 661,627 impressions and 4,067 new followers.

That's about 25x the impressions for my bracket.

It's also more than the median for an account four times my size, because 50K accounts sit at 385,000.

Impressions up 185% on my own previous quarter, followers up 41%.

Impressions don't book calls though. That's a separate build, and it's the part people actually ask me about 🙈

But anyway, here are four things that have helped me still pull consistent engagement on LinkedIn (hint: copy me)

1. A post going wide and a post getting you a call are two different animals.

I kept making the first one and waiting for the second one to just happen.

Wide posts get you in the room, that's their whole job and they do it well, and then they stand around in there.

You write the one that books a call for a handful of people, maybe one. It says their problem back to them in the words they'd use in their own Slack.

What you're after is the DM that says: ok, how do you know this about me.

2. The hook and the body want opposite things.

Took me a while to see that one. The hook has to be greedy, it grabs at something everybody walks around with, usually that low panic about being left behind, and that's what carries it past the people who already follow you.

Then inside? Get rude with the specifics.

"Your pipeline is broken" goes out to thousands who nod at it and keep scrolling. Put the revenue in. Put the exact stage where they keep losing demos. Now hardly anyone sees it, and I still don't fully love that trade, but that's where the calls come from.

3. Read your comment section properly.

I ignored mine for a long time, treated it like a scoreboard, a number to feel good or bad about.

Typing a real opinion under your own full name, somewhere your boss scrolls past it, costs something.

When somebody writes "we're dealing with this exact thing right now," they've told me more than the whole like count. I say this on calls and then watch people scroll straight to the likes anyway 🙃

4. None of it is about writing more.

Mine runs off one file: a voice profile you get to by talking for a while instead of filling anything in, because as if anyone has ever answered "what is your tone" honestly in a box.

Then a grader, five dimensions out of 50, anything under 38 goes back with the fixes named.

AI writes the first one, I go in and rough it back up, and the file sits there so it can't slowly sand me down into everybody else.

That's what I build for founders and their teams at @Frontal_AI 🤭

article_title: How to Build an AI Content Twin That Sounds Just Like You

text:
356 sales meetings in under 3 months, all from LinkedIn content. Zero ads, one person running the machine.

Here's how to actually get results like the above from LinkedIn: (bookmark for later)

1/ Profile first
Posting into an unoptimized profile is pouring water into a cracked glass. Banner, headline, About, a Featured section with proof and one clear link. The profile converts, the posts only bring people to it.

2/ Research that isn't you guessing
Ideas come from real places. Client-call transcripts in Fireflies, the highest-signal source and the one everyone leaves rotting in a folder. What's performing, via Apify. How buyers complain on Reddit. The live fights on X. Frameworks worth adapting on YouTube.

3/ The Client OS
One folder per person. A voice profile captured through a 25-question conversation, an ICP doc with 3 buyer tiers in their own words, and the pillars every post traces back to. A well-structured folder remembers who you are, so the model never gets to fill that in for you.

4/ The 40/20/40 mix
Reach at the top, authority in the middle, pipeline at the bottom. Hold that balance and the account grows and books meetings in the same week.

5/ The production line
20+ hook options per idea, one survives. A full draft in the documented voice. Then the gates: a de-AI pass that strips the tells, a score out of 50 where below 38 goes back, a check against the account's own feedback log, and a human sign-off. Mine 🙂

6/ The calendar
Posts scheduled and balanced by job, so no week quietly turns into all reach and no pipeline.

7/ The learning loop
Every session logs itself. Every five sessions the system flags what keeps getting rewritten, which is where a voice is drifting. Fresh call transcripts feed the voice profile, and the loop runs again.

I ran it on our own team first. 24 people posting, $153,000 in new MRR in 87 days, zero ads underneath.

Every layer, in build order, is in the article below. Clone it block by block. The taste part still has to be a person 🥲

I'm not an engineer, and Claude Code still runs our whole content operation. 27 skills, one terminal, and most of the code scrolling past me is a mystery 🙃

Which makes it sound like the tool is doing all the work. Anthropic just read 400,000 Claude Code sessions and the numbers say otherwise.

The same model, on the same subscription, hands people very different amounts.

Expert sessions pulled around 12 actions and 3,200 words out of one prompt, while beginner sessions got 5 actions and 600 words.

What separated them was how exactly they asked, and who ended up correcting who. Knowing the subject predicted more than knowing how to code.

And I only understood that last part properly after arguing with Claude about an iceberg infographic.

It told me, very confidently, that it could make the clean shapes on its own. It could not, and I only knew because we had already made a pile of ugly icebergs before that 🙈

So the confidence is not the signal. It sounds the same when it is right and when it is wrong, and you only catch the difference if you already know the work. That is the part the tool cannot do for you. You will still have to chip in.

Anyway. Back to the terminal, someone has to keep telling Claude no 😭

Every AI voice tool opens the same way. Describe your tone. Pick three adjectives.

I do this for a living and I still can't answer it about myself. Nobody can. That's why your twin keeps coming back sounding like a polite stranger.

So I've cracked the perfect system to build myself an AI content twin, and here's how you can do the same too:

1/ The three adjectives
Voice works like breathing. You do it all day and you've never watched it happen. So you guess. And the guess flatters: sharper, funnier, more decisive than you are. The machine takes the wish seriously, that's its job, and you get a twin of your highlight reel. So I stopped asking people to describe themselves. Now I just interview them.

2/ The 25-question conversation
A conversation, not a form. Style questions are the weakest ones in it. Ask about style, you get self-report, the thing that already failed. Five do the work:
→ what everyone in your field says that you think is wrong
→ what annoys you about how people in your space talk
→ what you'd defend out loud, at a dinner
→ what you believed two years ago and don't now
→ a time this went badly for you

3/ The last question
Watch that one. Nobody delivers a story in brand voice. The vocabulary narrows, sentences go short or run long, somebody makes a joke at their own expense. That's the voice 🙂 It was never going to show up in an adjective.

4/ What goes in the file
→ how the sentences move, and where the short ones land
→ the vocabulary, written down as they said it
→ the banned list, from what they avoided saying out loud
→ the beliefs they'll defend, which is what stops content going to agreeable mush
→ the humor, how they soften a hard opinion
→ the texture to protect
(this is the one to bookmark)

5/ The line every editing pass deletes
The grammar wobble, the odd pairing, the tic. Our reflex when we improve writing is smoother and more correct, and for voice that's backwards. A draft that comes back frictionless has had something polished out of it. (mine is the slightly weird way I pair words in English, I stopped sanding it 🤣)

6/ ICP and pillars, right next to it
Nobody's tracking how consistent you are, they notice whether you're the same person twice. Three buyer tiers, each mapped to the words that tier types when they go hunting. A CFO and a practitioner describe the same problem in completely different sentences. Then three to five pillars, everything traces back to one.

7/ The layer you're on
Layer 1 is "5 tips for better marketing". Layer 2 is structured, hooked, CTA at the bottom, swap the name at the top and nothing changes. Layer 3 has a real client story behind it and a number from the actual business. Layer 4 teaches from this quarter. Most founders say 3. I open the feed, it's 2 with some cosmetic work (mine slides there too on a rushed week 🙃). What closes that gap is knowing what only you can say, written down outside your head.

8/ Grading, by counting
Ask a model to score soul out of 10, you get a 7 today and a 9 tomorrow on the same paragraph. So the number has to come from counting. Each of the 5 dimensions is five yes-or-no checks, two points each. 25 checks, out of 50. Below 38 goes back. Then the floor: any single dimension at 5 or under goes back anyway. 42 with a 4 in soul is a well-built post with nobody inside it. A threshold doesn't get tired.

9/ The drift calendar
Weeks 1 to 3 are the honeymoon. Output is fast, it feels like you cracked something. Around week 4 you stop noticing every post opens the same way, your audience gets there first. By week 6 it's flat and nobody can say why, so people post more of it 😭 The jokes go first. Humor is the most fragile thing in a voice file. Every 5 sessions a pattern check, monthly a refresh, quarterly the pillars.

10/ Your own hand-edits
The highest-signal data in the system is the stuff you already rewrite by hand, without meaning to. It's the gap between what the file thinks you sound like and what you sound like. Feed it those.

This is the system I run. 24 people posting, $153,000 MRR in 87 days, 27 skills in one terminal.

And it will still hand me the wrong idea, beautifully written, because it can't know that the story from Tuesday was the way in.

That part stays mine. Nudging one circle on a visual, recoloring one pill, changing my mind ten times until it feels right..

Anyway, the full length guide is in the article below. Bookmark it for later.

For someone rated expert at the task, Claude produced around 12 actions and 3,200 words per prompt. For a novice: 5 actions, 600 words.

I'm not an engineer. Claude Code runs our entire content operation and I still can't read many of the code lines what scrolls past me .

What I can read is the output. Two seconds and I know if a sentence is dead or an infographic is ugly. Apparently that one piece of knowing is what buys the work .

Those numbers come from Anthropic, 400,000 Claude Code sessions, 235,000 users.

They also split who decides what. Users made around 70% of the planning calls. Claude made around 80% of the execution ones.

So the planning half never left our hands, which is the half I actually have .

The results followed.

→ Novice sessions reached verified success 15% of the time. Intermediate and expert sessions, 28 to 33%.

→ Novices abandoned the session 19% of the time. Everyone else, 5 to 7%.

So your expertise rate now gets printed on the receipt: tokens spent + session finished or abandoned.

Probably the most underrated (borderline ridiculous) Claude Code hack I know of:

Make it call me "Your Majesty"

And yes, it is a real productivity thing, I promise 🤣

I picked it up from a Chinese post on X originally.

The idea is to put one ridiculous word in your instruction file, something the model has no reason to ever say unless it is still reading that file. Then you forget about it and wait.

Because a few hours into a session your instructions slide into a blind spot. The answers get dumber and the tone stays exactly as confident as it was at the start. From there the work just gets worse.

So when it stops calling me Your Majesty mid-session, I know it's drifting. Probably time to close that and start a new session.

Most employee LinkedIn programs are dead by month 3.

The one I run inside Frontal just crossed 175K+ followers combined  + brought in 27 new clients and +$153K MRR in under 3 months.

And the team is more motivated to post now than at the start, because their writing keeps getting sharper. This is how we do it:

Layer 1. The operating setup.

Voice capture happens in a real conversation. A Google Form asking "what is your tone?" has never once been answered truthfully 🙂

One editor reads every draft and sends it back in twenty minutes>

The followers and the DMs belong to the employee. Put them on the company page and nobody stays motivated past week 6.

Distribution gets planned like everything else: who engages in the first hour, where each post gets reshared, which posts turned into booked calls.

Layer 2. Three kinds of voices, publishing in parallel.

Founders and execs open and close the story. They carry the point of view, and they are the names buyers want to trust before handing over money.

Operators sit in the middle. AEs, engineers, RevOps, talking about the work itself, with proof and real opinions.

Customers and the wider network bring the one thing nobody inside the company can fake: the testimonial and the warm intro.

All three running together is what turns content into a GTM channel.

Layer 3. The program answers to pipeline.

- Warm DMs from prospects who arrive half-sold before the first call.
- Paid budget goes to posts that already won organically, instead of random boosts on the corporate page.

Deals close faster because the buyer spent two months reading the seller. And the sales team believes what they sell, because they see themselves in the content.

Reach shows up anyway when all three layers run. It was never the goal.

Check which layer is missing on your side.

At 9:00 every morning, an agent sends me the content ideas that cleared my quality bar.

But before building the agent, I wrote the standard down.

The agent, Hermes, just enforces that line so I never have to trust my 11pm judgment again. Here is what it beats ideas against, in an order you can run by hand:

➤ Fix where ideas come from.

Mine come from a watch-list of creators on LinkedIn, X and YouTube,
from forums like Reddit and Quora where buyers describe problems with no audience to impress,
from the blogs and newsletters my buyers read,
and from topic searches that catch the people I don't follow yet.

➤ Measure posts against their author's average.

A post counts only when it clearly beats that author's usual numbers. 800 likes from someone who always gets 800 tells you not much.

➤ Run 4 checks before an idea gets your attention:

The same story from three sources becomes one theme, counted once.
Topics on your banned list never make it in.
Every number keeps a link to its source.
Each survivor gets a score on one question: would the people you want to reach care?

➤ Then this hard part: let the bar say no.

On a day nothing clears it, Hermes sends nothing. The empty mornings are what make the full ones trustworthy.

Hermes logs every idea I take or skip and tunes its scoring to match those calls.

💾 Save this post to build your own AI scout agent!

Our entire content operation runs through Claude from one terminal, and everything we ship for founders passes through it.

So this should be the news that ends me. It changes almost nothing.

A mark means content may have been processed by Claude. MAY.

And it does not run the other way. A missing mark proves nothing, it only tells you they used a different LLM.

What it does change is the hiding. For two years the skill worth having was making AI writing undetectable. That skill now has a much shorter shelf life.

This leaves us with what was always doing the work : whether the person had something to say before they opened the tool.

I am oddly glad about this one.

Clay announced 12 products in 12 weeks this month and built an automation to find the paying customers who still had not touched any of them.

This is such a great strategy imo.

On launch day only a slice of your customers actually see the thing. So we don't mark a launch done on the day it goes live.

Now I let the launch carry itself for 6 weeks:

1. Launch day: The announcement. One line item out of seven.

2. Day 3: What the customer used to do instead. Source: call transcripts.

3. Day 7: Screenshot of the old workflow next to the new one. Source: your own account.

4. Day 14: The unexpected use case. Source: support tickets and usage data.

5. Day 21: The reason people are not adopting, answered in public. Source: your sales team.

6. Day 30.: A customer explaining it in their words, quoted exactly. Source: transcripts again.

7. Day 45: The launch message again, rebuilt from whichever of the six performed.

Launch day is the day you are least useful to a buyer, because nobody wakes up needing your changelog.

Test it on your last launch. Can a paying customer describe what your new launch does after 3 weeks without opening your changelog?

Lovable went from zero to a $500M run rate in 19 months on $2M of marketing. I went looking for the growth engine behind that.

Their Head of Growth @ElenaVerna says 60 to 70% of the tactics she used before do not work anymore.

So I went through what replaced them, and none of them look like marketing:

1. Shipping is the distribution.

I opened their changelog and counted. 53 releases between May 18 and August 7, which is almost every weekday. Each one hands the team something to talk about.

2. 146 people post, and the first two hours are coordinated.

They call it beeswarming. Every employee builds something on Lovable and posts it, and an internal channel tells the rest of the team to go engage in the first two hours so the post never lands alone.

3. Community gets staffed like a job.

Their Discord is nothing fancy. What makes it work is that engineers and PMs show up in it themselves, user work gets spotlighted, and the people who help get early access.

4. Social replaced search.

Ranking a blog post used to bring traffic for years. Now people ask an AI the same question and never click through, so the article sits there earning nothing. Lovable put that effort into feeds instead. Leadership posts, the whole team is visible daily, and creators do a lot of the rest.

I scrolled back through @antonosika posts from before the product existed. Raw numbers, failed experiments, hiring photos. The audience existed before the product did.

5. The free tier is the ad budget.

They hand out credits like candy. Free users, hackathons, events.

One free day in March turned into 500K projects instead of the usual 200,000. Real paid acquisition did not start until they were past $300M ARR.

6. Features are commoditized, so they compete on how it feels.

In a market with hundreds of competitors everyone gets the same capability within weeks. What survives is how it feels to use, and whether you can see the people building it.

text: This might be one of the most insightful thing I've read all month from Clay about growth at software companies. https://t.co/G50xWxdunU

Lemlist crossed its first million in revenue without a single salesperson on the team. Their very first hires were content creators, developers, product people.

By year two, most of the growth was inbound, and lemlist reached $10M in ARR without paying for a single customer.

The numbers: $1M ARR in 2019. $10M by 2021. $28M by 2024 and it sits at $53M in 2026 . Close to 90% of that revenue came through inbound content, on zero ad spend. The real sales team came later, once content had already built the company.

I build content systems for a living, so here is what lemlist actually got right, and where teams go wrong copying it.

1. They staffed content before the revenue justified it.

In most companies content is the last hire made, once sales is covered and there is budget to spare. Lemlist did the reverse and put creators on payroll while a salesperson was still years away.

You cannot bolt a content engine on at $5M and expect it to compound, so the head start is the whole advantage, and lemlist took it before it had the revenue to justify it.

2. They posted the tactic, not the product.

Lemlist's content taught one thing: how to write cold email that actually gets replies. That is the exact thing lemlist does. So every useful post was a live demo, and the product showed up only as the tool the method ran on.

The content and the pitch were the same object.

This is the part most teams cannot copy, because it only works when your product is a teachable tactic.

3. Posting was everyone's job, modeled from the top.

The cadence started with the founders, then the whole company ran it. Product, engineering, support, all posting in public. That is the genuinely hard part, and it is why the reach never depended on one person's calendar.

4. They understood the engine well enough to sell it.

lempire, lemlist's parent, went on to build the tools other people use to do exactly this: Taplio, Tweet Hunter. When a company can productize its own content playbook, the playbook was never an accident.

Tell me whose LinkedIn you want pulled apart next.

text:
Most of my week at Frontal goes into un-writing.

Everyone on the team posts with AI, and left alone they all drift into one voice wearing different profile pictures. I call it linguistic monoculture.

I assumed the hard part would be volume. Volume is easy.

What saved it was one decision: where the human goes.

Almost everyone puts the person in at the front, briefs the AI, lets it write. We do the reverse. The model gets a draft to 80%. Then a real person spends the last 20% putting back everything it removed:

- the word pairing that looks like a mistake
- the detail so specific it seems useless
- the sentence that runs too long because that's how they actually breathe.

That last pass sounds optional. It's the entire job.

The machine is extremely good at making writing correct, and the feed is already drowning in correct.

I think about this more than I should, because English is my second language. I once wrote that Claude had become the most ruined name for human. Not a sentence. I left it in anyway.

So now I write them down on purpose and tell the system to protect them instead of smoothing them out.

If your content sounds fine and lands on no one, fine is the problem. Put your weird back in.

Clay has the most interesting company-led LinkedIn strategy right now. Across 12 months, posts from its employee accounts earned around 73,000 likes.

But one of their co-founders had published only five posts all year.

So where was all that attention coming from?

a. Distribution is the easy half.
Any company can launch an advocacy program and get a team posting. 3 weeks later they all sound like the same LinkedIn robot. Keeping every voice distinct is the hard half, and it is the half that earns the reach.

b. Go account by account and you see it.
Growth essays, career and AI lessons, memes, support advice, founder updates, video. All employees have personal interests, it doesn't feel anything corporate

c. A style guide is where voice goes to die.
Add one brand voice, run every draft through the same AI prompt, and everyone drifts to the same average until the feed reads like one tired person wrote it. Clay kept its people off the average. That is the achievement.

A form asking for tone words usually gives you “clear, authentic, conversational.”

Which is useful if your goal is to sound like everyone on the internet 😂

That is the result I keep building toward: remove the name and logo, and you can still tell who wrote each post.

In 87 days our teams' posts signed 27 new clients and added +$153,000 MRR.

ZERO paid ads with only ONE terminal.

This is the exact one we run, top to bottom.

1. Profile
Before a single post goes out, the profile has to convert the visitor that post sends. Banner, headline, About, and a Featured section that leads with proof. One CTA, not four.

2. Strategy
5 sources feed every idea:
→ Fireflies transcripts from client calls, the highest signal I get
→ Competitor and viral posts pulled through Apify
→ Reddit for how buyers describe the pain
→ YouTube for frameworks worth stealing
→ X for the live debates

3. The engine
Everything runs in one terminal on Claude Code. The brain is a folder per person, 3 documents:

→ Voice profile: a 25-question conversation, captured before AI touches a word
→ ICP: 3 buyer tiers and the words each tier actually uses
→ Pillars: 3 to 5 themes every post traces back to

4. Content mix
Every week balances reach at the top, authority in the middle, pipeline at the bottom. We hold it near 40/20/40, so the account grows and books meetings at the same time.

5. Development
59 hook patterns, 20+ openings per idea. A full draft in the documented voice. Then 4 gates every post clears: a de-AI pass, a grader scoring 5 dimensions out of 50 (below 38 goes back), a check against that person's own feedback log, and a human sign-off. Gemini for visuals, Figma and Canva to finish.

6. Calendar
Scheduled and balanced by job, so no week leans too hard one way.

7. Learning loop
Every session logs itself. Every 5 sessions it flags what keeps getting rewritten and where a voice is drifting. Once a quarter we re-check the pillars and refresh the voice from new transcripts.

AI drafts. The human sharpens. The folder is what keeps the model from filling in who you are.

That is the part people skip, and it is the only part that stops 24 accounts from sounding like one

I mapped all 7 stages in-detail so you can start the implementation today itself

Comment SYSTEM and I'll send it over 👇
(You gotta follow me so the DM lands)

This post by Laura gave Dreamdata its best-ever day for website traffic, form submissions, and demo bookings.

The company turned that result into a team experiment. They targeted 300,000 impressions the following quarter and finished around 520,000.

Employee-led ads earned 3-4x the engagement rate of ads from the company page. And 83% of Dreamdata’s closed-won deals in the past year were influenced by LinkedIn.

I build content systems for a living. Dreamdata passed four checks I use before building a company-wide engine around one person’s post.

1. Did the post leave a trace beyond the feed?

Dreamdata was around 10 people when account executive Laura Erdem wrote about a sales win. The post took off, and the company recorded its highest website traffic, form submissions, and demo bookings that day.

The activity on LinkedIn had left a trace somewhere closer to the business.

A same-day spike cannot prove which actions the post caused. It gives the content team a reason to investigate before the moment disappears.

My first check is simple: did anything change outside the post’s own metrics?

2. Would the story lose authority if someone else told it?

Laura had lived the sale she wrote about. The detail belonged to her before it belonged to the content calendar.

In the usual employee advocacy workflow, marketing supplies the idea, language, and opinion. The employee is left supplying a face and an audience.

Dreamdata kept the knowledge attached to the person who had earned it.

Remove Laura’s lived experience and the post loses its authority.

3. Did the audience help select what deserved scale?

Dreamdata watched which employee videos people chose to spend time with. The strongest posts later received additional distribution as ads.

The company gathered evidence on the person, subject, and format before paying to expand the audience. Organic content became the selection layer.

4. Could the company add structure without taking authorship?

The first team sprint had a 300,000-impression target and dinner attached to it. That got people posting together. The freedom to use their own voices helped the habit survive the experiment.

So before I scale an employee post, I want four clear answers:

- Did it leave a trace beyond the feed?
- Would it lose authority in someone else’s voice?
- Did organic response validate it?
- Can the company support it without rewriting it?

Four yeses mean there may be a content system hiding inside the post.

Dreamdata’s four answers were yes. Laura’s sales story became the beginning of its company-wide system.

Tell me whose LinkedIn you want pulled apart next.

How I built an infinite content idea engine👇

You don't need to invent a new idea everyday.
Better a system that produces more raw material than you can possibly publish.

Mine has 2 inputs: an external system and an internal system.

The external system tracks what the market is already saying.

I keep a watchlist (creators & triggering keyword) across @LinkedIn, @X and @YouTube, but I don't stop there.

I look at @Reddit and @Quora for problems people describe without an audience to impress, blogs and newsletters my buyers read, and topic searches that surface people I don't already follow.

Otherwise your watchlist becomes an echo chamber.

The internal system captures what only I have:
client questions, sales objections, things from calls, interesting examples, mistakes, half-formed arguments, screenshots and voice notes.

I don't decide whether something is “content” when I capture it. I just save it. When I need to publish, I go back through the archive.

The 2 systems then compound.

- An external signal gives me a subject.
- My internal archive gives me a perspective.

A successful post about AI replacing marketers might meet a client conversation about bad positioning, a sales objection about AI-generated content and a result showing that more content didn't produce more leads.

One signal has now created several original directions.

I also look at successful posts in my niche specifically to find the question underneath them.

I don't copy the post but ask what I would add, challenge or explain differently.

Then one idea can become several pieces: the argument for it, the argument against it, the mistake it corrects, the example that proves it, or the experience that complicates it.

That's where “infinite” comes from.

I rate ideas green, yellow or red based on alignment and feasibility.

I also check whether the original idea actually demonstrated demand, whether I've already saturated the topic, whether the evidence is still current and whether I have something meaningful to add.

The objective is to keep supply of ideas large enough to not get stuck.

The loop is:

Market → capture → combine with experience → develop multiple angles → filter → publish → learn → feed the results back into the system.

Build that loop once and “what should I post today?” stops being a creative crisis. It becomes an inventory problem.

And inventory is much easier to solve.

text:
We have the most sophisticated tools for content creation. But why have our feeds gotten worse?

AI can structure the argument, clean up the writing, generate variations, sharpen a headline, personalise a message, repurpose an idea, and turn a rough draft into something publishable in minutes.

The mechanics of making content have never been cheaper.

And yet we all can feel the fatigue of reading AI slop.

I want to be precise about why, because “AI content is bad” is the lazy explanation.

AI is not necessarily writing badly, but part of the blame lies in the prompts.

Look at the prompts people use:
“Make this more engaging.”
“Make the hook stronger.”
“Make it sound thought-provoking.”
“Make it punchier.”
“Add a CTA.”

You have essentially asked it to produce the statistical middle of everything ever written. And nothing that differentiates you from others.

AI has made it incredibly cheap to polish emptiness.

The better sequence is:

Experience → Idea → Thinking → AI → Editing → Judgment → Publish.

AI belongs in the middle as a production step. It can never substitute for having something to say. And the time AI gives us back is supposed to go somewhere.

If drafting takes ten minutes instead of two hours, that should give you more time to question the argument, find the weak sentence, check the claim, add the example, remove the cliché and ask whether the whole thing deserves to exist.

Instead, we often spend the time saved on volume.

Which brings me to the skill I think is becoming much more valuable: Taste.

Someone has to recognise that the opening is technically strong but intellectually empty.

Someone has to say, “This sounds good, but what are we actually saying?”

When everyone has access to the same generative tools, differentiation moves away from production and towards selection.

There is a market reason for this too.

The cost of publishing has collapsed. The supply of human attention has not.

Everyone can produce content now. The competition is whether what you produced deserves twenty seconds from someone who has hundreds of other things competing for the same twenty seconds.

So I don't think AI has lowered the bar for good content.

It has lowered the cost of reaching the bar.

Which means we have fewer excuses for not trying.

I spent a morning with the six citation studies published this year, LinkedIn’s own two guides, a survey of 45 more, and a crawl test on 4 live post pages.

A citation is the moment an AI answer links your post as its source.
It is not a mention of your name and it is not a view.
It is the engine deciding your sentence was the cleanest one available on that question.

Here are 8 edits that will make your LinkedIn post get cited by AI 👇

1/ Set the post to Anyone.

A Connections-only post is invisible to every engine. A public one is served in full, and its first 195 characters become the page title.

2/ Put the point in line one/hook, in the words a buyer would type.

My calendar post last week opened “Founders send me their content strategy fairly often.” The line an engine could quote was in paragraph four: “A calendar answers one question, which is when.” Next time it goes first, and the scene goes second.

3/ Name the tool, the number and the date.

In a causal model on 12,000 LinkedIn posts:
technical detail lifted citations 77%
named companies and tools 33%
a specific topic 18 percent

→ A vague post has no sentence worth lifting.

4/ Write the list as a list.

Every cited post LinkedIn checked carried a bulleted or numbered list

5/ Type in plain letters.

Pasted bold symbols cut citations 58 percent in the same model.
The symbols are not the word.

6/ Write it yourself.

95 percent of cited posts are original

7/ Keep posting.

3 in 4 cited authors publish 5 or more times/ 4 weeks, and about half of cited content is under 3 months old.
Nobody has shown the cadence causes the citation. The people being cited have it.

8/ Put the claim in the text.

A fact placed only inside an image was extracted by no engine, 3 correct answers in 120 runs.
An image post gets alt text. A carousel has no alt field, so its caption has to carry every number on the slides.

You could see by this point, what held up is mostly editing, and the human reader loses almost nothing.

At Frontal, the one thing we don't let AI run on its own is content. And it's our single biggest source of pipeline: 50+ inbound meetings a month.

But now content has become a commodity.

Type a prompt, get something clean, and it reads like the 100 other LinkedIn creators who prompted the same thing that same hour.

Running content for one profile, you can wing it. Running it for dozens without them all blurring into the same voice takes a system.

This is the exact content system we run, top to bottom 👇

1/ Profile
Before a single post goes out, we rebuild the profile to convert a visitor into a lead. Banner, headline, About, and a Featured section that leads with proof (a lead magnet works very well here), then one clear CTA.

2/ Strategy
5 sources feed every idea:
→ Real call transcripts, the highest-signal source we have
→ Competitor and viral posts pulled through Apify
→ Live research across Reddit, YouTube, X
→ Performance data from what already worked
→ A swipe file of the account's own best posts

3/ The engine
Everything runs in one terminal on Claude Code. The brain is a Client OS: one folder per person, 3 foundation docs.
→ Voice profile: a real conversation that captures how you actually talk, before AI writes a word
→ ICP: 3 buyer tiers and the words each one uses
→ Pillars: 5-6 themes every post traces back to

4/ Content mix
Every week balances 3 jobs: reach at the top, authority in the middle, pipeline at the bottom.
We hold it near 40/20/40, so the account grows and books meetings at the same time.

5/ Development
59 hook templates, 20+ openings per idea. A full draft in the documented voice.
Then 4 gates every post clears: a de-AI pass, a quality score out of 50 (under 38 goes back), a check against the account's own feedback log, and a final sign-off. Visuals built in AI, finished by human judgment.

6/ Calendar
Posts scheduled and balanced by job, so no week leans too hard one way.

7/ Learning loop
Every session logs itself. Every 5 sessions the system flags what keeps getting rewritten and where a voice is drifting. Once a quarter we re-check the pillars against the market and refresh the voice from fresh transcripts.

That's how content made it to our #1 acquisition channel, our employees's brand (170K+ combined followers) out-pulling the company page many times over.

The biggest lie in B2B:
You're marketing towards another corporate entity.
You’re not. 

You’re marketing to a human who scrolls in the bathroom and makes emotional decisions.

In 7 years, we went from 2 guys in a Rotterdam office to the #1 B2B agency in Europe. Today we're 70 people across 20+ nationalities, working with 100+ B2B clients from San Francisco to Sweden, on track to $9M ARR this year.

And not one of those clients came from outbound.

We've never run an SDR team, sent a cold email, or chased anyone down.

Every single one came to us.

We pulled that off by doing almost everything the marketing industry warns you against.

We posted videos that were way too long for LinkedIn, cursed in our content, and made people laugh while everyone else was busy being a thought leader.

And we did it five times a week, every week, for years, until my own friends started complaining they saw my face too often.

It worked.

Last year my personal LinkedIn did 9 million impressions against 90,000 visitors to our website, which means people see us about 100 times more often off our site than on it.

These days we get more inbound than we can handle.

So after seven years and more than a hundred companies, here's what I actually believe about B2B marketing:

- Niche-famous beats famous. You're selling to maybe a few hundred companies that will ever need what you do, so the whole game is being the name they already trust the moment they're ready to move.

- Lead gen is the tax you pay for not having a brand. No ad campaign or cold sequence will ever out-produce a name people already know, and most companies have the order backwards: they treat brand as the reward for success when it's the thing that creates it.

- Almost everyone overspends capturing the sliver of the market that's shopping today, while starving the demand generation that fills next year's pipeline. Then they wonder why growth quietly stalled.

- And the person blocking most of this is usually the founder. I'd know, because for a long time I was that bottleneck myself.

Underneath all of it sits one idea: in B2B you're only as real as you are visible.

A buyer can't choose a company they've forgotten exists, which makes being seen the whole game rather than the vanity metric most people dismiss it as.

I'm going to put all of it here.

The playbooks we actually run, the contrarian takes that get me in trouble, and the numbers behind what works and what just burns money.

An AI answer can feel cheap even when it is completely right. There is a name for the effect, and once you see it you cannot unsee it in your own product.

Two Harvard researchers, Ryan Buell and Michael Norton, called it the labor illusion. In their 2011 studies, people shown a travel site that displayed its work, searching one airline, now the next, often valued the result more than an identical result that appeared instantly.

Some even preferred the site that made them wait, because the visible effort made the outcome feel earned. Seeing the labor triggered a sense of reciprocity, and that changed what the answer was worth to them.

> Why this hits AI products hardest

Most categories carry friction that signals effort.

AI stripped it out on purpose. The answer arrives in a second, polished and confident, with none of the work on display. So the buyer's gut prices it like it took a second and marks it down, no matter how strong the analysis underneath was.

The faster and better the model, the worse this gets, because speed reads as cheapness.

> Show the work that already happened

You do not need to fake a delay to earn trust. In a good AI product the effort is real, it is just buried under a clean answer. Bring it to the surface:

- Name the sources it read, and how many.
- Surface the signals it weighed, and the ones it ruled out.
- Show the path from raw input to conclusion, so the reasoning is legible.
- Let people click into the evidence instead of trusting a black box.

When the effort is genuine, revealing it is not a trick. It is the difference between handing someone a verdict and handing them a receipt.

> The takeaway if you build with AI

People do not value the output. They value the work they believe produced it. If your product does something genuinely hard and hides it behind a tidy answer, you are training buyers to underprice you.

What the pattern showed

What the client did with it

They built a comparison page that answered those two objections by name, in the customer's own language. Then they aimed a small paid campaign at people searching the competitor's brand. No cold outreach, no manufactured urgency.

What came back

I stopped giving away free pilots, and engagement went up roughly 10x.

For months I'd let prospects try before they bought. No cost, no commitment. Engagement was blah. The logins were mediocre, the feedback was slow, and champions went quiet after week two. Every one of those pilots also took manual work on my side to spin up, so all the effort was coming from me.

Then I switched to paid pilots. Same product, same onboarding. The only change was that money moved upfront.

Engagement jumped, and it weeded out the folks who were never serious to begin with.

Part of that is the sunk cost effect... paying makes skipping feel like wasting the money. Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer found it in a paper published in 1985. They had Ohio University's theater randomly give some season-ticket buyers a discount and charge the rest full price, and over the first half of the season, the full-price buyers went to more plays.

By the second half, the gap was gone.

So the fee seems to buy attention early on, and after that it's up to the product to hold it.

A Carnegie Mellon-led study presented this year flagged about 6 million suspected fake stars on GitHub.

Stars are the number people tend to check first on a dev-tools rival, and they're cheap to fake.

The better counters sit in the package registries. npm shows weekly downloads on every package page. PyPI's download data is public through the PyPI Stats site and a public BigQuery dataset. Docker Hub shows pulls on public images. GitHub adds a "Used by" count to packages with more than 100 dependent repos.

A few ways to read them.

Watch the slope. Build servers, mirrors and bots all add noise, and npm has said to treat its numbers as directional. The shape of a rival's line over six months is the part to read.

Calibrate against yourself. You know your own real usage, so your download line gives you a rough ruler for theirs.

Count the dependents. A project that depends on their library had to write code to get there.

Read the spikes. A jump right after a launch or a conference talk can show you which of their moves landed with developers.

Some of the most revealing things a competitor publishes are PDFs hardly anyone links to.

Some partner programs spell out the discount at each tier, in writing.

PDFs usually get written for someone who needs the details: a partner, a procurement team, the engineer doing the install. So they say more.

A few to hunt for:

> Partner program guides. Tiers, requirements, what a reseller has to sell to move up a level. That's their channel strategy on paper.

> Datasheets. Specs, limits, supported integrations... and the limits are the part their sales team hopes you skim.

> Security whitepapers. Where the data lives, which certifications they hold, which regulated buyers they're getting ready for.

> Implementation guides. The setup steps show how the product is put together, and where it gets clunky.

> Google's site: and filetype:pdf operators turn up plenty of them on their domain. Others never get indexed at all, because nothing public links to them anymore.

We pull non-indexed PDFs into https://t.co/UE0nqa71cL with everything else.

Whoever wrote the install guide wasn't thinking about who else might open it.

Your competitor asks job candidates about the work it needs done next, and some of those candidates tell Glassdoor.

Interview reviews there cover the role, how hard the interview was, whether an offer came, and the questions themselves, and you can sort them by date.

The questions describe the job to be done.

Picture a sales candidate getting asked how they'd break into hospital systems. That's a healthcare push, and probably an early one. An engineer quizzed on data residency says something about the customers they're chasing.

Watch the volume as well.

A run of interview reviews for a function the company barely had last year means a team is being built.

Go easy on any single review. People with strong feelings, good or bad, post more often than people who feel fine about the place, so look for the same theme coming from several people.

Then read the employee reviews from the same quarter. Mentions of new leadership, a reorg or a quota change, clustered in a few weeks, usually mean something moved inside.

Engineers love explaining how they built things, including the parts their marketing team wouldn't put on the website.

KubeCon's November schedule, hundreds of sessions with speakers and abstracts, went up in early August.

A competitor's talk can tell you:

→ what they migrated to, and why
→ the scale they're running at, sometimes with real numbers
→ what broke along the way
→ which teams exist now, going by the speakers and the work they describe

Where they speak counts as well. A dev tools company on the agenda at a healthcare conference is courting a new buyer.

Read the abstracts closely.

A lot of them were written to get past a program committee, so they tend to lead with the most impressive detail the company's allowed to share. Recordings usually follow the event, so you get the story a second time, slides included.

Conference talks sit in https://t.co/UE0nqa71cL's  sources right next to the job posts... a speaker lineup is an org chart they published themselves.

Many private fundraises leave a public filing with the SEC, and anyone can read it for free.

It's called Form D. Under the SEC's Regulation D rules, a company has 15 days after its first sale of securities to file one, and it goes on EDGAR, the SEC's public filing database.

What's on it:

> Date of first sale. The day the first investor signed on. (A box can also say the first sale hasn't happened yet.)

> Total offering, amount sold and amount remaining. How big the round is, and how much of it was sold at the time of filing.

> Number of investors so far.

> Industry group and a revenue range, from "No Revenues" up to "Over $100,000,000." A company can also pick "Decline to Disclose," and hedge funds and other investment funds report a net asset value range in place of revenue.

> Executive officers, directors and promoters, by name.

To find one, search the company on EDGAR and look for filings labeled D. The Type of Filing box marks each one as a new notice or an amendment.

Read the date printed on the form.

A Form D can be filed before the first sale, and companies file amendments as a round continues, so one raise can show up more than once. Open the earlier filing next to the latest one and compare the amount sold, the investor count and the names.

Three limits.

The form has no line for valuation and none for the names of the investors. The revenue range is the company's own answer. Raises under other exemptions need not file one at all.

Together it makes a dated record of a private rival's fundraise, filed by the rival itself.

On June 16, 2025, Cursor's $20 Pro plan went from a 500-request monthly limit to what the company's blog post called "unlimited-with-rate-limits."

The post was edited on June 30 "to improve its clarity," and by July 4 Cursor was apologizing. Its follow-up said the pricing changes were "not communicated clearly." Pro, it explained, includes $20 of model usage at API pricing, and "unlimited" covered Tab and Auto only. Anyone charged unexpectedly between June 16 and July 4 was offered a full refund.

The Wayback Machine kept both versions of the page, which is how the wording change is still visible.

A pricing page has three lines worth a screenshot, and this story touches each one:

> The unit. Requests before, dollars of usage after.

> What "unlimited" covers. Tab and Auto.

> What happens at the limit. You buy more usage at cost.

Screenshot the plan and its FAQ, then put the old and new wording side by side on the first of each month.
