Customers will lie to you, politely and to your face. People want to be encouraging. They nod, say "interesting," and tell you they'd probably use it, and none of it costs them anything. That's how founders end up in a design partner death spiral.

So early on, I watch what people do. I run four channels, and each one gives me a different kind of signal. Each one lies to you in its own way too, so the downside goes next to the upside.

1. Cold email

The hardest channel to crack, and the strongest signal I get. It's cheap and fast, you can aim it at named accounts, and people reply with why a message landed or didn't. The price is setup: sending domains, warmup and email authentication (DKIM and DMARC), all dialed in for a shot at the inbox.

2. Cold LinkedIn

Response rates run higher than email, and you can pick the exact person. I run into a ceiling of about 30 outreaches a day.

3. Meta ads

Easy to spin up, and a real test costs $50 to $100 a day. Auto-targeting chooses the audience for you, so watch who the algorithm decides your buyer is. B2B buyers on the platform are fewer, and there are more of them than you'd expect.

4. Google ads

Searchers are typing the problem in right now, and their words are the words buyers use for their own pain, so there's no guessing at your framing. It costs more, it validates demand that already exists, and it can't see demand you'd have to create.

I run all four as experiments. The goal is a clear picture of who leans in, and why.

That VP of Sales isn't going to fix your sales problem.

You can't hire your way to product-market fit (PMF). A great sales hire is a multiplier. Your own selling is what they multiply, and it's also how you'll judge whether they're doing the job well.

The same goes for the growth marketer, the agency and the fractional CRO (a part-time chief revenue officer). Hiring ahead of PMF adds burn and gives you someone to blame.

Founders sell first. Hiring comes after you know what works.

Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, Sony and Thomson Reuters are all on the public roster of W3C's Web Applications Working Group.

W3C is a body that develops web standards. Each of its working groups has a participants page, which shows every person's name with their company underneath and a link to sort the list by company (this one is as of Oct 19).

The roster is a public record of which companies have a person in that group. Three things to do with one:

> Find the group closest to your rival's product on W3C's list of groups.

> Look for your rival's name, and note who appears and the date you looked.

> Search the rival's job posts for the name of a standard that group works on.

Large companies belong to many groups, so a single name says little. Come back next quarter, compare the two lists and look at what changed. The names added since your last look... those are the news.

A Product Marketing Manager , described a competitor feature that was retired with no announcement:

"The only trace was a small edit buried in their developer docs. https://t.co/UE0nqa71cL flagged it."

Developer docs are one place a retirement shows up... the API itself is another.

Every answer an API sends back carries a few lines of extra information called headers. Two of them exist for retirements, and both are defined in public standards :

> Deprecation. The point in time an endpoint was, or will be, flagged as on its way out. It's written as a timestamp.

> Sunset. The point in time it's expected to stop responding.

A third line, a Link header marked rel="deprecation", can point to documentation about the change.

To look, take an endpoint from a rival's public API reference and run curl -i on it in a terminal (curl is a free command-line tool, and -i shows the headers along with the response). Endpoints that need a key will turn you away, and not every API sets these headers.

The docs stay the main source.

Apple lets an app change its privacy label any time, with no app update needed.

The label lists the kinds of data an app collects, such as Location, Contacts, Health & Fitness, Financial Info or Browsing History. It has to cover the code from other companies inside the app too, like analytics and ad tools.

Open a rival's App Store page, scroll to App Privacy and screenshot it.

Look again next month, and the month after. A new data type on the list may mean the app started collecting it, or that the company corrected an earlier answer. The release notes around then may say which.

Labels are self-reported and can trail the product. The Apple App Store and Google Play are two of the sources we read at ForesightIQ.

A public company's annual report shows what the company has decided to stop counting.

Meta is the clearest case.

For years it told investors how many people used Facebook each day and each month. Its 2023 annual report said that from the first quarter of 2024 it would stop reporting those Facebook counts and report one daily count across all its apps. Meta's stated reason was that many people use more than one of its apps.

The last Facebook figures, from December 2023, were 2.11 billion daily users and 3.07 billion monthly users. The new all-apps count for the same month was 3.19 billion. In its SEC filings, Facebook's own trend line stops there.

Twitter made a similar move.

In February 2019 it told investors that after the first quarter it would stop reporting monthly active users and report a daily count of logged-in users on its website or on apps that can show ads. The last monthly figure, in April 2019, was 330 million, down 2% from a year earlier. The daily count for the same quarter was 134 million, up 11%.

Public companies file an annual report (the 10-K) with the SEC, and EDGAR has every one for free. To check a rival's:

1. Open its last two annual reports and find the page of key metrics.
2. Write down every number that's missing from the newer one.
3. Read the definition of anything new. Twitter's counted logged-in users on a website or app that can show ads.
4. Check the footnotes, because a changed definition can hide in one.

A missing number is a question for the next earnings call.

Stripe publishes a file on its main site that's written for AI assistants to read. It starts with "# Stripe", then a one-paragraph summary of the company, then a "## Payments" section of links.

The format is llms.txt. Jeremy Howard proposed it in September 2024. It usually sits at /llms.txt on a company's domain, and some companies put one in a subfolder too, like /docs/llms.txt. Anthropic's developer docs publish one.

To read a rival's, type their homepage address into your browser, add /llms.txt to the end, and press Enter.

The format is short:

> A title, the only required part.

> A summary in a quote block.

> Sections of links, each with an optional note.

> An "Optional" section, for pages an AI can skip.

On a rival's file, the summary paragraph is how they'd like an AI to describe them. The sections show which products they chose to list, and in what order. The Optional section holds the pages they're comfortable having skipped.

Keep a dated copy and open the file again in a month or two. A new section, or a summary rewritten around a different buyer, is worth a closer look.

Plenty of companies don't publish one yet... and nothing obliges an AI tool to read it.

Every UK company files its paperwork on one public register, including the UK arms of American companies. Searching it is free and needs no login.

The register is Companies House. Search the company name on its free "Find and update company information" service and open the company's page. It covers:

> Filing history. Every document since the company was formed, dated. Most come as a free PDF (some older ones cost £3 to request).

> Officers. Current directors and the ones who've resigned, with dates.

> People, then Persons with significant control. Usually anyone holding more than 25% of the shares or votes. Home addresses and exact birth dates stay off the public page.

> Charges. A lender's registered claim on company assets, usually tied to a loan.

> Previous company names, which give you the rebrand history.

> An Insolvency tab, which shows up only for companies with an insolvency case on record.

How I'd work through a UK rival or acquisition target:

Start with the latest accounts. Private companies get nine months after their year end to file, so the numbers are always a little old. Smaller companies can file shortened accounts (micro-entities even shorter), so a small rival's filing may skip the full income statement.

Then read the officer list in date order. A new finance director, or three resignations in one quarter, is worth checking against their news.

Check the charges next. A new one means a lender has registered a claim on something the company owns, which usually goes with new borrowing.

Look at people with significant control too. A change there is a reason to find out who now holds the shares or votes.

Last, create a free https://t.co/AVmhePZiav One Login and click "Follow this company." Companies House will email you about each new filing it accepts.

Companies House doesn't check the accuracy of what companies file... every document is the company's own account of itself.

US employers put a job title, a work city and a salary on one line for each H-1B application they file... and the Department of Labor publishes it.

The form is a Labor Condition Application, which an employer files before sponsoring a worker on an H-1B visa, for new hires and extensions alike. The data comes out quarterly as Excel files, grouped by federal fiscal year (October 1 to September 30), on the Labor Department's foreign labor "Performance Data" page.

The columns to keep:

> EMPLOYER_NAME and JOB_TITLE.

> WORKSITE_CITY and WORKSITE_STATE, for the first worksite.

> WAGE_RATE_OF_PAY_FROM and WAGE_UNIT_OF_PAY (hourly, weekly, bi-weekly, monthly or yearly, so compare like with like).

> CASE_STATUS, DECISION_DATE and TOTAL_WORKER_POSITIONS.

Filter EMPLOYER_NAME to the rival, trying a few versions of their legal name (Inc., LLC, subsidiaries). Keep the rows marked Certified, with VISA_CLASS set to H-1B. Then sort by DECISION_DATE and look for job titles and cities that are new for them.

A certified application is permission paperwork, and plenty never become a hire. Only roles that need visa sponsorship show up, and the main file lists the first worksite only. Read it for the direction their hiring is heading.

Grammarly's Chrome extension listing showed 41,000,000 users on October 28, with version 14.1342.0 and an "Updated October 26, 2026" date.

Every Chrome Web Store listing shows those same details, plus size.

To track a rival's extension:

1. Search their name in the Chrome Web Store.
2. Copy the users, the version and the updated date into a sheet, next to today's date.
3. Do it again at the start of each month.

A few months of rows show how fast it's growing and how often they ship.

Google doesn't publish how the user count is calculated, the number is reported to be rounded, and some extensions have been caught inflating theirs. Treat it as a trend line.

A rival's homepage source can list every language and country version of that page.

To see it in Chrome or Edge, right-click the page, choose View page source, and search for hreflang (Ctrl+F, or Cmd+F on a Mac). Each match pairs a URL with a code:

> "de" is German.

> "en-GB" is English for the UK.

> "x-default" is the fallback page.

Some sites keep these tags in their sitemap. Add /sitemap.xml to the homepage address, or find the Sitemap: line in /robots.txt, and search it too. Some sitemaps are just an index of other sitemaps, so open the ones it lists.

Save the list. A code that wasn't there last time, like "ja" (Japanese) or "pt-BR" (Portuguese for Brazil), means they've built a page for that market. Then check whether their language menu links to it yet.

Insurers file new products and rates with state regulators, and many states put those filings online for free.

The system is SERFF, run by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC). Its public side is SERFF Filing Access: pick a state, choose a business type, then search by company name, product name, submission dates and type of insurance.

Start with a state where your rival sells and check that it's on SERFF Filing Access (Florida, for one, runs its own system). Search the company name and read their newest filings first.

What the filings can show:

> A new product name, filed with its policy forms.

> Rate filings, meaning the prices they've filed with the state.

> Which states they've filed in lately (each state has its own search, so run it in each one).

Each state decides what goes public. Texas shows only filings the company or the regulator marked for public access, and New Jersey keeps health insurance rate filings out of public view. A missing filing tells you very little.

Put the latest filing date for each rival in a sheet and check back each quarter.

Each edit to a company's Wikipedia page is logged with a date and the editor's name. And editors paid by the company have to say so.

That rule has been in Wikimedia's terms of use since June 16, 2014.

Paid editors disclose it on their user page, on the article's talk page, or in the edit summary. Wikipedia's conflict-of-interest guideline also strongly discourages people with a stake from editing the article directly, and asks them to post an edit request on the talk page.

The routine on a rival's page:

1. Open View history (a tab at the top of the page on desktop). Every change is listed by date, with the editor and a short summary. Select two versions and click "Compare selected revisions" to see exactly what changed.

2. Read the edit summaries for disclosures, and click through to the user pages of the most frequent editors. A stated employer or client tells you whose edits they are.

3. Open the talk page and its archives, and search for "conflict of interest." Each flagged edit request comes from someone with an actual or apparent conflict of interest, and it shows the change they asked for, accepted or not.

4. Line up the dates. An opening sentence rewritten the week of a launch or a funding round is worth noting.

Things worth watching for:

> Products removed or renamed.

> A new acquisition added to the history section.

> The first sentence, where the page says what the company does.

Anyone can edit, and administrators can hide some edits from public view, so a change may come from a fan or a critic as easily as from the company. An edit belongs to the company only where a disclosure says so.
